exceptions_and_qualifications: Mere concealment alone is not enough — it must be coupled with 'reason to believe' a cognizable offence is being planned; innocent reasons for concealment (e.g., avoiding harassment, personal safety) don't satisfy the threshold.
breakdown.how_to_read: Short and self-contained — the whole test is in the single sentence. Compare its narrower scope against Section 129's much longer list of specific habitual-offender categories.

sections.title: Security for good behaviour from habitual offenders

breakdown.plain_summary: The longest and broadest of the good-behaviour categories, aimed squarely at habitual criminals. It lists seven overlapping categories: habitual robbers/house-breakers/thieves/forgers; habitual knowing receivers of stolen property; habitual protectors/harbourers of thieves or handlers of stolen property; habitual kidnapping/abduction/extortion/cheating/mischief offenders (or offences under the BNS's public-tranquillity-adjacent Chapter X or specific public-servant-related sections); habitual breach-of-the-peace offenders; habitual offenders under a named list of regulatory statutes (Drugs and Cosmetics, Foreigners Act, EPF Act, Essential Commodities, Protection of Civil Rights, Customs, Food Safety) or any other hoarding/profiteering/adulteration/corruption law; and finally a catch-all — anyone "so desperate and dangerous" that being at large without security would be hazardous to the community. Uniquely among this quartet of good-behaviour sections, this one carries the longer three-year maximum bond period (matching Section 125's post-conviction ceiling), reflecting the seriousness of chronic, repeat offending it targets.
essential_elements: Seven distinct qualifying categories (a)-(g), any one of which suffices.
'Habitually' is the recurring qualifier for most categories — a single incident generally won't do; a pattern is required.
Category (f) incorporates a specific list of regulatory/economic-offence statutes plus a residual clause for hoarding/profiteering/adulteration/corruption laws generally.
Category (g) is a broad residual 'desperate and dangerous' catch-all independent of any specific offence pattern.
Maximum bond period: three years — the longest among the preventive (non-conviction) good-behaviour sections.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The 'habit' element under sections 128, 129 categories (a)-(f) can be proved by evidence of general repute, not just specific proven instances — see Section 135(4) later in this Chapter, which supplies the evidentiary rule.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat categories (a)-(f) as fact-specific pigeonholes to check the person against, and category (g) as the fallback if none of the specific categories quite fit but the person is still clearly dangerous. Remember the cross-reference to Section 135(4) for how 'habit' gets proved at the inquiry stage.

sections.title: Order to be made
sections.raw_text: 130. Order to be made.—When a Magistrate acting under section 126, section 127, section 128 or section 129, deems it necessary to require any person to show cause under such section, he shall make an order in writing, setting forth the substance of the information received, the amount of the bond to be executed, the term for which it is to be in force and the number of sureties, after considering the sufficiency and fitness of sureties.

breakdown.plain_summary: The formal gateway order that kicks off the show-cause procedure under any of Sections 126-129. It must be in writing and specify four things: the substance of the information received, the bond amount, how long the bond will run, and the number of sureties required — the Magistrate must have already turned their mind to the sufficiency and fitness of sureties before issuing it.
essential_elements: Applies uniformly across all four preventive-security grounds: Sections 126, 127, 128, and 129.
Mandatory written order — not oral.
Must state: substance of information, bond amount, bond duration, and number of sureties.
The Magistrate must have already considered surety sufficiency and fitness before making the order.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the procedural hinge connecting the four substantive grounds (Sections 126-129) to the common inquiry machinery that follows (Sections 131 onward) — every peace/good-behaviour case, regardless of which ground triggered it, starts here.

sections.title: Procedure in respect of person present in Court
sections.raw_text: 131. Procedure in respect of person present in Court.—If the person in respect of whom such order is made is present in Court, it shall be read over to him, or, if he so desires, the substance thereof shall be explained to him.

breakdown.plain_summary: A simple fair-notice rule: if the person against whom a Section 130 order is made happens to already be present in Court, the order must be read out to them (or, if they'd prefer, its substance explained), so they understand exactly what they're being asked to show cause about.
essential_elements: Applies only where the person is already present in Court when the order is made.
Two options: the order is read out verbatim, or its substance is explained if the person prefers.
breakdown.how_to_read: Short procedural section — its counterpart for a person not present in Court is Section 132, immediately following.

sections.title: Summons or warrant in case of person not so present
sections.raw_text:
132. Summons or warrant in case of person not so present.—If such person is not present in Court, the Magistrate shall issue a summons requiring him to appear, or, when such person is in custody, a warrant directing the officer in whose custody he is to bring him before the Court:
    Provided that whenever it appears to such Magistrate, upon the report of a police officer or upon other information (the substance of which report or information shall be recorded by the Magistrate), that there is reason to fear the commission of a breach of the peace, and that such breach of the peace cannot be prevented otherwise than by the immediate arrest of such person, the Magistrate may at any time issue a warrant for his arrest.

breakdown.plain_summary: The mirror image of Section 131 for a person who isn't already in Court: the Magistrate issues a summons to bring them in, or, if they're already in custody for some other reason, a warrant directing the custodial officer to produce them. There's an emergency override: if the Magistrate has reason to fear an imminent breach of the peace that can only be averted by immediate arrest, they can skip straight to an arrest warrant at any time — bypassing the ordinary summons-first approach.
essential_elements: Default route: summons to appear (person not in custody) or warrant to the custodial officer (person already in custody).
Emergency override: immediate arrest warrant where breach of the peace is feared and cannot otherwise be prevented.
The report or information grounding the emergency override must be recorded in substance by the Magistrate.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The emergency-arrest proviso is available 'at any time' — it isn't limited to the initial stage, and can override the ordinary summons-first sequence whenever the urgency threshold is met.
breakdown.how_to_read: Pair with Section 133 immediately following — every summons or warrant issued under this section must carry a copy of the Section 130 order.

sections.title: Copy of order to accompany summons or warrant
sections.raw_text: 133. Copy of order to accompany summons or warrant.—Every summons or warrant issued under section 132 shall be accompanied by a copy of the order made under section 130, and such copy shall be delivered by the officer serving or executing such summons or warrant to the person served with, or arrested under, the same.

breakdown.plain_summary: A fair-notice safeguard mirroring Section 131 for people who weren't already in Court: whenever a Section 132 summons or warrant is issued, a copy of the underlying Section 130 order must travel with it and actually be delivered to the person when served or arrested — so an arrested or summoned person always knows the specific grounds (information, bond terms, sureties required) behind the process against them.
essential_elements: Applies to every summons or warrant issued under Section 132.
The copy of the Section 130 order must be physically delivered to the person served or arrested.
breakdown.how_to_read: Closes the loop opened by Sections 131-132 — between the two, every person subject to a Section 130 order gets to know its contents, whether present in Court or brought in later.

sections.title: Power to dispense with personal attendance
sections.raw_text: 134. Power to dispense with personal attendance.—The Magistrate may, if he sees sufficient cause, dispense with the personal attendance of any person called upon to show cause why he should not be ordered to execute a bond for keeping the peace or for good behaviour and may permit him to appear by an advocate.

breakdown.plain_summary: A convenience/dignity provision: the person called upon to show cause doesn't necessarily have to attend in person throughout — if the Magistrate sees sufficient cause, they can dispense with personal attendance and let the person be represented by an advocate instead.
essential_elements: Discretionary power — the Magistrate must see 'sufficient cause' before dispensing with personal attendance.
The alternative is representation by an advocate.
breakdown.how_to_read: A practical relief provision — useful to invoke for a client who faces genuine hardship attending every hearing of a good-behaviour/peace-security inquiry.

sections.title: Inquiry as to truth of information
sections.raw_text:
135. Inquiry as to truth of information.—(1) When an order under section 130 has been read or explained under section 131 to a person present in Court, or when any person appears or is brought before a Magistrate in compliance with, or in execution of, a summons or warrant, issued under section 132, the Magistrate shall proceed to inquire into the truth of the information upon which action has been taken, and to take such further evidence as may appear necessary.
    (2) Such inquiry shall be made, as nearly as may be practicable, in the manner hereinafter prescribed for conducting trial and recording evidence in summons-cases.
    (3) After the commencement, and before the completion, of the inquiry under sub-section (1), the Magistrate, if he considers that immediate measures are necessary for the prevention of a breach of the peace or disturbance of the public tranquillity or the commission of any offence or for the public safety, may, for reasons to be recorded in writing, direct the person in respect of whom the order under section 130 has been made to execute a bond or bail bond, for keeping the peace or maintaining good behaviour until the conclusion of the inquiry, and may detain him in custody until such bond or bail bond is executed or, in default of execution, until the inquiry is concluded:
    Provided that—
        (a) no person against whom proceedings are not being taken under section 127, section 128, or section 129 shall be directed to execute a bond or bail bond for maintaining good behaviour;
        (b) the conditions of such bond, whether as to the amount thereof or as to the provision of sureties or the number thereof or the pecuniary extent of their liability, shall not be more onerous than those specified in the order under section 130.
    (4) For the purposes of this section the fact that a person is a habitual offender or is so desperate and dangerous as to render his being at large without security hazardous to the community may be proved by evidence of general repute or otherwise.
    (5) Where two or more persons have been associated together in the matter under inquiry, they may be dealt with in the same or separate inquiries as the Magistrate shall think just.
    (6) The inquiry under this section shall be completed within a period of six months from the date of its commencement, and if such inquiry is not so completed, the proceedings under this Chapter shall, on the expiry of the said period, stand terminated unless, for special reasons to be recorded in writing, the Magistrate otherwise directs:
    Provided that where any person has been kept in detention pending such inquiry, the proceeding against that person, unless terminated earlier, shall stand terminated on the expiry of a period of six months of such detention.
    (7) Where any direction is made under sub-section (6) permitting the continuance of proceedings, the Sessions Judge may, on an application made to him by the aggrieved party, vacate such direction if he is satisfied that it was not based on any special reason or was perverse.

breakdown.plain_summary: The heart of the Chapter IX procedure — the actual inquiry into whether the Section 130 order's underlying information is true. It runs roughly like a summons-case trial (evidence recording, etc.). Mid-inquiry, if the Magistrate thinks immediate action is needed to prevent a breach of the peace, disturbance, an offence, or for public safety, they can order an interim bond (and detain the person if they don't comply) pending the inquiry's conclusion — but only for people actually facing good-behaviour proceedings under Sections 127-129 (not the plain peace-keeping track), and the interim bond terms can't be harsher than what the original Section 130 order specified. For habitual-offender or "desperate and dangerous" findings, general repute evidence is expressly allowed, not just specific proven acts. Multiple associated persons can be inquired into jointly or separately, at the Magistrate's discretion. There's a hard six-month completion deadline — miss it, and proceedings automatically terminate (with an even harder rule if the person has been detained: termination at six months of detention regardless), unless the Magistrate records special reasons to continue, and even that continuation is subject to Sessions Judge review on an aggrieved party's application if the special reasons look pretextual or perverse.
essential_elements: Inquiry follows the summons-case trial procedure, as nearly as practicable.
Interim bond power during the inquiry: available only for good-behaviour proceedings (Sections 127-129), on recorded reasons, capped at the original order's terms.
General-repute evidence is expressly permissible to prove habitual-offender or desperate-and-dangerous status.
Six-month hard deadline for completing the inquiry, with automatic termination on expiry absent recorded special reasons.
A stricter six-month cap applies specifically where the person has been detained pending inquiry.
Sessions Judge oversight: can vacate a continuation direction found not to rest on genuine special reasons, or found perverse.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The interim-bond power under sub-section (3) is expressly unavailable for pure peace-keeping proceedings (Section 126) — only good-behaviour tracks (127-129) permit it.
The six-month detention cap is an independent, stricter ceiling that overrides the general six-month inquiry deadline where actual detention has occurred.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the longest and most procedurally dense section in the Chapter — read the six-month deadline and its detention-specific proviso as the key liberty safeguard, and the Sessions Judge review in sub-section (7) as the check against Magistrates rubber-stamping indefinite extensions.

sections.title: Order to give security

breakdown.plain_summary: The final, operative order following a completed Section 135 inquiry — if the inquiry proves the security is actually necessary, the Magistrate must order it. Three built-in limits protect the person: the final bond can't exceed the nature, amount, or duration set out in the original Section 130 order (no escalation after the fact); the amount must be reasonable and not excessive given the case's circumstances; and — a specific child-protection rule — if the person is a child, they personally cannot be made to execute the bond at all; only sureties on the child's behalf can.
essential_elements: Triggered only if the inquiry proves necessity for keeping the peace or maintaining good behaviour.
Cap: the final security cannot exceed the nature, amount, or period specified in the Section 130 order.
The bond amount must be fixed with due regard to the case's circumstances and must not be excessive.
Child-specific rule: a bond in respect of a child must be executed only by sureties, never by the child personally.
breakdown.how_to_read: The child proviso (c) is the standout safeguard here — always check the age of the person concerned before an order under this section is finalised.

sections.title: Discharge of person informed against
sections.raw_text: 137. Discharge of person informed against.—If, on an inquiry under section 135, it is not proved that it is necessary for keeping the peace or maintaining good behaviour, as the case may be, that the person in respect of whom the inquiry is made, should execute a bond, the Magistrate shall make an entry on the record to that effect, and if such person is in custody only for the purposes of the inquiry, shall release him, or, if such person is not in custody, shall discharge him.

breakdown.plain_summary: The flip side of Section 136 — if the inquiry fails to prove that security is necessary, the person must be let go. The Magistrate records this outcome formally, and if the person was held in custody solely for the inquiry, they're released; if never in custody, they're simply discharged from the proceedings.
essential_elements: Triggered when the inquiry fails to prove necessity.
A formal record entry of this outcome is mandatory.
In-custody-for-the-inquiry-only persons are released; not-in-custody persons are discharged.
breakdown.how_to_read: The natural counterpart to Section 136 — every Section 135 inquiry ends in one or the other of these two outcomes.

sections.title: Commencement of period for which security is required
sections.raw_text:
138. Commencement of period for which security is required.—(1) If any person, in respect of whom an order requiring security is made under section 125 or section 136, is at the time such order is made, sentenced to, or undergoing a sentence of, imprisonment, the period for which such security is required shall commence on the expiration of such sentence.
    (2) In other cases such period shall commence on the date of such order unless the Magistrate, for sufficient reason, fixes a later date.

breakdown.plain_summary: Clarifies when the clock actually starts running on a security order made under either Section 125 (post-conviction) or Section 136 (post-inquiry). If the person is already serving (or has just been sentenced to) imprisonment when the order is made, the security period only begins once that sentence ends — it doesn't run concurrently with imprisonment, since the person poses no liberty-related risk while locked up. In all other cases, the period starts from the date of the order itself, unless the Magistrate has sufficient reason to fix a later start date.
essential_elements: Applies to security orders under Section 125 or Section 136.
If the person is under (or sentenced to) imprisonment: the security period starts only when that sentence expires.
Otherwise: the period starts on the date of the order, unless the Magistrate fixes a later date for sufficient reason.
breakdown.how_to_read: A short but practically important timing rule — always check whether the person concerned was serving a sentence at the time of the order before calculating when a peace/good-behaviour bond period actually begins and ends.

sections.title: Contents of bond
sections.raw_text: 139. Contents of bond.—The bond or bail bond to be executed by any such person shall bind him to keep the peace or to be of good behaviour, as the case may be, and in the latter case the commission or attempt to commit, or the abetment of, any offence punishable with imprisonment, wherever it may be committed, is a breach of the bond or bail bond.

breakdown.plain_summary: Defines what the bond actually promises. A "keep the peace" bond binds the person simply to that. A "good behaviour" bond is broader in its breach trigger: committing, attempting, or abetting any imprisonable offence — anywhere, not just within the Magistrate's jurisdiction — counts as a breach of the bond.
essential_elements: Two bond types with different content: 'keep the peace' vs. 'good behaviour.'
For good-behaviour bonds specifically: any commission, attempt, or abetment of an imprisonable offence is a breach, regardless of where it's committed.
breakdown.how_to_read: Note how much broader the good-behaviour trigger is compared to keep-the-peace — an unrelated offence committed far away can still breach a good-behaviour bond, which is a key point for anyone advising a person currently bound under one.

sections.title: Power to reject sureties
sections.raw_text:
140. Power to reject sureties.—(1) A Magistrate may refuse to accept any surety offered, or may reject any surety previously accepted by him or his predecessor under this Chapter on the ground that such surety is an unfit person for the purposes of the bail bond:
    Provided that before so refusing to accept or rejecting any such surety, he shall either himself hold an inquiry on oath into the fitness of the surety, or cause such inquiry to be held and a report to be made thereon by a Magistrate subordinate to him.
    (2) Such Magistrate shall, before holding the inquiry, give reasonable notice to the surety and to the person by whom the surety was offered and shall, in making the inquiry, record the substance of the evidence adduced before him.
    (3) If the Magistrate is satisfied, after considering the evidence so adduced either before him or before a Magistrate deputed under sub-section (1), and the report of such Magistrate (if any), that the surety is an unfit person for the purposes of the bail bond, he shall make an order refusing to accept or rejecting, as the case may be, such surety and recording his reasons for so doing:
    Provided that before making an order rejecting any surety who has previously been accepted, the Magistrate shall issue his summons or warrant, as he thinks fit, and cause the person for whom the surety is bound to appear or to be brought before him.

breakdown.plain_summary: Gives the Magistrate quality control over sureties — both at the offering stage and even after a surety has already been accepted (by the same Magistrate or a predecessor). Rejection can't be arbitrary: a formal on-oath fitness inquiry (held personally or delegated to a subordinate Magistrate who reports back) is mandatory first, with reasonable notice to both the surety and the person who offered them, and a recorded evidentiary record. Only after that inquiry, and only with recorded reasons, can the Magistrate reject the surety. If a previously-accepted surety is being rejected (as opposed to a fresh offer being refused), there's an extra procedural step: the person for whom the surety stood must be summoned or brought before the Magistrate before the rejection order is made.
essential_elements: Applies to both fresh surety offers and previously-accepted sureties.
Mandatory fitness inquiry on oath before any refusal/rejection — either held personally or delegated with a report back.
Reasonable notice must be given to both the surety and the person who offered the surety.
Rejection requires recorded reasons.
Rejecting a previously-accepted surety additionally requires summoning/producing the person for whom the surety is bound before the order is made.
breakdown.how_to_read: Note the escalating procedural protection: rejecting a brand-new offer needs the fitness inquiry; rejecting an already-accepted surety needs that plus the additional summons/production step — reflecting the greater disruption caused by pulling the rug out from under an existing arrangement.

sections.title: Imprisonment in default of security
sections.raw_text:
141. Imprisonment in default of security.—(1)(a) If any person ordered to give security under section 125 or section 136 does not give such security on or before the date on which the period for which such security is to be given commences, he shall, except in the case next hereinafter mentioned, be committed to prison, or, if he is already in prison, be detained in prison until such period expires or until within such period he gives the security to the Court or Magistrate who made the order requiring it;
    (b) if any person after having executed a bond or bail bond for keeping the peace in pursuance of an order of a Magistrate under section 136, is proved, to the satisfaction of such Magistrate or his successor-in-office, to have committed breach of the bond or bail bond, such Magistrate or successor-in-office may, after recording the grounds of such proof, order that the person be arrested and detained in prison until the expiry of the period of the bond or bail bond and such order shall be without prejudice to any other punishment or forfeiture to which the said person may be liable in accordance with law.
    (2) When such person has been ordered by a Magistrate to give security for a period exceeding one year, such Magistrate shall, if such person does not give such security as aforesaid, issue a warrant directing him to be detained in prison pending the orders of the Sessions Judge and the proceedings shall be laid, as soon as conveniently may be, before such Court.
    (3) Such Court, after examining such proceedings and requiring from the Magistrate any further information or evidence which it thinks necessary, and after giving the concerned person a reasonable opportunity of being heard, may pass such order on the case as it thinks fit:
    Provided that the period (if any) for which any person is imprisoned for failure to give security shall not exceed three years.
    (4) If security has been required in the course of the same proceeding from two or more persons in respect of any one of whom the proceedings are referred to the Sessions Judge under sub-section (2) such reference shall also include the case of any other of such persons who has been ordered to give security, and the provisions of sub-sections (2) and (3) shall, in that event, apply to the case of such other person also, except that the period (if any) for which he may be imprisoned, shall not exceed the period for which he was ordered to give security.
    (5) A Sessions Judge may in his discretion transfer any proceedings laid before him under sub-section (2) or sub-section (4) to an Additional Sessions Judge and upon such transfer, such Additional Sessions Judge may exercise the powers of a Sessions Judge under this section in respect of such proceedings.
    (6) If the security is tendered to the officer in charge of the jail, he shall forthwith refer the matter to the Court or Magistrate who made the order, and shall await the orders of such Court or Magistrate.
    (7) Imprisonment for failure to give security for keeping the peace shall be simple.
    (8) Imprisonment for failure to give security for good behaviour shall, where the proceedings have been taken under section 127, be simple, and, where the proceedings have been taken under section 128 or section 129, be rigorous or simple as the Court or Magistrate in each case directs.

breakdown.plain_summary: The enforcement teeth of the whole Chapter: what happens if a person ordered to give security under Section 125 or 136 simply doesn't. Default consequence: committal to (or continued detention in) prison until the security period expires or the security is actually given. Separately, breach of an already-executed peace-keeping bond can itself lead to arrest and imprisonment for the bond's remaining period, on recorded proof of the breach — and this is on top of, not instead of, any other legal punishment the breach might attract. There's a jurisdictional escalation for longer orders: if the required security period exceeds one year, the Magistrate can't just imprison the person on their own authority — they must refer the matter to the Sessions Judge, who reviews the record, can call for more evidence, must give the person a hearing, and then decides — subject to an absolute three-year cap on imprisonment for security default. Multiple co-accused persons from the same proceeding get bundled into the same Sessions Judge reference if any one of them triggers it, though each person's own imprisonment cap tracks their own originally-ordered security period. A Sessions Judge can delegate to an Additional Sessions Judge. Tendering the security to the jail officer (rather than the Court directly) is expressly allowed — the jail officer just refers it up. Finally, the type of imprisonment differs by track: peace-keeping default is always simple imprisonment; good-behaviour default is simple for Section 127 (dissemination) cases, but the Court/Magistrate's choice between rigorous or simple for Sections 128-129 (suspected persons / habitual offenders) cases.
essential_elements: Default consequence: committal to or continued detention in prison until the security is given or the period expires.
Bond breach (post-execution) can independently trigger arrest and imprisonment for the bond's unexpired period, without prejudice to other legal consequences.
Mandatory Sessions Judge reference where the required security period exceeds one year — the Magistrate cannot imprison unilaterally in such cases.
Absolute cap: imprisonment for security default cannot exceed three years.
Imprisonment type varies by track: simple for peace-keeping and Section 127 good-behaviour defaults; Court/Magistrate's choice of simple or rigorous for Section 128/129 defaults.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Multiple-persons bundling under sub-section (4) still respects each individual's own security-period cap when fixing their imprisonment term.
Tendering security directly to the jail officer under sub-section (6) is a valid alternative channel — the officer must refer it onward and await orders, not decide unilaterally.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the section to reach for whenever advising a detained client on a peace/good-behaviour bond default — check first whether the required period exceeded one year (Sessions Judge reference required), then check the three-year absolute ceiling, then check which imprisonment type applies to their specific track.

sections.title: Power to release persons imprisoned for failing to give security
sections.raw_text:
142. Power to release persons imprisoned for failing to give security.—(1) Whenever the District Magistrate in the case of an order passed by an Executive Magistrate under section 136, or the Chief Judicial Magistrate in any other case is of opinion that any person imprisoned for failing to give security under this Chapter may be released without hazard to the community or to any other person, he may order such person to be discharged.
    (2) Whenever any person has been imprisoned for failing to give security under this Chapter, the High Court or Court of Session, or, where the order was made by any other Court, District Magistrate, in the case of an order passed by an Executive Magistrate under section 136, or the Chief Judicial Magistrate in any other case, may make an order reducing the amount of the security or the number of sureties or the time for which security has been required.
    (3) An order under sub-section (1) may direct the discharge of such person either without conditions or upon any conditions which such person accepts:
    Provided that any condition imposed shall cease to be operative when the period for which such person was ordered to give security has expired.
    (4) The State Government may prescribe, by rules, the conditions upon which a conditional discharge may be made.
    (5) If any condition upon which any person has been discharged is, in the opinion of District Magistrate, in the case of an order passed by an Executive Magistrate under section 136, or the Chief Judicial Magistrate in any other case by whom the order of discharge was made or of his successor, not fulfilled, he may cancel the same.
    (6) When a conditional order of discharge has been cancelled under sub-section (5), such person may be arrested by any police officer without warrant, and shall thereupon be produced before the District Magistrate, in the case of an order passed by an Executive Magistrate under section 136, or the Chief Judicial Magistrate in any other case.
    (7) Unless such person gives security in accordance with the terms of the original order for the unexpired portion of the term for which he was in the first instance committed or ordered to be detained (such portion being deemed to be a period equal to the period between the date of the breach of the conditions of discharge and the date on which, except for such conditional discharge, he would have been entitled to release), District Magistrate, in the case of an order passed by an Executive Magistrate under section 136, or the Chief Judicial Magistrate in any other case may remand such person to prison to undergo such unexpired portion.
    (8) A person remanded to prison under sub-section (7) shall, subject to the provisions of section 141, be released at any time on giving security in accordance with the terms of the original order for the unexpired portion aforesaid to the Court or Magistrate by whom such order was made, or to its or his successor.
    (9) The High Court or Court of Session may at any time, for sufficient reasons to be recorded in writing, cancel any bond for keeping the peace or for good behaviour executed under this Chapter by any order made by it, and District Magistrate, in the case of an order passed by an Executive Magistrate under section 136, or the Chief Judicial Magistrate in any other case may make such cancellation where such bond was executed under his order or under the order of any other Court in his district.
    (10) Any surety for the peaceable conduct or good behaviour of another person ordered to execute a bond under this Chapter may at any time apply to the Court making such order to cancel the bond and on such application being made, the Court shall issue a summons or warrant, as it thinks fit, requiring the person for whom such surety is bound to appear or to be brought before it.

breakdown.plain_summary: The Chapter's safety-valve/clemency section, closing it out. It gives senior authorities — the District Magistrate (for Executive Magistrate orders under Section 136) or the Chief Judicial Magistrate (for other cases) — power to release, on their own opinion, a person imprisoned for security default who can safely be let out without hazarding the community. Separately, the High Court, Court of Session, or the same District Magistrate/Chief Judicial Magistrate can reduce the security amount, number of sureties, or the time period, easing the terms without a full release. Release can be unconditional or conditional (conditions automatically lapse once the original security period would have expired anyway); the State Government can prescribe by rule what kinds of conditions are permissible. If a conditionally-discharged person breaches their conditions, they can be re-arrested without warrant and brought before the releasing authority, then remanded to serve out the unexpired portion of their original sentence unless they now give the required security — though they can still buy their way out at any point during that remand by finally giving the security. Independently, the High Court/Court of Session (or the District Magistrate/Chief Judicial Magistrate in their own district) can cancel any peace/good-behaviour bond outright for recorded sufficient reasons. And finally, a surety themselves — not just the principal — can apply to be released from their own surety obligation, triggering a summons/warrant to bring the principal back before the Court to sort out a replacement arrangement.
essential_elements: Release power vested in the District Magistrate (Section 136 orders) or Chief Judicial Magistrate (other cases), on their opinion that release is safe.
Separate power (High Court/Sessions Court or District/Chief Judicial Magistrate) to reduce security amount, surety count, or time period without full release.
Conditional discharge is permitted; conditions automatically lapse at the original security period's expiry; the State Government can prescribe permissible conditions by rule.
Breach of discharge conditions: warrantless arrest, production before the releasing authority, and possible remand for the unexpired portion — avoidable by finally furnishing the security.
Independent bond-cancellation power for the High Court/Sessions Court (any time, recorded reasons) or the District/Chief Judicial Magistrate (within their own district's orders).
A surety can apply to be discharged from their own obligation, triggering process to bring the principal back before the Court.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The 'unexpired portion' calculation on remand under sub-section (7) is specifically tied to the gap between the conditional-discharge breach date and the date the person would otherwise have been entitled to release — not simply the full original term.
Remand under sub-section (7) remains subject to Section 141's rules (e.g., the three-year absolute imprisonment cap), so it isn't an unlimited re-imprisonment power.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read this as the release/relief counterpart to Section 141's enforcement machinery — whenever a client has been imprisoned for security default, this is the section to check for a path back out, whether via outright release, term reduction, or conditional discharge.

sections.title: Security for unexpired period of bond
sections.raw_text:
143. Security for unexpired period of bond.—(1) When a person for whose appearance a summons or warrant has been issued under the proviso to sub-section (3) of section 140 or under sub-section (10) of section 142, appears or is brought before the Magistrate or Court, the Magistrate or Court shall cancel the bond or bail bond executed by such person and shall order such person to give, for the unexpired portion of the term of such bond, fresh security of the same description as the original security.
    (2) Every such order shall, for the purposes of sections 139 to 142 (both inclusive) be deemed to be an order made under section 125 or section 136, as the case may be.

breakdown.plain_summary: The closing section of Chapter IX ties off two loose ends created earlier in the Chapter: what happens when a previously-accepted surety is rejected (Section 140(3) proviso) or when a surety applies to be discharged from their own obligation (Section 142(10)), and the principal is accordingly summoned or brought before the Court. In either case, once the person appears, the Magistrate or Court must cancel the existing bond and order fresh security of the same kind, running only for whatever portion of the original bond's term remains — not a fresh full term. That new order is then deemed, for all the purposes of Sections 139-142 (bond contents, surety rejection, imprisonment in default, and release/relief), to be an original order made under Section 125 or Section 136, so the whole Chapter's machinery applies to it exactly as if it were a first-time order.
essential_elements: Applies specifically where a person is summoned/brought before the Court under the Section 140(3) proviso (rejected surety) or Section 142(10) (surety's own discharge application).
The existing bond is cancelled and fresh security of the same description is ordered.
The fresh security covers only the unexpired portion of the original bond's term.
The fresh order is deemed, for Sections 139-142 purposes, to be an order under Section 125 or Section 136.
breakdown.how_to_read: A short mechanical closing section — its main function is the 'deeming' clause in sub-section (2), which folds fresh-security orders back into the same enforcement/relief framework (Sections 139-142) rather than creating a separate, undefined procedural track.

sections.title: Order for maintenance of wives, children and parents
sections.raw_text:
144. Order for maintenance of wives, children and parents.—(1) If any person having sufficient means neglects or refuses to maintain—
        (a) his wife, unable to maintain herself; or
        (b) his legitimate or illegitimate child, whether married or not, unable to maintain itself; or
        (c) his legitimate or illegitimate child (not being a married daughter) who has attained majority, where such child is, by reason of any physical or mental abnormality or injury unable to maintain itself; or
        (d) his father or mother, unable to maintain himself or herself,
a Magistrate of the first class may, upon proof of such neglect or refusal, order such person to make a monthly allowance for the maintenance of his wife or such child, father or mother, at such monthly rate as such Magistrate thinks fit and to pay the same to such person as the Magistrate may from time to time direct:
    Provided that the Magistrate may order the father of a female child referred to in clause (b) to make such allowance, until she attains her majority, if the Magistrate is satisfied that the husband of such female child, if married, is not possessed of sufficient means:
    Provided further that the Magistrate may, during the pendency of the proceeding regarding monthly allowance for the maintenance under this sub-section, order such person to make a monthly allowance for the interim maintenance of his wife or such child, father or mother, and the expenses of such proceeding which the Magistrate considers reasonable, and to pay the same to such person as the Magistrate may from time to time direct:
    Provided also that an application for the monthly allowance for the interim maintenance and expenses of proceeding under the second proviso shall, as far as possible, be disposed of within sixty days from the date of the service of notice of the application to such person.
    Explanation.—For the purposes of this Chapter, "wife" includes a woman who has been divorced by, or has obtained a divorce from, her husband and has not remarried.
    (2) Any such allowance for the maintenance or interim maintenance and expenses of proceeding shall be payable from the date of the order, or, if so ordered, from the date of the application for maintenance or interim maintenance and expenses of proceeding, as the case may be.
    (3) If any person so ordered fails without sufficient cause to comply with the order, any such Magistrate may, for every breach of the order, issue a warrant for levying the amount due in the manner provided for levying fines, and may sentence such person, for the whole or any part of each month's allowance for the maintenance or the interim maintenance and expenses of proceeding, as the case may be, remaining unpaid after the execution of the warrant, to imprisonment for a term which may extend to one month or until payment if sooner made:
    Provided that no warrant shall be issued for the recovery of any amount due under this section unless application be made to the Court to levy such amount within a period of one year from the date on which it became due:
    Provided further that if such person offers to maintain his wife on condition of her living with him, and she refuses to live with him, such Magistrate may consider any grounds of refusal stated by her, and may make an order under this section notwithstanding such offer, if he is satisfied that there is just ground for so doing.
    Explanation.—If a husband has contracted marriage with another woman or keeps a mistress, it shall be considered to be just ground for his wife's refusal to live with him.
    (4) No wife shall be entitled to receive an allowance for the maintenance or the interim maintenance and expenses of proceeding, from her husband under this section if she is living in adultery, or if, without any sufficient reason, she refuses to live with her husband, or if they are living separately by mutual consent.
    (5) On proof that any wife in whose favour an order has been made under this section is living in adultery, or that without sufficient reason she refuses to live with her husband, or that they are living separately by mutual consent, the Magistrate shall cancel the order.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the BNSS's carry-forward of the well-known summary maintenance remedy (the old CrPC Section 125). It lets a Magistrate of the first class order a person of sufficient means, who neglects or refuses to maintain a dependant, to pay a monthly allowance — covering a wife unable to maintain herself, a legitimate or illegitimate child (married or not) unable to maintain itself, an adult child unable to maintain itself due to physical/mental abnormality or injury (except a married daughter), or a father or mother unable to maintain themselves. A special sub-rule lets the Magistrate order a female child's father to pay until she turns 18 if her husband (if married) lacks sufficient means. Interim maintenance and litigation-expense orders are available while the main proceeding is pending, and applications for interim relief should, as far as possible, be decided within sixty days of notice being served — a built-in speed guarantee recognising that dependants often can't wait for a full trial. "Wife" is defined broadly to include a divorced woman who hasn't remarried. Payment runs from the order date, or an earlier application date if the Magistrate so directs. Non-compliance is enforced like a fine — levied by warrant, escalating to up to one month's imprisonment per unpaid instalment (or until payment, if sooner) — but recovery applications must be made within one year of the amount falling due, or the warrant route is barred. A husband's mere offer to resume cohabitation doesn't automatically defeat the wife's claim; the Magistrate can still order maintenance if her stated grounds for refusal are just — and bigamy or keeping a mistress is expressly deemed a just ground by the Explanation. Conversely, a wife is disentitled altogether if she's living in adultery, refuses to live with her husband without sufficient reason, or the couple is separated by mutual consent — and an existing order must be cancelled on proof of any of these.
essential_elements: Four categories of dependants: wife unable to maintain herself; child (legitimate/illegitimate, married or not) unable to maintain itself; a non-married adult child unable to maintain itself due to physical/mental abnormality or injury; parent unable to maintain themselves.
Threshold: the person ordered to pay must have 'sufficient means' and must have 'neglected or refused' to maintain the dependant.
Interim maintenance and proceeding-expenses orders are available pending the main case, targeted for disposal within sixty days of notice.
'Wife' expressly includes an un-remarried divorced woman.
Enforcement: warrant for levying the amount as a fine, with up to one month's imprisonment per unpaid instalment — but a strict one-year limitation on when a recovery application can be made.
Bigamy or keeping a mistress is deemed 'just ground' for a wife's refusal to resume living with her husband, defeating his cohabitation-offer defence.
Wife's disentitlement: living in adultery, refusing to live with husband without sufficient reason, or living separately by mutual consent — grounds for both refusing and cancelling an order.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The one-year limitation on enforcement applications is calculated from when each instalment 'became due' — a running clock per instalment, not a single deadline for the whole order.
Imprisonment for default doesn't wipe out the debt — the arrears remain recoverable; imprisonment is coercive, not a substitute for payment ('or until payment if sooner made').
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a high-volume, practically important section — read sub-section (1)'s four dependant categories first to check standing, then sub-section (4)'s disentitlement grounds as the standard defence checklist, then sub-section (3)'s enforcement mechanics and one-year limitation for the recovery stage.

sections.title: Procedure
sections.raw_text:
145. Procedure.—(1) Proceedings under section 144 may be taken against any person in any district—
        (a) where he is; or
        (b) where he or his wife resides; or
        (c) where he last resided with his wife, or as the case may be, with the mother of the illegitimate child; or
        (d) where his father or mother resides.
    (2) All evidence in such proceedings shall be taken in the presence of the person against whom an order for payment of maintenance is proposed to be made, or, when his personal attendance is dispensed with, in the presence of his advocate, and shall be recorded in the manner prescribed for summons-cases:
    Provided that if the Magistrate is satisfied that the person against whom an order for payment of maintenance is proposed to be made is wilfully avoiding service, or wilfully neglecting to attend the Court, the Magistrate may proceed to hear and determine the case ex parte and any order so made may be set aside for good cause shown on an application made within three months from the date thereof subject to such terms including terms as to payment of costs to the opposite party as the Magistrate may think just and proper.
    (3) The Court in dealing with applications under section 144 shall have power to make such order as to costs as may be just.

breakdown.plain_summary: Deliberately claimant-friendly venue and evidentiary rules for maintenance proceedings. Venue is flexible — proceedings can be brought wherever the respondent currently is, where he or his wife resides, where he last resided with his wife (or the illegitimate child's mother), or where his parents reside — sparing a dependant claimant from having to chase the respondent to a distant or inconvenient forum. Evidence follows the summons-case procedure and must ordinarily be taken in the respondent's presence (or their advocate's, if personal attendance is dispensed with), but a Magistrate satisfied the respondent is wilfully dodging service or wilfully skipping Court can proceed ex parte — with a three-month window for the respondent to apply to set aside that ex parte order on good cause, potentially subject to a costs condition. The Court also has general power to award costs as it sees fit in these proceedings.
essential_elements: Four alternative venue options, all favouring the claimant's convenience over the respondent's.
Default evidentiary rule: taken in the respondent's presence (or advocate's, where attendance is dispensed with), following summons-case procedure.
Ex parte proceeding permitted on proof of wilful evasion of service or wilful non-attendance.
Ex parte orders can be set aside on an application within three months, for good cause, potentially on costs terms.
General discretionary costs power for the Court.
breakdown.how_to_read: The multiple-venue rule in sub-section (1) is the standout access-to-justice feature — always check all four options when advising a maintenance claimant on where to file, not just the respondent's current residence.

sections.title: Alteration in allowance

breakdown.plain_summary: Closes Chapter X with the mechanics of adjusting, cancelling, or coordinating a Section 144 maintenance order over time. General alteration power: either party (payer or payee) can seek a change in the allowance on proof of a change in circumstances — the Magistrate has full discretion on the new amount. Civil Court deference: if a competent Civil Court's decision makes the existing Section 144 order inappropriate, the Magistrate must cancel or vary it accordingly — the summary criminal maintenance order yields to a subsequent civil adjudication. Divorce-specific cancellation triggers for a wife who was divorced: remarriage cancels the order from the remarriage date; receipt of the full customary/personal-law divorce settlement sum cancels it (with the cancellation date depending on whether that sum was paid before or after the order); and voluntary surrender of her maintenance rights post-divorce cancels it from the surrender date. Finally, a coordination rule prevents double recovery: when a Civil Court later grants a maintenance or dowry decree, it must account for and set off whatever has already been paid or recovered under the Section 144 order.
essential_elements: General alteration on proof of changed circumstances — available to either the paying or receiving party.
Mandatory cancellation/variation where a competent Civil Court's decision requires it.

Three specific divorce-related cancellation triggers for a divorced wife: remarriage, receipt of the full customary/personal-law settlement sum, or voluntary surrender of maintenance rights — each with its own effective cancellation date.
Civil Court maintenance/dowry decrees must set off sums already paid/recovered under the Section 144 order, preventing double recovery.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The cancellation-date rule for receipt of the full settlement sum (sub-section (3)(b)) varies depending on timing: from the order date if the sum was paid before the order, or from the expiry of the period maintenance was actually paid if paid after.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat sub-sections (1)-(2) as the general variation/deference rules and sub-section (3) as a specific divorced-wife checklist — three distinct triggers, each cancelling the order from a different calculated date. Sub-section (4) is the anti-double-recovery coordination clause worth flagging whenever a civil maintenance/dowry decree follows an existing Section 144 order.

sections.title: Enforcement of order of maintenance
sections.raw_text:
147. Enforcement of order of maintenance.—A copy of the order of maintenance or interim
maintenance and expenses of proceedings, as the case may be, shall be given without payment to the person
in whose favour it is made, or to his guardian, if any, or to the person to whom the allowance for the
maintenance or the allowance for the interim maintenance and expenses of proceeding, as the case may be,
is to be paid; and such order may be enforced by any Magistrate in any place where the person against
whom it is made may be, on such Magistrate being satisfied as to the identity of the parties and the
non-payment of the allowance, or as the case may be, expenses, due.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section closes out Chapter X by making a maintenance order actually enforceable wherever the defaulting person happens to be, not just in the court that passed it. The person who is entitled to receive the money (or their guardian, or whoever collects it on their behalf) gets a free copy of the order — no court fee. If the husband, father, or son who was ordered to pay moves to another district, the claimant doesn't have to chase him back to the original court: any Magistrate in the place where he currently is can enforce the order, as long as that Magistrate is satisfied about two things — that the parties are who they say they are, and that the allowance really is unpaid.
essential_elements: A certified copy of the maintenance order (or interim maintenance and expenses order) is supplied free of cost
The copy goes to the person entitled to the money, their guardian, or the person authorised to collect the payment on their behalf
The order can be enforced by any Magistrate — not only the Magistrate who originally passed it — in whatever place the defaulter is found
Enforcement requires the enforcing Magistrate to be satisfied on two points: identity of the parties, and non-payment of the allowance/expenses due
exceptions_and_qualifications: The section only authorises enforcement (recovery of what's due) — it does not let a new Magistrate re-open or vary the amount of maintenance fixed by the original order
The 'free of payment' rule applies only to the copy of the order itself, not to other litigation costs
breakdown.how_to_read: Pair this with Section 144(3), which is the actual enforcement mechanism — a warrant to levy the amount as a fine, backstopped by up to one month's imprisonment per default. Section 147 is the portability rule that lets that machinery be triggered by whichever Magistrate the defaulter is presently within reach of, which matters enormously in practice since maintenance defaulters often relocate precisely to frustrate recovery.

sections.title: Dispersal of assembly by use of civil force
sections.raw_text:
148. Dispersal of assembly by use of civil force.—(1) Any Executive Magistrate or officer in charge
of a police station or, in the absence of such officer in charge, any police officer, not below the rank of a
sub-inspector, may command any unlawful assembly, or any assembly of five or more persons likely to
cause a disturbance of the public peace, to disperse; and it shall thereupon be the duty of the members of
such assembly to disperse accordingly.
    (2) If, upon being so commanded, any such assembly does not disperse, or if, without being so
commanded, it conducts itself in such a manner as to show a determination not to disperse, any Executive
Magistrate or police officer referred to in sub-section (1), may proceed to disperse such assembly by force,
and may require the assistance of any person, not being an officer or member of the armed forces and acting
as such, for the purpose of dispersing such assembly, and, if necessary, arresting and confining the persons
who form part of it, in order to disperse such assembly or that they may be punished according to law.
key_terms: officer in charge of a police station

breakdown.plain_summary: This opens Chapter XI's scheme for handling assemblies that threaten public order, and it's meant to be a graduated response — force is the last resort, not the first. An Executive Magistrate, or the senior police officer at a station (or, if that officer isn't around, any sub-inspector-or-above), can order an unlawful assembly — or even a lawful gathering of five or more people that looks likely to cause a disturbance — to disperse. Once that command is given, every member of the crowd is legally obliged to leave. Only if the crowd ignores the order, or is visibly refusing to break up even without being told to, does sub-section (2) kick in: the Magistrate or officer may then use civil force to physically disperse the assembly, and can rope in ordinary members of the public to help — though not soldiers acting in their military capacity — including, where necessary, arresting people from the crowd.
essential_elements: The power to command dispersal belongs to an Executive Magistrate, the officer in charge of a police station, or (in that officer's absence) any police officer of sub-inspector rank or above
It applies to any 'unlawful assembly' as well as to any assembly of five or more persons that is likely to disturb the public peace, even if not technically unlawful yet
Once commanded, dispersal becomes a legal duty of every member of the assembly
Force may be used only if the assembly fails to disperse after being commanded, or shows a clear determination not to disperse even without a command
Civilian assistance can be requisitioned for dispersal and, if needed, arrest — but this assistance may not be drawn from armed-forces personnel acting in that capacity
exceptions_and_qualifications: Force is a second-stage power — it cannot be used as the first response unless the assembly has already shown a determination not to disperse
The civilian-assistance power expressly excludes officers or members of the armed forces acting as such; the armed forces route is separately governed by sections 149 and 150
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 148 is the civil-force tier of a three-tier escalation ladder that runs through sections 149 and 150 (armed-forces assistance) and is capped by section 151 (good-faith protection from prosecution). When examining any dispersal action, first check whether a clear command to disperse was given and disobeyed (or manifest defiance shown) before force was used — that sequencing is the crux of whether the action was lawful.

sections.title: Use of armed forces to disperse assembly
sections.raw_text:
149. Use of armed forces to disperse assembly.—(1) If any assembly referred to in sub-section (1) of
section 148 cannot otherwise be dispersed, and it is necessary for the public security that it should be
dispersed, the District Magistrate or any other Executive Magistrate authorised by him, who is present, may
cause it to be dispersed by the armed forces.
    (2) Such Magistrate may require any officer in command of any group of persons belonging to the
armed forces to disperse the assembly with the help of the armed forces under his command, and to arrest
and confine such persons forming part of it as the Executive Magistrate may direct, or as it may be necessary
to arrest and confine in order to disperse the assembly or to have them punished according to law.
    (3) Every such officer of the armed forces shall obey such requisition in such manner as he thinks fit,
but in so doing he shall use as little force, and do as little injury to person and property, as may be consistent
with dispersing the assembly and arresting and detaining such persons.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the next rung up the ladder from Section 148: when civil force alone can't break up the assembly and public security genuinely demands it, the District Magistrate — or another Executive Magistrate he has authorised, and who is actually present at the scene — can call in the armed forces. The Magistrate directs an officer commanding a unit to disperse the crowd and, if needed, arrest people from it. The armed-forces officer decides the tactical 'how,' but is bound by a built-in restraint: use the minimum force and cause the least possible injury to people and property that is still consistent with actually getting the job done.
essential_elements: Triggered only when the assembly cannot otherwise be dispersed and public security necessitates dispersal
The calling authority must be the District Magistrate, or another Executive Magistrate specifically authorised by him, and that Magistrate must be present
The Magistrate requisitions an armed-forces officer in command of a group to disperse the assembly and arrest/confine persons as directed or as necessary

The armed-forces officer has tactical discretion on method, but is legally bound to use as little force and cause as little injury to person and property as is consistent with achieving dispersal and arrest
exceptions_and_qualifications: This power is conditional on civil-force dispersal under section 148 having failed or being plainly inadequate — it is not a freestanding first option
Presence of the authorising Magistrate at the scene is a precondition, distinguishing this from section 150 which applies precisely when no Magistrate can be reached
breakdown.how_to_read: Read sections 148-150 as one continuum of escalating force, each stage gated by the failure or unavailability of the previous one, and read all three against section 151's good-faith immunity — which is the practical mechanism that shields officers acting under this section from criminal prosecution provided they stayed within the 'least force necessary' constraint.

sections.title: Power of certain armed force officers to disperse assembly
sections.raw_text:
150. Power of certain armed force officers to disperse assembly.—When the public security is
manifestly endangered by any such assembly and no Executive Magistrate can be communicated with, any
commissioned or gazetted officer of the armed forces may disperse such assembly with the help of the
armed forces under his command, and may arrest and confine any persons forming part of it, in order to
disperse such assembly or that they may be punished according to law; but if, while he is acting under this
section, it becomes practicable for him to communicate with an Executive Magistrate, he shall do so, and
shall thenceforward obey the instructions of the Magistrate, as to whether he shall or shall not continue such
action.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the emergency, no-Magistrate-available fallback. If public security is obviously and seriously threatened by an assembly, and genuinely no Executive Magistrate can be reached in time, a commissioned or gazetted officer of the armed forces can act on his own authority — disperse the crowd and arrest people from it — without waiting for civilian sign-off. But this independent authority is temporary by design: the moment it becomes practically possible for him to get in touch with an Executive Magistrate, he must do so, and from that point on he has to follow the Magistrate's instructions on whether to keep going or stand down.
essential_elements: Applies only when public security is manifestly (obviously, seriously) endangered by the assembly
Applies only when no Executive Magistrate can be communicated with at that time
The acting officer must be commissioned or gazetted (not any lower-ranking officer)
He may disperse the assembly and arrest/confine members of it using the armed forces under his command
As soon as communication with an Executive Magistrate becomes practicable, he must establish it and thereafter obey the Magistrate's instructions on continuing or discontinuing the action
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a stopgap power that yields automatically to civilian magisterial control the instant that control becomes reachable — it is not a standing parallel authority
Unlike section 149, no advance requisition from a Magistrate is needed here precisely because none is available; that is the whole justification for the provision
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 150 exists for genuine command-and-control gaps — remote areas, communication breakdowns, or a sudden crisis. The key fact question in any dispute over this section is almost always whether a Magistrate truly could not be reached, and, if reached mid-operation, whether the officer promptly deferred to the Magistrate's instructions as required.

sections.title: Protection against prosecution for acts done under sections 148, 149 and 150
sections.raw_text:
151. Protection against prosecution for acts done under sections 148, 149 and 150.—(1) No
prosecution against any person for any act purporting to be done under section 148, section 149 or
section 150 shall be instituted in any Criminal Court except—
       (a) with the sanction of the Central Government where such person is an officer or member of the
    armed forces;
        (b) with the sanction of the State Government in any other case.
    (2) (a) No Executive Magistrate or police officer acting under any of the said sections in good faith;
    (b) no person doing any act in good faith in compliance with a requisition under section 148 or
section 149;
    (c) no officer of the armed forces acting under section 150 in good faith;
   (d) no member of the armed forces doing any act in obedience to any order which he was bound to
obey,
shall be deemed to have thereby committed an offence.
    (3) In this section and in the preceding sections of this Chapter,—
        (a) the expression "armed forces" means the army, naval and air forces, operating as land forces
    and includes any other armed forces of the Union so operating;
        (b) "officer", in relation to the armed forces, means a person commissioned, gazetted or in pay as
    an officer of the armed forces and includes a junior commissioned officer, a warrant officer, a petty
    officer, a non-commissioned officer and a non-gazetted officer;
        (c) "member", in relation to the armed forces, means a person in the armed forces other than an
    officer.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the accountability valve for the dispersal powers in sections 148-150 — it doesn't grant blanket immunity, but it does erect two separate protections. First, a procedural bar: nobody can even be prosecuted for something done (or purporting to be done) under those sections unless the Central Government sanctions it (if the person is armed-forces personnel) or the State Government sanctions it (in every other case) — so a criminal case can't be launched against a Magistrate, police officer, or soldier without that government-level gatekeeping first. Second, a substantive shield: acts genuinely done in good faith under these sections — by a Magistrate or police officer, by a civilian who was requisitioned to help, by an armed-forces officer acting under section 150, or by any armed-forces member simply obeying a lawful order he was bound to obey — are deemed not to be offences at all. Sub-section (3) then locks down the definitions of 'armed forces,' 'officer,' and 'member' used throughout this Part, so there's no ambiguity about who these protections cover.
essential_elements: Prosecution for acts under sections 148, 149, or 150 requires prior sanction: Central Government sanction if the accused is an armed-forces officer/member, State Government sanction in any other case
Good-faith acts by an Executive Magistrate or police officer under any of these sections are deemed not to be offences
Good-faith compliance by a civilian requisitioned under section 148 or 149 is likewise deemed not an offence
Good-faith acts by an armed-forces officer under section 150 are deemed not an offence
An armed-forces member simply obeying an order he was bound to obey is deemed not to have committed an offence

'Armed forces' is defined as army, naval and air forces operating as land forces, plus any other Union armed forces so operating; 'officer' and 'member' are correspondingly defined to cover the full rank spectrum
exceptions_and_qualifications: The good-faith protection in sub-section (2) is not automatic — good faith must actually be established; it is not a licence for excessive or malicious force
The sanction requirement in sub-section (1) is a bar to institution of prosecution, not a bar to investigation or a permanent immunity — sanction can still be granted after due consideration
breakdown.how_to_read: Always read section 151 together with whichever of 148/149/150 is actually invoked — it is the safety net that makes the escalation ladder workable in practice, but its protection is conditional on good faith, and prosecution (even if barred without sanction) is not permanently foreclosed, only gated behind government sanction. This mirrors the classic Indian criminal-procedure device of requiring 'previous sanction' before prosecuting public servants and armed-forces personnel for official acts.

sections.title: Conditional order for removal of nuisance
sections.raw_text:
152. Conditional order for removal of nuisance.—(1) Whenever a District Magistrate or a
Sub-divisional Magistrate or any other Executive Magistrate specially empowered in this behalf by the
State Government, on receiving the report of a police officer or other information and on taking such
evidence (if any) as he thinks fit, considers—
       (a) that any unlawful obstruction or nuisance should be removed from any public place or from any
    way, river or channel which is or may be lawfully used by the public; or
        (b) that the conduct of any trade or occupation, or the keeping of any goods or merchandise, is
    injurious to the health or physical comfort of the community, and that in consequence such trade or
    occupation should be prohibited or regulated or such goods or merchandise should be removed or the
    keeping thereof regulated; or
        (c) that the construction of any building, or, the disposal of any substance, as is likely to occasion
    conflagration or explosion, should be prevented or stopped; or
         (d) that any building, tent or structure, or any tree is in such a condition that it is likely to fall and
    thereby cause injury to persons living or carrying on business in the neighbourhood or passing by, and
    that in consequence the removal, repair or support of such building, tent or structure, or the removal or
    support of such tree, is necessary; or
        (e) that any tank, well or excavation adjacent to any such way or public place should be fenced in
    such manner as to prevent danger arising to the public; or
        (f) that any dangerous animal should be destroyed, confined or otherwise disposed of,
such Magistrate may make a conditional order requiring the person causing such obstruction or nuisance,
or carrying on such trade or occupation, or keeping any such goods or merchandise, or owning, possessing
or controlling such building, tent, structure, substance, tank, well or excavation, or owning or possessing
such animal or tree, within a time to be fixed in the order—
        (i) to remove such obstruction or nuisance; or
        (ii) to desist from carrying on, or to remove or regulate in such manner as may be directed, such
    trade or occupation, or to remove such goods or merchandise, or to regulate the keeping thereof in such
    manner as may be directed; or
        (iii) to prevent or stop the construction of such building, or to alter the disposal of such
    substance; or
        (iv) to remove, repair or support such building, tent or structure, or to remove or support such
    trees; or
        (v) to fence such tank, well or excavation; or
        (vi) to destroy, confine or dispose of such dangerous animal in the manner provided in the said
    order, or, if he objects so to do, to appear before himself or some other Executive Magistrate subordinate
    to him at a time and place to be fixed by the order, and show cause, in the manner hereinafter provided,
    why the order should not be made absolute.
    (2) No order duly made by a Magistrate under this section shall be called in question in any Civil Court.
    Explanation.—A "public place" includes also property belonging to the State, camping grounds and
grounds left unoccupied for sanitary or recreative purposes.

breakdown.plain_summary: This opens Part B of Chapter XI, the public-nuisance machinery — a fast, summary way for a Magistrate to order a public nuisance fixed without waiting for a full civil suit. A District Magistrate, Sub-divisional Magistrate, or specially-empowered Executive Magistrate, acting on a police report or other information, can make a 'conditional order' covering six kinds of situations: obstructions blocking a public way/river/channel; a trade, occupation, or stored goods harming public health or comfort; construction or storage that risks fire or explosion; a building, tent, structure, or tree at risk of collapsing on people; an unfenced tank/well/excavation next to a public place; or a dangerous animal. The order tells the responsible person to either fix the problem within a set time, or — if they object — show up in court and explain why the order shouldn't be made permanent ('absolute'). Crucially, sub-section (2) insulates these orders from being challenged in a civil court — the whole point is speed, with the built-in show-cause hearing (sections 156-157) as the safeguard instead of parallel civil litigation.
essential_elements: The empowered Magistrates are the District Magistrate, Sub-divisional Magistrate, or an Executive Magistrate specially empowered by the State Government
The order can be triggered by a police report or any other information, plus whatever evidence the Magistrate chooses to take

Six categories of situations are covered: (a) obstruction/nuisance on a public way; (b) unhealthy trade or goods; (c) fire/explosion risk from construction or substances; (d) collapsing building/tent/structure/tree; (e) unfenced dangerous tank/well/excavation; (f) dangerous animals

The order is 'conditional': it directs the responsible person either to act (remove, desist, fence, destroy, etc.) within a fixed time, or to appear and show cause why the order should not be made absolute
Such an order cannot be challenged in any Civil Court
'Public place' is defined broadly by the Explanation to include State property, camping grounds, and grounds kept vacant for sanitary or recreational purposes
exceptions_and_qualifications: The order is only 'conditional' at this stage — it only becomes final and binding ('absolute') after the show-cause process in sections 154-157 runs its course
The civil-court ouster in sub-section (2) bars challenging the order itself, but does not eliminate the statutory show-cause remedy built into this very Chapter
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 152 is the trigger; sections 153-158 are the machinery that turns the conditional order into either an absolute order or a dropped proceeding. Map each of the six paragraphs (a)-(f) to real fact patterns — encroachments, polluting factories, fire hazards, unsafe structures, open wells, stray dangerous animals — since practitioners typically plead this section by pointing to the exact paragraph that matches their facts.

sections.title: Service or notification of order
sections.raw_text:
153. Service or notification of order.—(1) The order shall, if practicable, be served on the person
against whom it is made, in the manner herein provided for service of summons.
    (2) If such order cannot be so served, it shall be notified by proclamation published in such manner as
the State Government may, by rules, direct, and a copy thereof shall be stuck up at such place or places as
may be fittest for conveying the information to such person.

breakdown.plain_summary: This tells the Magistrate how to actually get the Section 152 order to the person it's aimed at. The default is personal service, done the same way a summons would be served. But if that's not practicable — the person can't be found, is evading service, or is simply unknown — the order is instead publicised by proclamation, in whatever manner the State Government has prescribed by rules, with a copy physically posted at whichever location is most likely to actually reach the person (for example, at the site of the nuisance itself).
essential_elements: Primary mode: service on the person, following the same procedure used for serving a summons
Fallback mode, used only if personal service isn't practicable: proclamation published per State Government rules, plus a copy stuck up at the most effective location for reaching that person
exceptions_and_qualifications: The fallback is only available when personal service is genuinely impracticable — it is not an alternative of first choice
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a purely procedural section but matters a great deal in practice: if the order was never properly served or proclaimed, the entire downstream obey-or-show-cause obligation in section 154 cannot attach, and any consequential absolute order is vulnerable to challenge for want of notice.

sections.title: Person to whom order is addressed to obey or show cause
sections.raw_text:
154. Person to whom order is addressed to obey or show cause.—The person against whom such
order is made shall—
    (a) perform, within the time and in the manner specified in the order, the act directed thereby; or
    (b) appear in accordance with such order and show cause against the same; and such appearance or
hearing may be permitted through audio-video conferencing.
