breakdown.plain_summary: Once served with (or proclaimed) a Section 152 order, the person named in it has exactly two lawful options: comply with what it directs, doing the act within the specified time and manner, or turn up and contest it by showing cause against the order. A modernising touch in the BNSS: the appearance or hearing to show cause can now be conducted through audio-video conferencing, so the person doesn't necessarily have to travel to appear in person.
essential_elements: Option one: perform the directed act within the time and manner the order specifies
Option two: appear and show cause against the order
Appearance/hearing for showing cause may be conducted via audio-video conferencing
exceptions_and_qualifications: There is no third option of simply ignoring the order — failure to do either triggers the penalty in section 155
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the fork in the road that determines what happens next: compliance ends the matter, while showing cause routes the case into the inquiry procedure of sections 156-157. The audio-video conferencing option is a practical BNSS-era convenience worth flagging for clients who are far from the court.

sections.title: Penalty for failure to comply with section 154
sections.raw_text:
155. Penalty for failure to comply with section 154.—If the person against whom an order is made
under section 154 does not perform such act or appear and show cause, he shall be liable to the penalty
specified in that behalf in section 223 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, and the order shall be made
absolute.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the consequence for doing neither of the two things section 154 requires. If the person neither performs the directed act nor shows up to contest it, two things happen automatically: they become liable to the penalty prescribed in Section 223 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (the substantive criminal offence for disobeying an order promulgated by a public servant), and — separately — the conditional order itself is made absolute, meaning it now has full binding force.
essential_elements: Applies only where the person has done neither of the two things required by section 154 — neither complied nor appeared to show cause
Triggers criminal liability under section 223 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
Also converts the conditional order automatically into an absolute order
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is distinct from the outcome under section 157, where the person does appear and show cause but the Magistrate is not satisfied — that follows a different (evidentiary) route to an absolute order
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 155 rewards default with the harshest combined consequence — criminal liability plus an automatically finalised order, with no evidentiary inquiry at all. This is precisely why section 154's audio-video conferencing option matters: it removes travel-distance as an excuse for total default.

sections.title: Procedure where existence of public right is denied
sections.raw_text:
156. Procedure where existence of public right is denied.— (1) Where an order is made under
section 152 for the purpose of preventing obstruction, nuisance or danger to the public in the use of any
way, river, channel or place, the Magistrate shall, on the appearance before him of the person against whom
the order was made, question him as to whether he denies the existence of any public right in respect of the
way, river, channel or place, and if he does so, the Magistrate shall, before proceeding under section 157,
inquire into the matter.
    (2) If in such inquiry the Magistrate finds that there is any reliable evidence in support of such denial,
he shall stay the proceedings until the matter of the existence of such right has been decided by a competent
Court; and, if he finds that there is no such evidence, he shall proceed as laid down in section 157.
    (3) A person who has, on being questioned by the Magistrate under sub-section (1), failed to deny the
existence of a public right of the nature therein referred to, or who, having made such denial, has failed to
adduce reliable evidence in support thereof, shall not in the subsequent proceedings be permitted to make
any such denial.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section handles a special wrinkle that can arise specifically in the public-way/river/channel category of Section 152 order (paragraph (a)): what if the person served with the order says there's no public right over that way, river, channel, or place at all — i.e., the public was never entitled to use it in the first place? When such a person appears, the Magistrate must specifically ask them whether they deny the existence of that public right. If they do deny it, the Magistrate has to pause and inquire into that specific question before moving to the ordinary show-cause hearing under section 157. If there's reliable evidence backing the denial, the whole proceeding is stayed until a competent civil court decides the public-right question definitively. If there's no reliable evidence for the denial, the Magistrate proceeds straight to section 157. And there's a use-it-or-lose-it rule: anyone who was asked and didn't deny the public right, or denied it but couldn't back it up with reliable evidence, is barred from raising that denial later in the proceedings.
essential_elements: Applies specifically to orders made under section 152 to prevent obstruction/nuisance/danger in the use of a way, river, channel, or place
On the person's appearance, the Magistrate must ask whether he denies the existence of any public right in that way/river/channel/place
If denied, the Magistrate must inquire into the denial before proceeding under section 157
If reliable evidence supports the denial, the proceedings are stayed pending a competent Court's decision on the existence of the right
If no reliable evidence supports the denial, the Magistrate proceeds directly under section 157
A person who fails to deny the right when asked, or denies it without adducing reliable evidence, is barred from raising that denial in later proceedings
exceptions_and_qualifications: This procedure is triggered only by an actual denial from the person — the Magistrate doesn't investigate public-right questions unprompted
The stay under sub-section (2) is not indefinite dismissal — it simply parks the criminal/summary proceeding until the civil question of the right's existence is resolved by a competent court
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat this as a jurisdictional screening step unique to public-way nuisance cases: it prevents a Magistrate exercising summary powers from having to conclusively adjudicate genuinely disputed questions of public right, which properly belong before a civil court, while also preventing endless unsubstantiated denials from derailing the summary process.

sections.title: Procedure where person against whom order is made under section 152 appears to show cause
sections.raw_text:
157. Procedure where person against whom order is made under section 152 appears to show
cause.—(1) If the person against whom an order under section 152 is made appears and shows cause against
the order, the Magistrate shall take evidence in the matter as in a summons-case.
     (2) If the Magistrate is satisfied that the order, either as originally made or subject to such modification
as he considers necessary, is reasonable and proper, the order shall be made absolute without modification
or, as the case may be, with such modification.
    (3) If the Magistrate is not so satisfied, no further proceedings shall be taken in the case:
    Provided that the proceedings under this section shall be completed, as soon as possible, within a period
of ninety days, which may be extended for the reasons to be recorded in writing, to one hundred and twenty
days.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the substantive show-cause hearing itself. If the person appears and contests the order (rather than defaulting under section 155, or being routed to a civil court under section 156), the Magistrate takes evidence following summons-case procedure — the same relatively streamlined evidentiary process used for less serious criminal cases. Based on that evidence, if the Magistrate is satisfied the order (as originally framed, or as modified) is reasonable and proper, it's made absolute, either unmodified or with whatever modification the Magistrate thinks fit. If the Magistrate isn't satisfied, the proceedings simply end there — no order is made absolute. There's also a built-in time discipline: the whole show-cause proceeding should wrap up within 90 days, extendable to a hard cap of 120 days, and only for reasons recorded in writing.
essential_elements: Triggered when the person appears and shows cause against a section 152 order
Evidence is taken following summons-case procedure
If satisfied the order (original or modified) is reasonable and proper, the Magistrate makes it absolute, with or without modification as warranted
If not satisfied, no further proceedings are taken — the matter simply drops
The proceedings must be completed within 90 days, extendable to a maximum of 120 days, and only for written reasons
exceptions_and_qualifications: The 90/120-day timeline is a statutory discipline on the process, not a limitation period barring the original order — its breach affects how long the show-cause matter can run, not whether the underlying nuisance order was valid
'Modification' power lets the Magistrate tailor the final absolute order rather than being locked into an all-or-nothing choice between the original order and no order at all
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the standard outcome-determining hearing for public-nuisance orders and the natural stage at which most contested Section 152 orders are finally resolved. Note the deliberate contrast with section 156: section 157 handles the merits of the nuisance/obstruction itself, while section 156 handles the threshold question of whether a public right existed at all.

sections.title: Power of Magistrate to direct local investigation and examination of an expert
sections.raw_text:
158. Power of Magistrate to direct local investigation and examination of an expert.—The
Magistrate may, for the purposes of an inquiry under section 156 or section 157—
        (a) direct a local investigation to be made by such person as he thinks fit; or
        (b) summon and examine an expert.

breakdown.plain_summary: This gives the Magistrate two practical evidence-gathering tools to use during either the public-right inquiry (section 156) or the show-cause hearing (section 157): ordering a local investigation by a person of the Magistrate's choosing (for instance, sending someone to physically inspect a disputed encroachment, structure, or water channel), or calling in and examining an expert witness (for example, an engineer to assess whether a building is genuinely at risk of collapse).
essential_elements: Available specifically for inquiries under section 156 (public right denial) or section 157 (show-cause hearing)
Option one: direct a local investigation, carried out by whichever person the Magistrate thinks fit to appoint
Option two: summon and examine an expert witness
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a discretionary evidentiary power, not a mandatory step — the Magistrate may proceed on the evidence already before him without invoking it
breakdown.how_to_read: This closing section of the first sub-batch equips the Magistrate to resolve genuinely technical or on-the-ground factual disputes — precisely the kind that arise in nuisance cases involving structural safety, encroachment boundaries, or watercourse rights — without having to rely solely on the parties' own competing evidence.

sections.title: Power of Magistrate to furnish written instructions, etc.
sections.raw_text:
159. Power of Magistrate to furnish written instructions, etc.—(1) Where the Magistrate directs a
local investigation by any person under section 158, the Magistrate may—
        (a) furnish such person with such written instructions as may seem necessary for his guidance;
        (b) declare by whom the whole or any part of the necessary expenses of the local investigation shall
    be paid.
    (2) The report of such person may be read as evidence in the case.
    (3) Where the Magistrate summons and examines an expert under section 158, the Magistrate may
direct by whom the costs of such summoning and examination shall be paid.

breakdown.plain_summary: This fills in the operational details of the local-investigation and expert-examination powers granted by section 158. When the Magistrate sends someone to conduct a local investigation, he can hand that person written instructions on exactly what to look into and how, and can also decide who bears the expense of the investigation. Once the investigator reports back, that report itself can be used as evidence in the case — the investigator doesn't necessarily need to be separately examined as a witness for the report to count. Similarly, when an expert is summoned and examined under section 158, the Magistrate can direct who pays the costs of bringing in that expert.
essential_elements: The Magistrate may furnish the local investigator with written instructions for guidance
The Magistrate may declare who bears the expenses (in whole or part) of the local investigation
The investigator's report may be read as evidence in the case
For an expert summoned under section 158, the Magistrate may direct who bears the costs of summoning and examining the expert
exceptions_and_qualifications: Allowing the report to be 'read as evidence' is a practical evidentiary shortcut for this summary jurisdiction — it does not by itself preclude a party from cross-examining the investigator if the Magistrate considers that necessary for fairness
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat section 159 as the logistics companion to section 158: 158 grants the power to investigate or consult an expert, and 159 answers the two questions that immediately follow — who pays, and how is the resulting material actually used as evidence.

sections.title: Procedure on order being made absolute and consequences of disobedience
sections.raw_text:
160. Procedure on order being made absolute and consequences of disobedience.—(1) When an
order has been made absolute under section 155 or section 157, the Magistrate shall give notice of the same
to the person against whom the order was made, and shall further require him to perform the act directed
by the order within the time to be fixed in the notice, and inform him that, in case of disobedience, he shall
be liable to the penalty provided by section 223 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
    (2) If such act is not performed within the time fixed, the Magistrate may cause it to be performed, and
may recover the costs of performing it, either by the sale of any building, goods or other property removed
by his order, or by the distress and sale of any other movable property of such person within or without
such Magistrate's local jurisdiction, and if such other property is without such jurisdiction, the order shall
authorise its attachment and sale when endorsed by the Magistrate within whose local jurisdiction the
property to be attached is found.
    (3) No suit shall lie in respect of anything done in good faith under this section.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is where an absolute order (made under either section 155's default route or section 157's contested-hearing route) actually gets executed. The Magistrate first gives formal notice to the person, fixing a fresh deadline to comply and warning them explicitly that disobedience means liability under BNS section 223. If the person still doesn't act within that time, the Magistrate doesn't have to keep waiting — he can get the act done himself (or through someone else) and recover the cost from the defaulter, either by selling property that was removed under the order, or by seizing and selling ('distress and sale') any other movable property belonging to that person, even property located outside the Magistrate's own jurisdiction (in which case a Magistrate with jurisdiction over that property's location must endorse the order for it to be executed there). Finally, sub-section (3) protects the Magistrate and anyone acting under his authority: no civil suit can be brought over anything done in good faith under this section.
essential_elements: Applies once an order has been made absolute under section 155 (default) or section 157 (contested hearing)
The Magistrate must give notice to the person, fixing a time to perform the directed act, and warning of liability under BNS section 223 for disobedience
If the act is not performed in time, the Magistrate may have it performed and recover costs by selling removed property or by distress and sale of the person's other movable property
Distress and sale can reach property outside the Magistrate's own jurisdiction, via endorsement by the Magistrate having jurisdiction over that property's location
No suit lies for anything done in good faith under this section
exceptions_and_qualifications: The notice-and-fresh-deadline step in sub-section (1) is a mandatory precondition before the Magistrate can step in and execute the order himself under sub-section (2)
The good-faith bar to suit in sub-section (3) does not protect acts done in bad faith or with gross irregularity
breakdown.how_to_read: This section is the enforcement backbone that gives the entire Section 152-158 scheme real teeth: without it, an 'absolute' order would just be a paper declaration. The distress-and-sale mechanism with cross-jurisdictional endorsement mirrors how fines and other monetary orders are typically enforced elsewhere in criminal procedure.

sections.title: Injunction pending inquiry
sections.raw_text:
161. Injunction pending inquiry.—(1) If a Magistrate making an order under section 152 considers
that immediate measures should be taken to prevent imminent danger or injury of a serious kind to the
public, he may issue such an injunction to the person against whom the order was made, as is required to
obviate or prevent such danger or injury pending the determination of the matter.
    (2) In default of such person forthwith obeying such injunction, the Magistrate may himself use, or
cause to be used, such means as he thinks fit to obviate such danger or to prevent such injury.
    (3) No suit shall lie in respect of anything done in good faith by a Magistrate under this section.

breakdown.plain_summary: This gives the Magistrate an emergency stopgap power that operates while the show-cause process under sections 154-157 is still playing out. If, at the very time he's making the section 152 order, the Magistrate sees that there's an imminent risk of serious danger or injury to the public — the kind of situation that can't wait for the full inquiry to finish — he can issue an injunction directly ordering the person to do whatever is necessary to avert that immediate danger, right away. If the person doesn't comply with the injunction immediately, the Magistrate himself can take direct action (or arrange for someone else to) to avert the danger or prevent the injury. As with section 160, anything done in good faith here is immune from civil suit.
essential_elements: Available only where the Magistrate, at the time of making a section 152 order, considers immediate measures necessary to prevent imminent danger or serious injury to the public
The injunction is issued to the person against whom the underlying order was made, requiring whatever action is needed to obviate or prevent the danger, pending final determination
If the person does not forthwith obey the injunction, the Magistrate may personally take, or arrange, whatever means he considers fit to avert the danger
No suit lies for anything done in good faith by the Magistrate under this section
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is an interim, provisional power tied to imminence and seriousness of risk — it is not a substitute for the underlying section 152-157 process, only a bridge across the time it takes to complete that process
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 161 functions like an interim injunction in civil practice, transplanted into the summary criminal-procedure nuisance scheme — it lets the Magistrate act instantly on genuine emergencies without waiting for the show-cause hearing to run its course, while the underlying dispute is still being determined under sections 152-157.

sections.title: Magistrate may prohibit repetition or continuance of public nuisance
sections.raw_text:
162. Magistrate may prohibit repetition or Continuance of public nuisance.—A District Magistrate
or Sub-divisional Magistrate, or any other Executive Magistrate or Deputy Commissioner of Police
empowered by the State Government or the District Magistrate in this behalf, may order any person not to
repeat or continue a public nuisance, as defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, or any special or
local law.
key_terms: public nuisance as defined in BNS

breakdown.plain_summary: This closes out Part B (Public Nuisances) with a simple, forward-looking prohibition power, distinct from the removal-focused machinery of sections 152-161. A District Magistrate, Sub-divisional Magistrate, other empowered Executive Magistrate, or an empowered Deputy Commissioner of Police can directly order a person not to repeat or continue committing a public nuisance — where 'public nuisance' takes its meaning from the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (the substantive criminal code) or from any applicable special or local law, rather than being separately defined here.
essential_elements: Empowered officers: District Magistrate, Sub-divisional Magistrate, another Executive Magistrate empowered by the State Government or District Magistrate, or a Deputy Commissioner of Police similarly empowered
The order simply prohibits a person from repeating or continuing a public nuisance
'Public nuisance' is defined by reference to the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, or any special or local law — not autonomously by this section
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a targeted, ongoing-conduct prohibition, distinct from the structured conditional-order-to-absolute-order pipeline in sections 152-158 — it doesn't require the show-cause procedure of those sections
breakdown.how_to_read: Note the inclusion of the Deputy Commissioner of Police alongside Executive Magistrates — this reflects how, in metropolitan/commissionerate policing areas, certain magisterial-style powers are extended to senior police officers. This section is a good quick-reference tool distinct from the more elaborate machinery preceding it.

sections.title: Power to issue order in urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger
sections.raw_text:
163. Power to issue order in urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger.— (1) In cases where,
in the opinion of a District Magistrate, a Sub-divisional Magistrate or any other Executive Magistrate
specially empowered by the State Government in this behalf, there is sufficient ground for proceeding under
this section and immediate prevention or speedy remedy is desirable, such Magistrate may, by a written
order stating the material facts of the case and served in the manner provided by section 153, direct any
person to abstain from a certain act or to take certain order with respect to certain property in his possession
or under his management, if such Magistrate considers that such direction is likely to prevent, or tends to
prevent, obstruction, annoyance or injury to any person lawfully employed, or danger to human life, health
or safety or a disturbance of the public tranquillity, or a riot, or an affray.
    (2) An order under this section may, in cases of emergency or in cases where the circumstances do not
admit of the serving in due time of a notice upon the person against whom the order is directed, be passed
ex parte.
    (3) An order under this section may be directed to a particular individual, or to persons residing in a
particular place or area, or to the public generally when frequenting or visiting a particular place or area.
    (4) No order under this section shall remain in force for more than two months from the making thereof:
     Provided that if the State Government considers it necessary so to do for preventing danger to human
life, health or safety or for preventing a riot or any affray, it may, by notification, direct that an order made
by a Magistrate under this section shall remain in force for such further period not exceeding six months
from the date on which the order made by the Magistrate would have, but for such order, expired, as it may
specify in the said notification.
    (5) Any Magistrate may, either on his own motion or on the application of any person aggrieved, rescind
or alter any order made under this section by himself or any Magistrate subordinate to him or by his
predecessor-in-office.
    (6) The State Government may, either on its own motion or on the application of any person aggrieved,
rescind or alter any order made by it under the proviso to sub-section (4).
    (7) Where an application under sub-section (5) or sub-section (6) is received, the Magistrate, or the
State Government, as the case may be, shall afford to the applicant an early opportunity of appearing before
him or it, either in person or by an advocate and showing cause against the order; and if the Magistrate or
the State Government, as the case may be, rejects the application wholly or in part, he or it shall record in
writing the reasons for so doing.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the famous emergency-order power (the BNSS's version of the old CrPC Section 144, widely used for prohibitory orders, curfews, and crowd-control directions) — opening Part C. When a District Magistrate, Sub-divisional Magistrate, or specially-empowered Executive Magistrate judges that there are sufficient grounds and the situation genuinely calls for immediate prevention or a speedy remedy, he can pass a written order — stating the material facts and served the same way as a Section 152 order — directing a specific person to abstain from an act, or to take some specified action regarding property in their possession or control, if that direction is likely to prevent obstruction, annoyance, or injury to lawfully-employed people, danger to human life/health/safety, disturbance of public tranquillity, a riot, or an affray. Because speed is the whole point, the order can be passed ex parte when the emergency doesn't allow time for advance notice. It can target one specific individual, people in a specific area, or the public generally when they're in a specific place. Such orders automatically expire after two months, though the State Government can extend that by notification for up to six more months if genuinely necessary to prevent danger to life/health/safety or a riot/affray. Any order (Magistrate's or State Government's) can be reconsidered — rescinded or altered — either on the deciding authority's own motion or on an aggrieved person's application, and if such an application is received, the person must be given an early opportunity to be heard, with any rejection recorded in writing with reasons.
essential_elements: Empowered authorities: District Magistrate, Sub-divisional Magistrate, or a specially-empowered Executive Magistrate
Requires the Magistrate's opinion that there are sufficient grounds and that immediate prevention or speedy remedy is desirable
The order must be in writing, state material facts, and be served as provided in section 153
It can direct a person to abstain from an act or to take a specified action regarding property in their possession/management
Justifying harms: obstruction/annoyance/injury to lawfully employed persons, danger to human life/health/safety, disturbance of public tranquillity, riot, or affray
Can be passed ex parte in emergencies or where timely notice isn't feasible
Can target a named individual, persons in a defined area, or the public generally frequenting a defined place
Maximum duration is two months from the date of making, extendable by State Government notification up to a further six months, only for danger to life/health/safety or to prevent a riot/affray
Any Magistrate (self, subordinate, or predecessor's order) or the State Government (for its own extension order) can rescind or alter such an order, on own motion or aggrieved person's application
Any application to rescind/alter must be given an early hearing opportunity, and rejection (wholly or in part) must be recorded in writing with reasons
exceptions_and_qualifications: The two-month default cap is a hard ceiling absent the specific State Government extension mechanism — a Magistrate cannot unilaterally extend his own order beyond two months

The extension proviso is narrower than the base power: it is available only for danger to life/health/safety or to prevent a riot/affray, not for the full range of harms (e.g., mere obstruction/annoyance) that justify the original order
Ex parte orders remain subject to the rescind-or-alter safeguard in sub-sections (5)-(7), which is the built-in due-process check against arbitrary or excessive urgent orders
breakdown.how_to_read: This is one of the most practically significant provisions in the whole Chapter — the modern-day successor to the classic 'Section 144 order' used for prohibitory/curfew directions, ranging from individual restraining directions to area-wide crowd-control orders. Always check the duration clock (2 months, extendable to a further 6 via State Government notification) and the mandatory review/hearing safeguard in sub-sections (5)-(7) when assessing whether such an order remains valid or has been properly challenged.

sections.title: Procedure where dispute concerning land or water is likely to cause breach of peace
sections.raw_text:
164. Procedure where dispute concerning land or water is likely to cause breach of
peace.—(1) Whenever an Executive Magistrate is satisfied from a report of a police officer or upon other
information that a dispute likely to cause a breach of the peace exists concerning any land or water or the
boundaries thereof, within his local jurisdiction, he shall make an order in writing, stating the grounds of
his being so satisfied, and requiring the parties concerned in such dispute to attend his Court in person or
by an advocate on a specified date and time, and to put in written statements of their respective claims as
respects the fact of actual possession of the subject of dispute.
    (2) For the purposes of this section, the expression "land or water" includes buildings, markets,
fisheries, crops or other produce of land, and the rents or profits of any such property.
    (3) A copy of the order shall be served in the manner provided by this Sanhita for the service of
summons upon such person or persons as the Magistrate may direct, and at least one copy shall be published
by being affixed to some conspicuous place at or near the subject of dispute.
    (4) The Magistrate shall, without reference to the merits or the claims of any of the parties to a right to
possess the subject of dispute, peruse the statements so put in, hear the parties, receive all such evidence as
may be produced by them, take such further evidence, if any, as he thinks necessary, and, if possible, decide
whether any and which of the parties was, at the date of the order made by him under sub-section (1), in
possession of the subject of dispute:
    Provided that if it appears to the Magistrate that any party has been forcibly and wrongfully
dispossessed within two months next before the date on which the report of a police officer or other
information was received by the Magistrate, or after that date and before the date of his order under
sub-section (1), he may treat the party so dispossessed as if that party had been in possession on the date of
his order under sub-section (1).
    (5) Nothing in this section shall preclude any party so required to attend, or any other person interested,
from showing that no such dispute as aforesaid exists or has existed; and in such case the Magistrate shall
cancel his said order, and all further proceedings thereon shall be stayed, but, subject to such cancellation,
the order of the Magistrate under sub-section (1) shall be final.
    (6) (a) If the Magistrate decides that one of the parties was, or should under the proviso to
sub-section (4) be treated as being, in such possession of the said subject of dispute, he shall issue an order
declaring such party to be entitled to possession thereof until evicted therefrom in due course of law, and
forbidding all disturbance of such possession until such eviction; and when he proceeds under the proviso
to sub-section (4), may restore to possession the party forcibly and wrongfully dispossessed;
    (b) the order made under this sub-section shall be served and published in the manner laid down in
sub-section (3).
    (7) When any party to any such proceeding dies, the Magistrate may cause the legal representative of
the deceased party to be made a party to the proceeding and shall thereupon continue the inquiry, and if any
question arises as to who the legal representative of a deceased party for the purposes of such proceeding
is, all persons claiming to be representatives of the deceased party shall be made parties thereto.
     (8) If the Magistrate is of opinion that any crop or other produce of the property, the subject of dispute
in a proceeding under this section pending before him, is subject to speedy and natural decay, he may make
an order for the proper custody or sale of such property, and, upon the completion of the inquiry, shall make
such order for the disposal of such property, or the sale-proceeds thereof, as he thinks fit.
    (9) The Magistrate may, if he thinks fit, at any stage of the proceedings under this section, on the
application of either party, issue a summons to any witness directing him to attend or to produce any
document or thing.
   (10) Nothing in this section shall be deemed to be in derogation of powers of the Magistrate to proceed
under section 126.

breakdown.plain_summary: This opens Part D (Disputes as to Immovable Property) — a distinctive summary mechanism where criminal courts step into what looks like a civil possession dispute, purely to prevent violence. When an Executive Magistrate is satisfied that a land-or-water dispute (which broadly includes buildings, markets, fisheries, and crops/produce, plus rents/profits from such property) risks causing a breach of the peace, he orders the parties to appear and file written statements about who is actually in possession — deliberately without going into who has the better legal right to possess it. After hearing evidence, he decides who was in actual possession as of the date of his initial order, with a special two-month look-back rule: if someone was forcibly and wrongfully thrown out of possession shortly before or during the proceedings, the Magistrate can treat them as if they were still in possession. Either party can short-circuit the whole thing by showing no real dispute exists, in which case the order is cancelled. Otherwise, the Magistrate declares the person found in possession entitled to remain until evicted through proper legal process, and forbids any disturbance of that possession in the meantime. The section also handles practical continuity — substituting a deceased party's legal representative, and ordering the sale or safekeeping of perishable produce caught up in the dispute — plus preserves the Magistrate's separate power to act under section 126 (security for good behaviour/keeping the peace) if that's also warranted.
essential_elements: Triggered when an Executive Magistrate is satisfied (from a police report or other information) that a land/water dispute within his jurisdiction risks a breach of the peace
'Land or water' is defined broadly to include buildings, markets, fisheries, crops/produce, and rents/profits of such property
The Magistrate orders the parties to appear and file written statements on actual possession — expressly without reference to who has the better legal title or claim
A special provision lets the Magistrate treat a party forcibly and wrongfully dispossessed shortly before or during the proceedings as if still in possession
Any party can show no genuine dispute exists, resulting in cancellation of the order and stay of further proceedings
The final order declares the party found in possession entitled to remain until evicted in due course of law, and forbids disturbance until then
Provisions exist for substituting a deceased party's legal representative, ordering safekeeping/sale of perishable disputed produce, and issuing witness summonses
This section does not derogate from the Magistrate's separate power under section 126 (security for keeping the peace)
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Magistrate's decision is confined to actual possession as of the date of the original order — it is not, and cannot be, a determination of legal title or ownership, which remains for a civil court
The order is expressly interim in nature: possession is protected 'until evicted therefrom in due course of law,' preserving the losing party's right to pursue a civil remedy
The finality stated in sub-section (5) (the order being final subject to cancellation) is finality within this summary jurisdiction only, not a bar to civil suit
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a well-known and heavily litigated provision (the BNSS successor to old CrPC section 145) precisely because possession disputes over land are common triggers for violence in India. The critical discipline for any practitioner is to keep possession and title strictly separate — this section is only ever about who was in actual possession on a specific date, as a peace-keeping measure, and it deliberately stays out of ownership questions, which is exactly why parties remain free to litigate title separately in a civil court.

sections.title: Power to attach subject of dispute and to appoint receiver
sections.raw_text:
165. Power to attach subject of dispute and to appoint receiver.— (1) If the Magistrate at any time
after making the order under sub-section (1) of section 164 considers the case to be one of emergency, or
if he decides that none of the parties was then in such possession as is referred to in section 164, or if he is
unable to satisfy himself as to which of them was then in such possession of the subject of dispute, he may
attach the subject of dispute until a competent Court has determined the rights of the parties thereto with
regard to the person entitled to the possession thereof:
    Provided that such Magistrate may withdraw the attachment at any time if he is satisfied that there is
no longer any likelihood of breach of the peace with regard to the subject of dispute.
    (2) When the Magistrate attaches the subject of dispute, he may, if no receiver in relation to such subject
of dispute has been appointed by any Civil Court, make such arrangements as he considers proper for
looking after the property or if he thinks fit, appoint a receiver thereof, who shall have, subject to the control
of the Magistrate, all the powers of a receiver appointed under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of
1908):
    Provided that in the event of a receiver being subsequently appointed in relation to the subject of dispute
by any Civil Court, the Magistrate—
         (a) shall order the receiver appointed by him to hand over the possession of the subject of dispute
    to the receiver appointed by the Civil Court and shall thereafter discharge the receiver appointed by
    him;
        (b) may make such other incidental or consequential orders as may be just.

breakdown.plain_summary: This handles the three situations where Section 164's possession-based approach breaks down: a genuine emergency, a finding that neither party was actually in possession, or the Magistrate simply being unable to determine who was in possession. In any of these cases, rather than declaring a winner, the Magistrate can freeze the situation entirely by attaching the disputed property until a competent civil court finally determines the parties' rights — though he can lift the attachment early if he becomes satisfied there's no longer any real risk of a breach of the peace. While the property is attached, the Magistrate looks after it either through whatever arrangement he considers proper, or by appointing a receiver with all the powers a receiver has under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 — but subject to the Magistrate's own control. And if a civil court later appoints its own receiver for the same property, the Magistrate's receiver has to hand over possession to the civil court's receiver and is then discharged, with the Magistrate free to pass whatever incidental orders are needed to make that handover work smoothly.
essential_elements: Applies where the case is an emergency, or the Magistrate finds neither party was in possession under section 164, or he cannot determine who was
The Magistrate may attach the subject of dispute until a competent Court determines the parties' rights to possession
Attachment may be withdrawn at any time if the Magistrate is satisfied breach-of-peace risk no longer exists
The Magistrate may make his own custodial arrangements, or appoint a receiver with the full powers of a CPC receiver, subject to his control — but only if no Civil Court has already appointed one

If a Civil Court subsequently appoints its own receiver, the Magistrate's receiver must hand over possession and be discharged, with the Magistrate empowered to pass just incidental/consequential orders
exceptions_and_qualifications: This power is a fallback triggered by the failure or unsuitability of the ordinary possession-determination route in section 164 — it is not a routine first option
The Magistrate's receiver is always subordinate in priority to a Civil Court's receiver over the same property, reflecting that final adjudication belongs to the civil forum
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 165 is the safety valve for the hardest possession disputes — genuine deadlocks where the summary criminal process can't confidently identify a possessor. Attachment plus receivership keeps the property intact and neutral while the real contest over rights is fought out in civil court, which is exactly where this Part always intends title disputes to ultimately be resolved.

sections.title: Dispute concerning right of use of land or water
sections.raw_text:
166. Dispute concerning right of use of land or water.— (1) Whenever an Executive Magistrate is
satisfied from the report of a police officer or upon other information, that a dispute likely to cause a breach
of the peace exists regarding any alleged right of user of any land or water within his local jurisdiction,
whether such right be claimed as an easement or otherwise, he shall make an order in writing, stating the
grounds of his being so satisfied and requiring the parties concerned in such dispute to attend his Court in
person or by an advocate on a specified date and time and to put in written statements of their respective
claims.
    Explanation.—For the purposes of this sub-section, the expression "land or water" has the meaning
given to it in sub-section (2) of section 164.
    (2) The Magistrate shall peruse the statements so put in, hear the parties, receive all such evidence as
may be produced by them respectively, consider the effect of such evidence, take such further evidence, if
any, as he thinks necessary and, if possible, decide whether such right exists; and the provisions of
section 164 shall, so far as may be, apply in the case of such inquiry.
    (3) If it appears to such Magistrate that such rights exist, he may make an order prohibiting any
interference with the exercise of such right, including, in a proper case, an order for the removal of any
obstruction in the exercise of any such right:
     Provided that no such order shall be made where the right is exercisable at all times of the year, unless
such right has been exercised within three months next before the receipt under sub-section (1) of the report
of a police officer or other information leading to the institution of the inquiry, or where the right is
exercisable only at particular seasons or on particular occasions, unless the right has been exercised during
the last of such seasons or on the last of such occasions before such receipt.
    (4) When in any proceedings commenced under sub-section (1) of section 164 the Magistrate finds that
the dispute is as regards an alleged right of user of land or water, he may, after recording his reasons,
continue with the proceedings as if they had been commenced under sub-section (1), and when in any
proceedings commenced under sub-section (1) the Magistrate finds that the dispute should be dealt with
under section 164, he may, after recording his reasons, continue with the proceedings as if they had been
commenced under sub-section (1) of section 164.

breakdown.plain_summary: This closes Chapter XI by extending the same breach-of-peace logic from Section 164 (disputes over possession) to a related but distinct problem: disputes over a right to use land or water — such as a right of way, a right to draw water, or any other easement-type right — rather than over possession itself. The procedure largely mirrors section 164: the Magistrate orders the parties to appear and file statements, then hears evidence and decides, so far as possible, whether the claimed right actually exists, applying section 164's procedural provisions to the extent they fit. If satisfied the right exists, the Magistrate can prohibit interference with it, including ordering removal of any obstruction — but only if the right has actually been recently exercised: for a right usable year-round, it must have been exercised within the three months before the police report/information that triggered the inquiry; for a seasonal or occasional right, it must have been exercised during the last such season or occasion. Finally, sub-section (4) provides a practical safety net: if a Magistrate realizes midway through a Section 164 possession proceeding that it's really a Section 166 usage-right dispute (or vice versa), he can simply continue the same proceeding under the correct section instead of starting over, as long as he records his reasons for the recharacterisation.
essential_elements: Triggered when an Executive Magistrate is satisfied a dispute over an alleged right of use (easement or otherwise) of land or water risks a breach of the peace
'Land or water' carries the same broad meaning defined in section 164(2)
Procedure mirrors section 164: written order, appearance, written statements, evidence, and a decision on whether the right exists, applying section 164's provisions so far as they apply
If the right is found to exist, the Magistrate may prohibit interference with it, including ordering removal of an obstruction

A recency-of-exercise proviso gates this remedy: a year-round right must have been exercised within 3 months before the triggering report/information; a seasonal/occasional right must have been exercised during the most recent relevant season/occasion
Proceedings mistakenly started under section 164 or section 166 can be continued under the correct section instead of being restarted, provided the Magistrate records reasons
exceptions_and_qualifications: As with section 164, this section decides only whether the alleged right exists for peace-keeping purposes at this summary stage — it does not conclusively adjudicate the right in the way a civil court's decree would
The recency proviso is a hard gate on the remedy (prohibiting interference/ordering removal), not on the underlying existence-of-right finding itself
breakdown.how_to_read: Read section 166 as section 164's sibling provision — same breach-of-peace trigger and broadly the same summary procedure, just aimed at use-rights (easements) rather than possession. The recency proviso is the feature to watch closely in practice: a long-dormant right, even if genuine, may not qualify for this summary protective remedy if it hasn't actually been exercised within the relevant recent window. The cross-recharacterisation safety valve in sub-section (4) is a useful practical point — it prevents needless procedural restarts when the two sections' subject matter is initially misidentified.

sections.title: Local inquiry
sections.raw_text:
167. Local inquiry.—(1) Whenever a local inquiry is necessary for the purposes of section 164, section
165 or section 166, a District Magistrate or Sub-divisional Magistrate may depute any Magistrate
subordinate to him to make the inquiry, and may furnish him with such written instructions as may seem
necessary for his guidance, and may declare by whom the whole or any part of the necessary expenses of
the inquiry shall be paid.
    (2) The report of the person so deputed may be read as evidence in the case.
    (3) When any costs have been incurred by any party to a proceeding under section 164, section 165 or
section 166, the Magistrate passing a decision may direct by whom such costs shall be paid, whether by
such party or by any other party to the proceeding, and whether in whole or in part or proportion and such
costs may include any expenses incurred in respect of witnesses and of advocates' fees, which the Court
may consider reasonable.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section closes out Chapter XI by giving the District Magistrate or Sub-divisional Magistrate a practical tool for the immovable-property dispute provisions (sections 164, 165, and 166): rather than conducting every factual on-site inquiry personally, he can depute a subordinate Magistrate to go and make the local inquiry, giving that Magistrate written instructions on what to look into and deciding who pays for it. Whatever that deputed Magistrate reports back can be used as evidence in the case, without needing a separate examination. Separately, once a decision is reached in any section 164/165/166 proceeding, the deciding Magistrate can allocate the costs of the proceeding between the parties as he sees fit — including witness expenses and reasonable advocates' fees — rather than each party automatically bearing its own.
essential_elements: Applies specifically to inquiries needed for the purposes of sections 164, 165, or 166 (disputes over possession, attachment/receivership, and use-rights)
The District Magistrate or Sub-divisional Magistrate may depute a subordinate Magistrate, with written instructions, to conduct the local inquiry
The deputing Magistrate may also decide who pays the expenses of that inquiry
The deputed Magistrate's report may be read as evidence in the case
The Magistrate deciding the underlying section 164/165/166 proceeding may allocate the costs of the proceeding among the parties, including witness expenses and reasonable advocates' fees
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a delegation-and-cost-allocation tool specific to the land/water dispute provisions immediately preceding it — it does not create a freestanding general inquiry power
breakdown.how_to_read: Pair this closely with sections 164-166: it is the practical machinery (delegation of fact-finding, and allocation of costs) that makes those substantive dispute-resolution provisions workable in practice, particularly in busy districts where the District/Sub-divisional Magistrate cannot personally visit every disputed site.

sections.title: Police to prevent cognizable offences
sections.raw_text:
168. Police to prevent cognizable offences.—Every police officer may interpose for the purpose of
preventing, and shall, to the best of his ability, prevent, the commission of any cognizable offence.

breakdown.plain_summary: This opens Chapter XII, which is about stopping crime before it happens rather than investigating it afterward. It states a police officer's general duty in the plainest possible terms: every police officer may step in to prevent a cognizable offence, and — this part is mandatory, not discretionary — must, to the best of his ability, actually prevent it from being committed.
essential_elements: Applies to every police officer, not just officers in charge of a station
The power to interpose (step in) to prevent a cognizable offence is permissive ('may')
The duty to actually prevent the offence, to the best of the officer's ability, is mandatory ('shall')
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a general foundational duty; the following sections (169-172) supply the specific tools — communication of information, preventive arrest, protection of public property, and enforcement of lawful directions — through which this duty is carried out
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat section 168 as the chapter's mission statement, with sections 169-172 as the concrete mechanisms that flesh out how a police officer is expected to discharge this preventive duty in practice.

sections.title: Information of design to commit cognizable offences
sections.raw_text:
169. Information of design to commit cognizable offences.—Every police officer receiving
information of a design to commit any cognizable offence shall communicate such information to the police
officer to whom he is subordinate, and to any other officer whose duty it is to prevent or take cognizance
of the commission of any such offence.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is a mandatory information-relay duty. If a police officer learns that someone is planning ('designing') to commit a cognizable offence, he cannot just sit on that information — he must pass it up to his superior officer, and also to any other officer whose job includes preventing or taking cognizance of that kind of offence, so that preventive action can actually be coordinated and taken.
essential_elements: Triggered whenever a police officer receives information of a design (plan/intention) to commit a cognizable offence
He must communicate that information to the officer to whom he is subordinate
He must also communicate it to any other officer whose duty is to prevent or take cognizance of such an offence
exceptions_and_qualifications: The duty is to communicate the information, not necessarily to personally investigate or arrest — the arrest power for such situations is separately supplied by section 170
breakdown.how_to_read: Read together with section 170: section 169 ensures information about a planned offence reaches the officers positioned to act on it, while section 170 supplies the actual power to arrest the would-be offender pre-emptively.

sections.title: Arrest to prevent commission of cognizable offences
sections.raw_text:
170. Arrest to prevent commission of cognizable offences.— (1) A police officer knowing of a design
to commit any cognizable offence may arrest, without orders from a Magistrate and without a warrant, the
person so designing, if it appears to such officer that the commission of the offence cannot be otherwise
prevented.
    (2) No person arrested under sub-section (1) shall be detained in custody for a period exceeding
twenty-four hours from the time of his arrest unless his further detention is required or authorised under
any other provisions of this Sanhita or of any other law for the time being in force.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the sharpest tool in the preventive-action chapter: a genuinely pre-emptive arrest power, used before any offence has actually been committed. If a police officer knows someone is planning to commit a cognizable offence, he can arrest that person immediately, with no Magistrate's order and no warrant — but only if it appears to him that arrest is truly necessary because the offence cannot be prevented any other way. Because this is such an exceptional power (arresting someone for something they haven't yet done), it comes with a strict clock: the person cannot be held in custody for more than 24 hours from arrest, unless some other provision of this Sanhita or another law separately authorises further detention.
essential_elements: The officer must actually know of a design to commit a cognizable offence — mere suspicion or rumour would not meet this
Arrest may be made without a Magistrate's order and without a warrant
The necessity threshold: it must appear to the officer that the offence cannot otherwise be prevented
Detention is capped at 24 hours from the time of arrest, unless further detention is required or authorised under another provision of this Sanhita or other law
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a last-resort power — the officer must reasonably conclude that no less intrusive measure (like the information-communication duty in section 169, or a warning) would prevent the offence

The 24-hour cap mirrors the constitutional and general arrest-procedure safeguard against prolonged detention without judicial oversight, and is not automatically extendable — it needs a separate legal basis to continue detention
breakdown.how_to_read: This is one of the most powerful and most scrutinised provisions in the preventive scheme precisely because it authorises arrest before any crime has occurred. Practitioners challenging such an arrest should focus on whether the officer genuinely 'knew' of a design (versus vague suspicion), whether prevention was truly impossible by lesser means, and whether the 24-hour custody limit was honoured.

sections.title: Prevention of injury to public property
sections.raw_text:
171. Prevention of injury to public property.—A police officer may of his own authority interpose
to prevent any injury attempted to be committed in his view to any public property, movable or immovable,
or the removal or injury of any public landmark, buoy or other mark used for navigation.

breakdown.plain_summary: This gives a police officer independent authority to physically intervene, on his own initiative, whenever he personally witnesses an attempt to damage public property — whether movable or immovable — or to remove or damage a public landmark, buoy, or other navigational marker.
essential_elements: The officer must witness the injury being attempted 'in his view' — this is not a power to act on secondhand reports
Covers injury to public property, whether movable or immovable
Also covers removal or injury of a public landmark, buoy, or other navigation mark
The officer acts on his own authority, without needing prior orders
exceptions_and_qualifications: The 'in his view' requirement narrows this to real-time, witnessed attempts — it is not a general enforcement power against property damage discovered after the fact
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a narrow, specific-purpose preventive power distinct from the broader cognizable-offence prevention duty in section 168 — it specifically protects public infrastructure and navigational aids, and is triggered only by direct, contemporaneous observation.

sections.title: Persons bound to conform to lawful directions of police
sections.raw_text:
172. Persons bound to conform to lawful directions of police.— (1) All persons shall be bound to
conform to the lawful directions of a police officer given in fulfilment of any of his duty under this Chapter.
    (2) A police officer may detain or remove any person resisting, refusing, ignoring or disregarding to
conform to any direction given by him under sub-section (1) and may either take such person before a
Magistrate or, in petty cases, release him as soon as possible within a period of twenty-four hours.

breakdown.plain_summary: This closes Chapter XII by giving legal force to the whole preventive scheme: every person is legally bound to follow the lawful directions a police officer gives while carrying out any of the duties described in this Chapter (sections 168-171). If someone resists, refuses, ignores, or disregards such a direction, the officer can detain or physically remove that person, and then either produce them before a Magistrate, or — for minor, petty matters — simply release them as soon as possible, within a maximum of 24 hours.
essential_elements: The obligation to conform applies to all persons, but only to directions given in fulfilment of a duty under this Chapter (sections 168-171)
The direction must be lawful — an unlawful or ultra vires direction does not trigger the obligation
On resistance, refusal, or disregard, the officer may detain or remove the person
The detained person must either be taken before a Magistrate, or, in petty cases, released as soon as possible and in any case within 24 hours
exceptions_and_qualifications: The 'lawful' qualifier is the key safeguard — only directions genuinely given in fulfilment of a Chapter XII duty carry this binding force; directions beyond that scope are not enforceable under this section
The 24-hour outer limit for petty-case release mirrors the general detention-without-magisterial-oversight safeguard seen elsewhere in the Sanhita (e.g., section 170)
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 172 is the enforcement backbone for the entire preventive-action chapter — without it, the preceding sections' preventive directions would have no teeth. Always check two things when this section is invoked: was the underlying direction genuinely 'lawful' and within the scope of Chapter XII's duties, and was the detained person's custody kept within the 24-hour petty-case limit or properly escalated before a Magistrate.

sections.title: Information in cognizable cases
sections.raw_text:
173. Information in cognizable cases.—(1) Every information relating to the commission of a
cognizable offence, irrespective of the area where the offence is committed, may be given orally or by
electronic communication to an officer in charge of a police station, and if given—
        (i) orally, it shall be reduced to writing by him or under his direction, and be read over to the
    informant; and every such information, whether given in writing or reduced to writing as aforesaid,
    shall be signed by the person giving it;
       (ii) by electronic communication, it shall be taken on record by him on being signed within three
    days by the person giving it,
and the substance thereof shall be entered in a book to be kept by such officer in such form as the State
Government may by rules prescribe in this behalf:
    Provided that if the information is given by the woman against whom an offence under section 64,
section 65, section 66, section 67, section 68, section 69, section 70, section 71, section 74, section 75,
section 76, section 77, section 78, section 79 or section 124 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 is alleged
to have been committed or attempted, then such information shall be recorded, by a woman police officer
or any woman officer:
    Provided further that—
        (a) in the event that the person against whom an offence under section 64, section 65, section 66,
    section 67, section 68, section 69, section 70, section 71, section 74, section 75, section 76, section 77,
    section 78, section 79 or section 124 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 is alleged to have been
    committed or attempted, is temporarily or permanently mentally or physically disabled, then such
    information shall be recorded by a police officer, at the residence of the person seeking to report such
    offence or at a convenient place of such person's choice, in the presence of an interpreter or a special
    educator, as the case may be;
        (b) the recording of such information shall be videographed;
        (c) the police officer shall get the statement of the person recorded by a Magistrate under clause (a)
    of sub-section (6) of section 183 as soon as possible.
     (2) A copy of the information as recorded under sub-section (1) shall be given forthwith, free of cost,
to the informant or the victim.
    (3) Without prejudice to the provisions contained in section 175, on receipt of information relating to
the commission of any cognizable offence, which is made punishable for three years or more but less than
seven years, the officer in charge of the police station may with the prior permission from an officer not
below the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police, considering the nature and gravity of the offence,—
        (i) proceed to conduct preliminary enquiry to ascertain whether there exists a prima facie case for
    proceeding in the matter within a period of fourteen days; or
        (ii) proceed with investigation when there exists a prima facie case.
    (4) Any person aggrieved by a refusal on the part of an officer in charge of a police station to record
the information referred to in sub-section (1), may send the substance of such information, in writing and
by post, to the Superintendent of Police concerned who, if satisfied that such information discloses the
commission of a cognizable offence, shall either investigate the case himself or direct an investigation to
be made by any police officer subordinate to him, in the manner provided by this Sanhita, and such officer
shall have all the powers of an officer in charge of the police station in relation to that offence failing which
such aggrieved person may make an application to the Magistrate.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the FIR section — arguably the single most consequential provision in the entire criminal procedure code, because it's the trigger that starts the whole investigative machinery. Information about a cognizable offence can be given to an officer in charge of any police station, from anywhere (no territorial restriction on where it's lodged), either orally (which the officer must write down, read back to the informant, and have signed) or electronically (which must be signed within three days). It's logged in a register in the prescribed format. For a specific list of serious offences against women (spanning several sexual-offence sections of the BNS), the information must be recorded by a woman officer; and if the victim is mentally or physically disabled, extra protections kick in — recording at her residence or chosen location, with an interpreter or special educator present, videographed, with a magistrate later recording her statement under section 183(6)(a). A free copy of the recorded information must go to the informant/victim immediately. A significant BNSS innovation appears in sub-section (3): for offences punishable between 3 and 7 years, the police can, with a Deputy Superintendent of Police's prior permission, run a 14-day preliminary enquiry first to check if there's even a prima facie case, before committing to a full investigation — this is meant to filter out weak complaints before triggering the full machinery of arrest and investigation. And if an officer refuses to record information at all, the aggrieved person has an escalation path: write to the Superintendent of Police, who must investigate or direct a subordinate to, failing which the person can approach the Magistrate.
essential_elements: Information about a cognizable offence may be given orally or electronically, to any officer in charge of a police station, regardless of where the offence occurred
Oral information must be reduced to writing, read back to the informant, and signed; electronic information must be signed within three days
The substance must be entered in a register in the State-Government-prescribed form
Information about specified sexual offences against a woman must be recorded by a woman police/other officer

Special safeguards for a mentally/physically disabled victim: recording at residence/chosen place, with interpreter/special educator, videographed, followed by a magisterial statement under section 183(6)(a)
A free copy of the recorded information must be given forthwith to the informant or victim
For offences punishable with 3 to 7 years, police may, with DSP-level prior permission, conduct a 14-day preliminary enquiry to check for a prima facie case before investigating
Refusal to record information can be escalated in writing to the Superintendent of Police, and ultimately to the Magistrate if that also fails
exceptions_and_qualifications: The preliminary-enquiry route under sub-section (3) is discretionary and available only for the specific 3-to-7-year punishment band — it is not available, and not needed, for the most serious offences where the duty to register an FIR and investigate is more direct (see section 175)
The escalation mechanism in sub-section (4) does not itself compel investigation — the Superintendent must first be satisfied a cognizable offence is disclosed
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the practitioner's starting point for virtually every criminal matter — the FIR's contents, timing, and manner of recording are frequently contested in later proceedings (e.g., delay in lodging, absence of a woman officer where required, or improper handling of a preliminary enquiry). The 3-to-7-year preliminary-enquiry mechanism in sub-section (3) is a genuinely new BNSS feature worth flagging distinctly from the old CrPC position, which generally mandated immediate FIR registration.

sections.title: Information as to non-cognizable cases and investigation of such cases
sections.raw_text:
174. Information as to non-cognizable cases and investigation of such cases.—(1) When
information is given to an officer in charge of a police station of the commission within the limits of such
station of a non-cognizable offence, he shall enter or cause to be entered the substance of the information
in a book to be kept by such officer in such form as the State Government may by rules prescribe in this
behalf, and,—
        (i) refer the informant to the Magistrate;
        (ii) forward the daily diary report of all such cases fortnightly to the Magistrate.
    (2) No police officer shall investigate a non-cognizable case without the order of a Magistrate having
power to try such case or commit the case for trial.
    (3) Any police officer receiving such order may exercise the same powers in respect of the investigation
(except the power to arrest without warrant) as an officer in charge of a police station may exercise in a
cognizable case.
   (4) Where a case relates to two or more offences of which at least one is cognizable, the case shall be
deemed to be a cognizable case, notwithstanding that the other offences are non-cognizable.

breakdown.plain_summary: This mirrors section 173 but for the less serious, non-cognizable category of offence. When such information comes in, the officer logs its substance in the prescribed register, but — unlike a cognizable case — doesn't automatically start investigating. Instead, he refers the informant to the Magistrate (who has to authorize any prosecution/investigation for such offences) and periodically reports all such entries to the Magistrate via a fortnightly diary. Police cannot investigate a non-cognizable case at all without a Magistrate's order; once that order is given, the investigating officer gets all the ordinary investigative powers of an officer in charge of a station in a cognizable case, except the power to arrest without a warrant — that specific power stays off-limits even with the Magistrate's order. Finally, sub-section (4) has a practically important rule: if a single case involves multiple offences and even one of them is cognizable, the whole case is treated as cognizable, even though the other offences by themselves would be non-cognizable — this prevents artificial splitting of a case to dodge the cognizable-offence investigative machinery.
essential_elements: Applies to information about a non-cognizable offence within the police station's limits
The officer logs the substance in the prescribed register, refers the informant to the Magistrate, and forwards a fortnightly diary report of such cases
No investigation of a non-cognizable case without a Magistrate's order (from a Magistrate empowered to try or commit the case)
Once ordered, the investigating officer has the same powers as in a cognizable case, except the power to arrest without a warrant
A case involving multiple offences, at least one of which is cognizable, is deemed a cognizable case in its entirety
exceptions_and_qualifications: The no-warrantless-arrest carve-out in sub-section (3) is absolute — even Magistrate-ordered investigation of a non-cognizable case does not restore the power of arrest without warrant
Sub-section (4)'s deeming rule is an anti-evasion device, ensuring that a complainant or accused cannot manipulate the classification by isolating the non-cognizable elements of a mixed case
breakdown.how_to_read: Always classify the offence(s) involved first — cognizable vs. non-cognizable determines whether police can act on their own initiative (section 173/175) or need prior magisterial authorization (this section). The multiple-offence deeming rule in sub-section (4) is a frequent point of contention worth checking whenever a case combines charges of different severity.

sections.title: Police officer's power to investigate cognizable case
sections.raw_text:
175. Police officer's power to investigate cognizable case.—(1) Any officer in charge of a police
station may, without the order of a Magistrate, investigate any cognizable case which a Court having
jurisdiction over the local area within the limits of such station would have power to inquire into or try
under the provisions of Chapter XIV:
    Provided that considering the nature and gravity of the offence, the Superintendent of Police may
require the Deputy Superintendent of Police to investigate the case.
    (2) No proceeding of a police officer in any such case shall at any stage be called in question on the
ground that the case was one which such officer was not empowered under this section to investigate.
    (3) Any Magistrate empowered under section 210 may, after considering the application supported by
an affidavit made under sub-section (4) of section 173, and after making such inquiry as he thinks necessary
and submission made in this regard by the police officer, order such an investigation as above-mentioned.
    (4) Any Magistrate empowered under section 210, may, upon receiving a complaint against a public
servant arising in course of the discharge of his official duties, order investigation, subject to—
        (a) receiving a report containing facts and circumstances of the incident from the officer superior
    to him; and
        (b) after consideration of the assertions made by the public servant as to the situation that led to the
    incident so alleged.
key_terms: power to investigate without Magistrate's order

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the core grant of investigative authority for cognizable offences: an officer in charge of a police station can investigate a cognizable case entirely on his own initiative, with no need for prior magisterial permission, as long as it's a case the local court would have jurisdiction to try under Chapter XIV's jurisdiction rules. For serious or grave offences, the Superintendent of Police can specifically direct that a Deputy Superintendent handle the investigation instead of a lower officer. Sub-section (2) is an important immunizing rule: even if it later turns out the investigating officer technically wasn't the right one empowered to investigate that particular case, that irregularity alone can't be used to challenge the proceedings at any stage — a pure jurisdictional technicality doesn't undo the investigation. Sub-section (3) creates a Magistrate-ordered route parallel to the direct police-initiated route, triggered by the section 173(4) affidavit-based escalation mechanism. And sub-section (4) adds a distinct, extra layer of protection specifically for complaints against public servants for acts done in the discharge of official duty: before a Magistrate can order investigation of such a complaint, he must first get a report on the facts from the public servant's superior officer, and must also consider the public servant's own explanation of what happened.
essential_elements: An officer in charge of a police station may investigate a cognizable case without a Magistrate's order, provided the local court would have jurisdiction over it under Chapter XIV
The Superintendent of Police may direct that the Deputy Superintendent handle investigation of a serious/grave case
A proceeding cannot be invalidated merely because the investigating officer was not, strictly, the one empowered under this section to investigate
A section 210 Magistrate may order investigation after considering an affidavit-supported application under section 173(4) and making any inquiry he considers necessary

For a complaint against a public servant arising from official-duty conduct, a section 210 Magistrate may only order investigation after receiving a superior officer's report on the incident and considering the public servant's own assertions
exceptions_and_qualifications: Sub-section (2)'s immunity is limited to the empowerment/jurisdictional technicality of who investigated — it does not cure substantive illegalities in how the investigation was conducted

Sub-section (4)'s extra safeguards for public servants apply specifically to conduct in the discharge of official duties — they would not extend to purely private conduct by a public servant unconnected to official functions
breakdown.how_to_read: This section is the practical backbone of police-initiated investigation, and sub-section (4) is a notable BNSS-era procedural safeguard for public servants — worth flagging distinctly whenever a complaint targets a government official's conduct in office, since the ordinary section 175(1) self-starting investigative power does not straightforwardly apply without these extra checks.

sections.title: Procedure for investigation
sections.raw_text:
176. Procedure for investigation.—(1) If, from information received or otherwise, an officer in charge
of a police station has reason to suspect the commission of an offence which he is empowered under
section 175 to investigate, he shall forthwith send a report of the same to a Magistrate empowered to take
cognizance of such offence upon a police report and shall proceed in person, or shall depute one of his
subordinate officers not being below such rank as the State Government may, by general or special order,
prescribe in this behalf, to proceed, to the spot, to investigate the facts and circumstances of the case, and,
if necessary, to take measures for the discovery and arrest of the offender:
    Provided that—
        (a) when information as to the commission of any such offence is given against any person by name
    and the case is not of a serious nature, the officer in charge of a police station need not proceed in
    person or depute a subordinate officer to make an investigation on the spot;
        (b) if it appears to the officer in charge of a police station that there is no sufficient ground for
    entering on an investigation, he shall not investigate the case:
    Provided further that in relation to an offence of rape, the recording of statement of the victim shall be
conducted at the residence of the victim or in the place of her choice and as far as practicable by a woman
police officer in the presence of her parents or guardian or near relatives or social worker of the locality and
such statement may also be recorded through any audio-video electronic means including mobile phone.
