    (2) In each of the cases mentioned in clauses (a) and (b) of the first proviso to sub-section (1), the
officer in charge of the police station shall state in his report the reasons for not fully complying with the
requirements of that sub-section by him, and, forward the daily diary report fortnightly to the Magistrate
and in the case mentioned in clause (b) of the said proviso, the officer shall also forthwith notify to the
informant, if any, in such manner as may be prescribed by rules made by the State Government.
    (3) On receipt of every information relating to the commission of an offence which is made punishable
for seven years or more, the officer in charge of a police station shall, from such date, as may be notified
within a period of five years by the State Government in this regard, cause the forensic expert to visit the
crime scene to collect forensic evidence in the offence and also cause videography of the process on mobile
phone or any other electronic device:
     Provided that where forensic facility is not available in respect of any such offence, the State
Government shall, until the facility in respect of that matter is developed or made in the State, notify the
utilisation of such facility of any other State.

breakdown.plain_summary: This lays down the operational how of investigation once a cognizable case is on the books. If the officer in charge has reason to suspect an offence he's empowered to investigate under section 175, he must promptly report it to the Magistrate empowered to take cognizance on a police report, and either go personally, or send a sufficiently senior subordinate, to the spot to investigate facts and circumstances — and, if needed, to find and arrest the offender. Two practical outs exist: he doesn't have to go to the spot personally or depute someone for minor named-accused cases that aren't serious, and he must not investigate at all if there's simply no sufficient ground to do so. Either way, he has to record his reasons and keep the Magistrate informed via the fortnightly diary, and in the no-sufficient-ground scenario, must also promptly notify the informant. A special protective procedure applies for rape cases: the victim's statement must be recorded at her residence or a place of her choosing, as far as practicable by a woman officer, with supportive people present, and can be recorded via audio-video electronic means including a mobile phone. The most significant BNSS innovation here is sub-section (3): for offences punishable with 7 years or more, a forensic expert must visit the crime scene to gather forensic evidence, with the process videographed — a mandatory step being phased in by State Governments within a 5-year notification window, with an inter-State-facility-sharing fallback where local forensic capacity isn't yet available.
essential_elements: Triggered when the officer in charge has reason to suspect a section-175-investigable offence
He must report to the cognizance-taking Magistrate and proceed (personally or via an appropriately senior subordinate) to the spot to investigate and, if necessary, arrest
Exception (a): no spot investigation needed for a minor, non-serious, named-accused case
Exception (b): must not investigate where there is no sufficient ground
In either exception, reasons must be recorded, a fortnightly diary sent to the Magistrate, and (for the no-ground exception) the informant notified
Rape-case statements must be recorded at the victim's residence/chosen place, as far as practicable by a woman officer, with supportive persons present, and may use audio-video electronic means

For offences punishable with 7+ years, forensic-expert crime-scene visits become mandatory (phased in over up to 5 years by State notification), with the process videographed and inter-State facility-sharing where local forensics aren't yet available
exceptions_and_qualifications: The two provisos in sub-section (1) are narrow carve-outs from the default spot-investigation duty, each requiring recorded reasons — they are not a general discretion to skip investigation

The forensic-expert mandate in sub-section (3) is being phased in over time (up to five years) rather than taking immediate nationwide effect, and has a built-in fallback where local facilities are unavailable
breakdown.how_to_read: Sub-section (3)'s mandatory forensic-evidence-collection requirement for serious offences is one of the most talked-about BNSS reforms — expect trials for 7-year-plus offences to increasingly turn on whether this forensic visit and videography actually happened, once the relevant State notification takes effect. The rape-victim statement safeguards echo and reinforce the protective mechanisms already seen in section 173.

sections.title: Report how submitted
sections.raw_text:
177. Report how submitted.—(1) Every report sent to a Magistrate under section 176 shall, if the State
Government so directs, be submitted through such superior officer of police as the State Government, by
general or special order, appoints in that behalf.
    (2) Such superior officer may give such instructions to the officer in charge of the police station as he
thinks fit, and shall, after recording such instructions on such report, transmit the same without delay to the
Magistrate.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is a purely administrative routing provision. If the State Government wants an extra layer of police supervision, it can direct that section 176 investigation reports be routed through a designated superior officer before reaching the Magistrate. That superior officer can add whatever instructions he thinks appropriate to the investigating officer, but must record those instructions on the report itself and then forward it to the Magistrate without delay — supervision cannot become an excuse to hold up or bypass the Magistrate's oversight.
essential_elements: Applies only where the State Government has specifically directed this routing-through-a-superior-officer procedure
The designated superior officer may add instructions for the investigating officer
Those instructions must be recorded on the report itself
The report must then be transmitted to the Magistrate without delay
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is an optional, State-Government-activated layer of oversight, not a default requirement in every district
breakdown.how_to_read: A minor but useful procedural provision to be aware of in States that have activated this supervisory routing — any added instructions become part of the visible record (recorded on the report), preserving transparency even while allowing an extra layer of senior police review.

sections.title: Power to hold investigation or preliminary inquiry
sections.raw_text:
178. Power to hold investigation or preliminary inquiry.—The Magistrate, on receiving a report
under section 176, may direct an investigation, or, if he thinks fit, at once proceed, or depute any Magistrate
subordinate to him to proceed, to hold a preliminary inquiry into, or otherwise to dispose of, the case in the
manner provided in this Sanhita.

breakdown.plain_summary: This gives the Magistrate who receives the section 176 report a flexible menu of options rather than a single fixed response. He can direct the police to investigate further; or he can personally step in right away and hold a preliminary inquiry himself; or he can delegate that preliminary inquiry to a subordinate Magistrate; or he can otherwise dispose of the case following whatever procedure this Sanhita provides for the situation at hand.
essential_elements: Triggered by receipt of a section 176 report
Option one: direct an investigation
Option two: personally hold a preliminary inquiry at once
Option three: depute a subordinate Magistrate to hold the preliminary inquiry
Option four: otherwise dispose of the case in the manner this Sanhita provides
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a discretionary menu, not a mandatory sequence — the Magistrate chooses whichever path fits the case, informed by the nature and quality of the report received
breakdown.how_to_read: This closing section of the sub-batch is the magisterial counterpart to the police's investigative powers in sections 175-176 — it confirms that judicial oversight sits above the police investigation from the very outset, with the Magistrate free to test, redirect, or independently inquire into the case as he judges appropriate.

sections.title: Police officer's power to require attendance of witnesses
sections.raw_text:
179. Police officer's power to require attendance of witnesses.—(1) Any police officer making an
investigation under this Chapter may, by order in writing, require the attendance before himself of any
person being within the limits of his own or any adjoining station who, from the information given or
otherwise, appears to be acquainted with the facts and circumstances of the case; and such person shall
attend as so required:
    Provided that no male person under the age of fifteen years or above the age of sixty years or a woman
or a mentally or physically disabled person or a person with acute illness shall be required to attend at any
place other than the place in which such person resides:
    Provided further that if such person is willing to attend at the police station, such person may be
permitted so to do.
    (2) The State Government may, by rules made in this behalf, provide for the payment by the police
officer of the reasonable expenses of every person, attending under sub-section (1) at any place other than
his residence.

breakdown.plain_summary: This gives an investigating officer a compulsory power to summon witnesses — anyone within his own or a neighbouring police station's area who appears, from the information available, to know something about the case can be ordered in writing to attend before him, and that person is legally obliged to comply. But there's a significant protective carve-out: certain vulnerable categories — boys under 15, men over 60, women of any age, mentally or physically disabled persons, and people with acute illness — cannot be compelled to attend anywhere except their own place of residence; the police must go to them instead. That said, if such a protected person is themselves willing to come to the police station, they're allowed to. Sub-section (2) adds a fairness mechanism: the State Government can make rules requiring the police to pay reasonable expenses to anyone who has to attend somewhere other than their own residence.
essential_elements: Applies to any police officer conducting an investigation under this Chapter
The order requiring attendance must be in writing
It can reach any person within the investigating officer's own station or an adjoining station who appears acquainted with the facts
Protected categories — males under 15 or over 60, women, mentally/physically disabled persons, persons with acute illness — cannot be required to attend anywhere but their own residence
A protected person may still voluntarily choose to attend at the police station
The State Government may make rules for reimbursing reasonable expenses to attendees summoned away from their residence
exceptions_and_qualifications: The residence-only protection is mandatory, not discretionary for the police officer — it cannot be waived by the officer even for investigative convenience, only by the protected person's own willingness to attend elsewhere
breakdown.how_to_read: This section balances the practical necessity of compelling witness cooperation against protecting vulnerable individuals from the burden and potential intimidation of police-station attendance — always check whether a witness falls into one of the protected categories before assuming compelled police-station attendance was proper.

sections.title: Examination of witnesses by police
sections.raw_text:
180. Examination of witnesses by police.—(1) Any police officer making an investigation under this
Chapter, or any police officer not below such rank as the State Government may, by general or special
order, prescribe in this behalf, acting on the requisition of such officer, may examine orally any person
supposed to be acquainted with the facts and circumstances of the case.
    (2) Such person shall be bound to answer truly all questions relating to such case put to him by such
officer, other than questions the answers to which would have a tendency to expose him to a criminal charge
or to a penalty or forfeiture.
    (3) The police officer may reduce into writing any statement made to him in the course of an
examination under this section; and if he does so, he shall make a separate and true record of the statement
of each such person whose statement he records:
    Provided that statement made under this sub-section may also be recorded by audio-video electronic
means:
    Provided further that the statement of a woman against whom an offence under section 64, section 65,
section 66, section 67, section 68, section 69, section 70, section 71, section 74, section 75, section 76,
section 77, section 78, section 79 or section 124 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 is alleged to have
been committed or attempted, shall be recorded, by a woman police officer or any woman officer.

breakdown.plain_summary: This authorizes police to interview witnesses during investigation — the investigating officer, or an officer of sufficient rank acting on that officer's requisition, can orally examine anyone thought to know something about the case. Sub-section (2) imposes a genuine legal duty to answer truthfully, but with a crucial constitutional-flavoured exception: the person cannot be compelled to answer questions whose answers would tend to incriminate them (expose them to a criminal charge, penalty, or forfeiture) — this is the statutory embodiment of the privilege against self-incrimination at the investigation stage. If the officer chooses to write down what's said, he must keep a separate, accurate record for each individual person examined; this can also be done by audio-video electronic means. And, continuing the protective pattern seen in sections 173 and 176, the statement of a woman alleging one of the listed sexual offences against her must specifically be recorded by a woman officer.
essential_elements: Applies to the investigating officer, or another officer of a State-Government-prescribed rank acting on that officer's requisition
The examination is oral, of any person supposed to be acquainted with the case's facts and circumstances
The examinee is bound to answer truly, except questions tending to self-incriminate (criminal charge, penalty, or forfeiture)
If a statement is reduced to writing, a separate, true record must be kept for each person examined
Statements may also be recorded via audio-video electronic means
A woman's statement, where she alleges one of the specified sexual offences, must be recorded by a woman officer
exceptions_and_qualifications: The self-incrimination exception is the central safeguard of this section — it exists precisely because sub-section (1)'s examination is unsworn, informal, and conducted outside a Magistrate's presence, unlike the confession-recording process of section 183
breakdown.how_to_read: This section is the everyday workhorse of witness examination during investigation, and its statements are governed by the important use-restriction in section 181 immediately following — always read the two together, since what's said here cannot simply be treated as courtroom testimony without going through section 181's filter.

sections.title: Statements to police and use thereof
sections.raw_text:
181. Statements to police and use thereof.—(1) No statement made by any person to a police officer
in the course of an investigation under this Chapter, shall, if reduced to writing, be signed by the person
making it; nor shall any such statement or any record thereof, whether in a police diary or otherwise, or any
part of such statement or record, be used for any purpose, save as hereinafter provided, at any inquiry or
trial in respect of any offence under investigation at the time when such statement was made:
    Provided that when any witness is called for the prosecution in such inquiry or trial whose statement
has been reduced into writing as aforesaid, any part of his statement, if duly proved, may be used by the
accused, and with the permission of the Court, by the prosecution, to contradict such witness in the manner
provided by section 148 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023; and when any part of such statement
is so used, any part thereof may also be used in the re-examination of such witness, but for the purpose only
of explaining any matter referred to in his cross-examination.
    (2) Nothing in this section shall be deemed to apply to any statement falling within the provisions of
clause (a) of section 26 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023; or to affect the provisions of the proviso
to sub-section (2) of section 23 of that Adhiniyam.
    Explanation.—An omission to state a fact or circumstance in the statement referred to in
sub-section (1) may amount to contradiction if the same appears to be significant and otherwise relevant
having regard to the context in which such omission occurs and whether any omission amounts to a
contradiction in the particular context shall be a question of fact.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is a foundational evidentiary safeguard: a statement made to police during investigation (a 'section 180 statement') is not signed by the person making it, and — critically — cannot generally be used at trial as substantive evidence of what happened. Its use is confined almost entirely to one narrow purpose: contradicting the witness if they say something different in court than what they told police. The accused can always use it for this contradiction purpose; the prosecution can only do so with the court's permission. If part of the statement is used to contradict the witness, the opposing side can bring in other parts during re-examination, but only to explain the point raised in cross-examination — not to bootstrap the whole statement in as truth. Two exceptions preserve other evidentiary provisions: statements admissible under section 26(a) of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (dying declarations, generally) and the proviso to section 23(2) of that Adhiniyam remain unaffected by this restriction. Finally, the Explanation makes clear that even a significant omission — something the witness left out when talking to police but includes at trial — can itself count as a 'contradiction' for these purposes, though whether it actually does is a fact-specific question.
essential_elements: A statement to police during investigation is not signed by its maker
As a general rule, it (or any part or record of it) cannot be used at the inquiry or trial for the offence under investigation, except as this section itself permits

Exception: where the maker becomes a prosecution witness, any duly proved part may be used by the accused (freely) or by the prosecution (with court permission) to contradict that witness, per section 148 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023
Where such contradiction is used, the statement may also be used in re-examination, but only to explain matters raised in cross-examination
Dying-declaration-type statements under BSA section 26(a), and the proviso to BSA section 23(2), are unaffected by this restriction
A significant, relevant omission in the police statement may itself amount to a contradiction, as a question of fact
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is the codified rule against treating police statements as substantive trial evidence — a core protection against convictions being built on unsworn, unsigned, non-cross-examined investigative statements
The contradiction mechanism is asymmetric: the accused's use of it is unrestricted, while the prosecution needs the court's specific permission
breakdown.how_to_read: This section is central to trial cross-examination strategy — the classic move of confronting a prosecution witness with what they told the police versus what they now say in court operates through this exact mechanism. Always check whether an omission being relied on is genuinely significant enough to count as a contradiction, since that determination is fact-specific under the Explanation.

sections.title: No inducement to be offered
sections.raw_text:
182. No inducement to be offered.—(1) No police officer or other person in authority shall offer or
make, or cause to be offered or made, any such inducement, threat or promise as is mentioned in
section 22 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023.
    (2) But no police officer or other person shall prevent, by any caution or otherwise, any person from
making in the course of any investigation under this Chapter any statement which he may be disposed to
make of his own free will:
    Provided that nothing in this sub-section shall affect the provisions of sub-section (4) of section 183.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section protects the voluntariness of statements made during investigation from both directions. First, it flatly bars police officers or anyone in authority from offering inducements, threats, or promises of the kind described in section 22 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (the evidence law's rule on what makes a confession involuntary and therefore inadmissible) — this protects against coerced statements. Second, and just as importantly, it prevents the opposite problem: police cannot use cautions or other means to stop someone from freely making a statement they genuinely want to make of their own accord. The proviso preserves section 183(4)'s specific procedure for confessions before a Magistrate (which does involve a formal caution that the person isn't bound to confess) — that separate, structured warning process isn't undermined by this section's general rule against discouraging voluntary statements.
essential_elements: Prohibits police officers or persons in authority from offering inducement, threat, or promise as described in BSA section 22
Equally prohibits preventing a person from making a statement they are freely disposed to make, whether by caution or other means
The proviso preserves the distinct caution procedure specifically required under section 183(4) for Magistrate-recorded confessions
exceptions_and_qualifications: The two halves of this section work in opposite directions — sub-section (1) protects against coercion, sub-section (2) protects against improper suppression of a voluntary statement — and both serve the same underlying goal of ensuring statements genuinely reflect free will
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a compact but important safeguard sitting between the general police-examination power (section 180) and the formal confession-recording procedure (section 183) — any confession or statement's admissibility can turn on whether this section's inducement/threat/promise prohibition, or its free-will protection, was honoured.

sections.title: Recording of confessions and statements
sections.raw_text:
183. Recording of confessions and statements.—(1) Any Magistrate of the District in which the
information about commission of any offence has been registered, may, whether or not he has jurisdiction
in the case, record any confession or statement made to him in the course of an investigation under this
Chapter or under any other law for the time being in force, or at any time afterwards but before the
commencement of the inquiry or trial:
    Provided that any confession or statement made under this sub-section may also be recorded by audio-
video electronic means in the presence of the advocate of the person accused of an offence:
    Provided further that no confession shall be recorded by a police officer on whom any power of a
Magistrate has been conferred under any law for the time being in force.
    (2) The Magistrate shall, before recording any such confession, explain to the person making it that he
is not bound to make a confession and that, if he does so, it may be used as evidence against him; and the
Magistrate shall not record any such confession unless, upon questioning the person making it, he has
reason to believe that it is being made voluntarily.
    (3) If at any time before the confession is recorded, the person appearing before the Magistrate states
that he is not willing to make the confession, the Magistrate shall not authorise the detention of such person
in police custody.
    (4) Any such confession shall be recorded in the manner provided in section 316 for recording the
examination of an accused person and shall be signed by the person making the confession; and the
Magistrate shall make a memorandum at the foot of such record to the following effect:—
        "I have explained to (name) that he is not bound to make a confession and that, if he does so, any
    confession he may make may be used as evidence against him and I believe that this confession was
    voluntarily made. It was taken in my presence and hearing, and was read over to the person making it
    and admitted by him to be correct, and it contains a full and true account of the statement made by him.
                                                                                              (Signed) A. B.
                                                                                                Magistrate.".
    (5) Any statement (other than a confession) made under sub-section (1) shall be recorded in such
manner hereinafter provided for the recording of evidence as is, in the opinion of the Magistrate, best fitted
to the circumstances of the case; and the Magistrate shall have power to administer oath to the person whose
statement is so recorded.
    (6) (a) In cases punishable under section 64, section 65, section 66, section 67, section 68, section 69,
section 70, section 71, section 74, section 75, section 76, section 77, section 78, section 79 or section 124
of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the Magistrate shall record the statement of the person against whom
such offence has been committed in the manner specified in sub-section (5), as soon as the commission of
the offence is brought to the notice of the police:
    Provided that such statement shall, as far as practicable, be recorded by a woman Magistrate and in her
absence by a male Magistrate in the presence of a woman:
    Provided further that in cases relating to the offences punishable with imprisonment for ten years or
more or with imprisonment for life or with death, the Magistrate shall record the statement of the witness
brought before him by the police officer:
    Provided also that if the person making the statement is temporarily or permanently, mentally or
physically disabled, the Magistrate shall take the assistance of an interpreter or a special educator in
recording the statement:
    Provided also that if the person making the statement is temporarily or permanently, mentally or
physically disabled, the statement made by the person, with the assistance of an interpreter or a special
educator, shall be recorded through audio-video electronic means preferably by mobile phone;
    (b) a statement recorded under clause (a) of a person, who is temporarily or permanently, mentally or
physically disabled, shall be considered a statement in lieu of examination-in-chief, as specified in section
142 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 such that the maker of the statement can be cross-examined
on such statement, without the need for recording the same at the time of trial.
    (7) The Magistrate recording a confession or statement under this section shall forward it to the
Magistrate by whom the case is to be inquired into or tried.
key_terms: not bound to make a confession

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the formal, judicially-supervised counterpart to the informal police examination of section 180 — the section that governs how a confession or statement is properly recorded before a Magistrate so that it can genuinely be relied on in court. Any District Magistrate can record such a confession or statement, even without jurisdiction over the actual case, and it can be done via audio-video electronic means with the accused's advocate present. Crucially, police officers who happen to hold magisterial powers under some other law are barred from recording confessions — this must be a genuinely independent judicial function. Before recording any confession, the Magistrate must warn the person that they're not bound to confess and that anything they say can be used against them, and must question them to form a genuine belief that the confession is voluntary. If the person says at any point before confessing that they don't actually want to confess, the Magistrate cannot then send them back into police custody — a critical safeguard against confession-by-coercion-through-remand. The confession is recorded per section 316's procedure, signed by the confessor, with the Magistrate appending a specific certifying memorandum confirming the warning was given, voluntariness was believed, and the record was read back and confirmed accurate. Non-confession statements are recorded in whatever manner best suits the circumstances, with the Magistrate empowered to administer an oath. Sub-section (6) then layers on the sexual-offence-victim protections seen throughout this Chapter: for the listed offences, the victim's statement must be recorded (via the sub-section (5) method) as soon as the offence is reported, preferably by a woman Magistrate (or a male Magistrate with a woman present), with an interpreter/special educator and audio-video recording for disabled persons, and for the gravest offences (10 years to life/death), the Magistrate must record the statement of the witness brought before him. A disabled victim's such statement can even substitute for a live examination-in-chief at trial, subject to cross-examination on it. Finally, whatever confession or statement is recorded here must be forwarded to the Magistrate who will actually inquire into or try the case.
essential_elements: Any District Magistrate can record a confession/statement, regardless of case jurisdiction; can be done via audio-video means with the accused's advocate present; police officers holding magisterial powers cannot record confessions
Before recording a confession, the Magistrate must warn the maker they are not bound to confess and that it may be used against them, and must be satisfied through questioning that it is voluntary
If the person declines to confess at any point before recording, the Magistrate must not remand them to police custody
The confession follows section 316's procedure, is signed by the maker, and is certified by the Magistrate's memorandum
Non-confession statements are recorded in whatever manner best fits the case, with power to administer oath
For specified sexual offences, the victim's statement must be recorded promptly, preferably by a woman Magistrate, with interpreter/special-educator and audio-video safeguards for disabled persons
For the gravest offences (10 years to life/death), the Magistrate must record the statement of the witness produced by police
A disabled victim's recorded statement can stand in place of live examination-in-chief, subject to cross-examination
The recording Magistrate must forward the confession/statement to the Magistrate who will inquire into or try the case
exceptions_and_qualifications: The bar on remanding a person who declines to confess is an absolute, mandatory protection — it cannot be overridden even if the investigating agency believes further custody would help secure a later confession

The 'preferably by a woman Magistrate' rule in sub-section (6) is a strong preference, not an absolute mandate — a male Magistrate may record the statement, but only with a woman present, and only 'in her absence' (i.e., no woman Magistrate being available)
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 183 is one of the most litigated provisions in criminal procedure because a confession's admissibility so often turns on strict compliance with its safeguards — the warning, the voluntariness inquiry, and the certifying memorandum. Always check each procedural step methodically when assessing whether a recorded confession will survive scrutiny, and treat the sexual-offence victim-statement protections in sub-section (6) as a distinct, additional layer serving witness/victim welfare rather than confession-voluntariness as such.

sections.title: Medical examination of victim of rape
sections.raw_text:
184. Medical examination of victim of rape.—(1) Where, during the stage when an offence of
committing rape or attempt to commit rape is under investigation, it is proposed to get the person of the
woman with whom rape is alleged or attempted to have been committed or attempted, examined
by a medical expert, such examination shall be conducted by a registered medical practitioner employed in
a hospital run by the Government or a local authority and in the absence of such a practitioner, by any other
registered medical practitioner, with the consent of such woman or of a person competent to give such
consent on her behalf and such woman shall be sent to such registered medical practitioner within
twenty-four hours from the time of receiving the information relating to the commission of such offence.
    (2) The registered medical practitioner, to whom such woman is sent, shall, without delay, examine her
person and prepare a report of his examination giving the following particulars, namely:—
        (i) the name and address of the woman and of the person by whom she was brought;
        (ii) the age of the woman;
        (iii) the description of material taken from the person of the woman for DNA profiling;
        (iv) marks of injury, if any, on the person of the woman;
        (v) general mental condition of the woman; and
        (vi) other material particulars in reasonable detail.
    (3) The report shall state precisely the reasons for each conclusion arrived at.
    (4) The report shall specifically record that the consent of the woman or of the person competent to
give such consent on her behalf to such examination had been obtained.
    (5) The exact time of commencement and completion of the examination shall also be noted in the
report.
    (6) The registered medical practitioner shall, within a period of seven days forward the report to the
investigating officer who shall forward it to the Magistrate referred to in section 193 as part of the
documents referred to in clause (a) of sub-section (6) of that section.
    (7) Nothing in this section shall be construed as rendering lawful any examination without the consent
of the woman or of any person competent to give such consent on her behalf.
    Explanation.—For the purposes of this section, "examination" and "registered medical practitioner"
shall have the same meanings as respectively assigned to them in section 51.

breakdown.plain_summary: This closes the sub-batch with the detailed procedure for medically examining a rape victim during investigation — a critical evidence-gathering step that this section deliberately hedges with consent protections at every turn. The examination must be done by a registered medical practitioner at a government/local-authority hospital where available (or, failing that, any registered practitioner), only with the woman's consent (or that of someone competent to consent on her behalf), and she must be sent for examination within 24 hours of the offence being reported. The examining practitioner must act without delay and produce a detailed report covering: identifying details, age, material collected for DNA profiling, injuries, general mental condition, and other relevant particulars — with precise reasoning for every conclusion reached, explicit confirmation that consent was obtained, and the exact start/end times of the examination logged. The report must reach the investigating officer within 7 days, who then forwards it to the trial-stage Magistrate referred to in section 193, as part of the documents bundled with the final investigation report. Sub-section (7) is an unambiguous, non-negotiable statement that nothing in this section legalizes an examination performed without valid consent — this section creates a careful evidentiary procedure, not a backdoor around the consent requirement.
essential_elements: Applies where, during investigation of rape or attempted rape, medical examination of the woman is proposed
Must be conducted by a government/local-authority-hospital registered medical practitioner, or (in their absence) any registered medical practitioner
Requires the woman's consent, or that of a person competent to consent on her behalf
The woman must be sent for examination within 24 hours of the offence being reported

The practitioner examines without delay and prepares a detailed report: identifying details, age, DNA-profiling material description, injuries, mental condition, other particulars, with reasoning for each conclusion, confirmation of consent, and exact examination timing
The report must be forwarded to the investigating officer within 7 days, who forwards it to the section 193 Magistrate as part of the final report's documents
Nothing in this section legalises an examination conducted without proper consent
'Examination' and 'registered medical practitioner' take the meanings defined in section 51
exceptions_and_qualifications: Consent is an absolute, non-derogable precondition — the entire elaborate procedural structure of this section presupposes valid consent and cannot be read as overriding its absence
The 24-hour and 7-day timelines are directed at ensuring evidence is not lost to delay, but do not themselves validate an examination conducted without consent
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 184 is a frequently-relied-on provision in sexual-offence trials, both for its evidentiary value (DNA profiling, injury documentation) and for procedural challenges (was consent genuinely obtained and recorded, was the 24-hour window honoured, was the report sufficiently detailed and reasoned). Cross-reference section 51's definitions of 'examination' and 'registered medical practitioner' for the precise scope of who may conduct this examination and what it may involve.

sections.title: Search by police officer
sections.raw_text:
185. Search by police officer.—(1) Whenever an officer in charge of a police station or a police officer
    making an investigation has reasonable grounds for believing that anything necessary for the purposes of
    an investigation into any offence which he is authorised to investigate may be found in any place within the
    limits of the police station of which he is in charge, or to which he is attached, and that such thing cannot
    in his opinion be otherwise obtained without undue delay, such officer may, after recording in writing the
    grounds of his belief in the case-diary and specifying in such writing, so far as possible, the thing for which
    search is to be made, search, or cause search to be made, for such thing in any place within the limits of
    such station.
    (2) A police officer proceeding under sub-section (1), shall, if practicable, conduct the search in person:
    Provided that the search conducted under this section shall be recorded through audio-video electronic
    means preferably by mobile phone.
    (3) If he is unable to conduct the search in person, and there is no other person competent to make the
    search present at the time, he may, after recording in writing his reasons for so doing, require any officer
    subordinate to him to make the search, and he shall deliver to such subordinate officer an order in writing,
    specifying the place to be searched, and so far as possible, the thing for which search is to be made; and
    such subordinate officer may thereupon search for such thing in such place.
    (4) The provisions of this Sanhita as to search-warrants and the general provisions as to searches
    contained in section 103 shall, so far as may be, apply to a search made under this section.
    (5) Copies of any record made under sub-section (1) or sub-section (3) shall forthwith, but not later
    than forty-eight hours, be sent to the nearest Magistrate empowered to take cognizance of the offence, and
    the owner or occupier of the place searched shall, on application, be furnished, free of cost, with a copy of
    the same by the Magistrate.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the police's own power to search a place for evidence during an investigation, without first getting a search-warrant from a court — but it comes wrapped in accountability requirements so the power isn't abused. An officer can search only within their own police-station area, only for something needed in an investigation they are authorised to conduct, and only if getting a warrant first would cause undue delay. Before searching, the officer must write down, in the case-diary, why they believe the thing is there and what they're looking for — a paper trail created before the fact, not invented afterward to justify it. The officer should search in person if at all possible, and under the new BNSS regime the search itself must be filmed, preferably on a mobile phone. If the officer genuinely cannot go in person and no one else suitable is around, they can delegate the search in writing to a subordinate. Ordinary search procedure (like the requirement for independent witnesses under section 103) still applies. And within 48 hours, copies of the search record must reach a Magistrate, who must give the owner or occupier of the searched place a free copy on request.
essential_elements: Officer in charge of a police station, or an officer making an investigation, may search
Search must be within the limits of that officer's own police station
Reasonable grounds to believe the thing sought is at that place, needed for an authorised investigation
The thing cannot otherwise be obtained without undue delay
Grounds of belief and the thing sought must be recorded in writing in the case-diary before the search
Search should be conducted in person if practicable, and must be recorded by audio-video means (preferably mobile phone)
If unable to search in person, may delegate in writing to a subordinate officer, recording reasons
General search-warrant and section 103 search provisions apply so far as may be
Copies of the search record must reach the nearest Magistrate within 48 hours
Owner/occupier of the searched place entitled to a free copy of the record from the Magistrate
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a warrantless search power — it substitutes for, rather than requires, a judicial search-warrant, which is precisely why the writing-first and audio-video-recording safeguards exist.
The 48-hour reporting deadline to the Magistrate is a hard outer limit; the audio-video recording requirement is a newer procedural safeguard not present in the old CrPC.
Delegation to a subordinate is permitted only when the officer genuinely cannot search in person and no other competent person is present — it isn't a free choice.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read sub-section (1) as the trigger conditions (reasonable grounds + urgency), sub-section (2)'s proviso as the new mandatory videography safeguard, sub-section (3) as the narrow delegation exception, and sub-sections (4)-(5) as tying this power back into the Sanhita's general search machinery and building in judicial oversight after the fact.

sections.title: When officer in charge of police station may require another to issue search-warrant
sections.raw_text:
186. When officer in charge of police station may require another to issue search-warrant.—(1)
    An officer in charge of a police station or a police officer not being below the rank of sub-inspector making
    an investigation may require an officer in charge of another police station, whether in the same or a different
    district, to cause a search to be made in any place, in any case in which the former officer might cause such
    search to be made, within the limits of his own station.
    (2) Such officer, on being so required, shall proceed according to the provisions of section 185, and
    shall forward the thing found, if any, to the officer at whose request the search was made.
    (3) Whenever there is reason to believe that the delay occasioned by requiring an officer in charge of
    another police station to cause a search to be made under sub-section (1) might result in evidence of the
    commission of an offence being concealed or destroyed, it shall be lawful for an officer in charge of a police
    station or a police officer making any investigation under this Chapter to search, or cause to be searched,
    any place in the limits of another police station in accordance with the provisions of section 185, as if such
    place were within the limits of his own police station.
    (4) Any officer conducting a search under sub-section (3) shall forthwith send notice of the search to
    the officer in charge of the police station within the limits of which such place is situate, and shall also
    send with such notice a copy of the list (if any) prepared under section 103, and shall also send to the
    nearest Magistrate empowered to take cognizance of the offence, copies of the records referred to in sub-
    sections (1) and (3) of section 185.
    (5) The owner or occupier of the place searched shall, on application, be furnished free of cost with a
    copy of any record sent to the Magistrate under sub-section (4).

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 185 only lets an officer search within their own police-station limits. This section bridges that gap for cases where the evidence sought is in a different station's territory — even a different district. Ordinarily, the investigating officer should ask the officer in charge of that other station to do the search on their behalf, under the same section 185 procedure, and hand over anything found. But where waiting for that request-and-response process risks the evidence being destroyed or hidden, the investigating officer is allowed to just go and search the other station's territory directly, as though it were their own — with extra notice obligations afterward (to the local station and to the Magistrate) to keep everyone informed and accountable.
essential_elements: Default rule: officer in charge (or an investigating officer of sub-inspector rank or above) may ask another station's officer-in-charge to search on their behalf
The requested officer follows section 185's procedure and forwards anything found to the requesting officer
Urgency exception: if delay in going through the other station risks concealment/destruction of evidence, the investigating officer may search that other station's area directly
Direct search under the urgency exception still follows section 185's procedure
Officer conducting a direct search must forthwith notify the local station-in-charge and send the Magistrate copies of the relevant records
Owner/occupier of the searched place is entitled to a free copy of the record sent to the Magistrate
exceptions_and_qualifications: The urgency/direct-search route under sub-section (3) is an exception to the ordinary request-based procedure, not a substitute for it in every case — it applies only where waiting genuinely risks loss of evidence.
Even when searching directly under sub-section (3), the officer must still follow section 185's own safeguards (writing, recording, etc.) as if the place were within their own station.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read sub-section (1)-(2) as the ordinary cooperative procedure between stations, and sub-section (3) as the emergency carve-out, with sub-sections (4)-(5) as the notice-and-transparency obligations that apply specifically when the emergency carve-out is used.

sections.title: Procedure when investigation cannot be completed in twenty-four hours
sections.raw_text:
187. Procedure when investigation cannot be completed in twenty-four hours.—(1) Whenever any
    person is arrested and detained in custody, and it appears that the investigation cannot be completed within
    the period of twenty-four hours fixed by section 58, and there are grounds for believing that the accusation
    or information is well-founded, the officer in charge of the police station or the police officer making the
    investigation, if he is not below the rank of sub-inspector, shall forthwith transmit to the nearest Magistrate
    a copy of the entries in the diary hereinafter specified relating to the case, and shall at the same time forward
    the accused to such Magistrate.
    (2) The Magistrate to whom an accused person is forwarded under this section may, irrespective of
    whether he has or has no jurisdiction to try the case, after taking into consideration whether such person
    has not been released on bail or his bail has been cancelled, authorise, from time to time, the detention of
    the accused in such custody as such Magistrate thinks fit, for a term not exceeding fifteen days in the whole,
    or in parts, at any time during the initial forty days or sixty days out of detention period of sixty days or
    ninety days, as the case may be, as provided in sub-section (3), and if he has no jurisdiction to try the case
    or commit it for trial, and considers further detention unnecessary, he may order the accused to be forwarded
    to a Magistrate having such jurisdiction.
    (3) The Magistrate may authorise the detention of the accused person, beyond the period of fifteen days,
    if he is satisfied that adequate grounds exist for doing so, but no Magistrate shall authorise the detention of
    the accused person in custody under this sub-section for a total period exceeding—
        (i) ninety days, where the investigation relates to an offence punishable with death, imprisonment
    for life or imprisonment for a term of ten years or more;
        (ii) sixty days, where the investigation relates to any other offence, and, on the expiry of the said
    period of ninety days, or sixty days, as the case may be, the accused person shall be released on bail if
    he is prepared to and does furnish bail, and every person released on bail under this sub-section shall
    be deemed to be so released under the provisions of Chapter XXXV for the purposes of that Chapter.
    (4) No Magistrate shall authorise detention of the accused in custody of the police under this section
    unless the accused is produced before him in person for the first time and subsequently every time till the
    accused remains in the custody of the police, but the Magistrate may extend further detention in judicial
    custody on production of the accused either in person or through the audio-video electronic means.
    (5) No Magistrate of the second class, not specially empowered in this behalf by the High Court, shall
    authorise detention in the custody of the police.
    Explanation I.—For the avoidance of doubts, it is hereby declared that, notwithstanding the expiry of
    the period specified in sub-section (3), the accused shall be detained in custody so long as he does not
    furnish bail.
    Explanation II.—If any question arises whether an accused person was produced before the Magistrate
    as required under sub-section (4), the production of the accused person may be proved by his signature on
    the order authorising detention or by the order certified by the Magistrate as to production of the accused
    person through the audio-video electronic means, as the case may be:
    Provided that in case of a woman under eighteen years of age, the detention shall be authorised to be
    in the custody of a remand home or recognised social institution:
    Provided further that no person shall be detained otherwise than in police station under police custody
    or in prison under judicial custody or a place declared as prison by the Central Government or the State
    Government.
    (6) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1) to sub-section (5), the officer in charge of
    the police station or the police officer making the investigation, if he is not below the rank of a
    sub-inspector, may, where a Magistrate is not available, transmit to the nearest Executive Magistrate, on
    whom the powers of a Magistrate have been conferred, a copy of the entry in the diary hereinafter specified
    relating to the case, and shall, at the same time, forward the accused to such Executive Magistrate, and
    thereupon such Executive Magistrate, may, for reasons to be recorded in writing, authorise the detention of
    the accused person in such custody as he may think fit for a term not exceeding seven days in the aggregate;
    and, on the expiry of the period of detention so authorised, the accused person shall be released on bail
    except where an order for further detention of the accused person has been made by a Magistrate competent
    to make such order; and, where an order for such further detention is made, the period during which the
    accused person was detained in custody under the orders made by an Executive Magistrate under this sub-
    section, shall be taken into account in computing the period specified in sub-section (3):
    Provided that before the expiry of the period aforesaid, the Executive Magistrate shall transmit to the
    nearest Judicial Magistrate the records of the case together with a copy of the entries in the diary relating
    to the case which was transmitted to him by the officer in charge of the police station or the police officer
    making the investigation, as the case may be.
    (7) A Magistrate authorising under this section detention in the custody of the police shall record his
    reasons for so doing.
    (8) Any Magistrate other than the Chief Judicial Magistrate making such order shall forward a copy of
    his order, with his reasons for making it, to the Chief Judicial Magistrate.
    (9) If in any case triable by a Magistrate as a summons-case, the investigation is not concluded within
    a period of six months from the date on which the accused was arrested, the Magistrate shall make an order
    stopping further investigation into the offence unless the officer making the investigation satisfies the
    Magistrate that for special reasons and in the interests of justice the continuation of the investigation beyond
    the period of six months is necessary.
    (10) Where any order stopping further investigation into an offence has been made under
    sub-section (9), the Sessions Judge may, if he is satisfied, on an application made to him or otherwise, that
    further investigation into the offence ought to be made, vacate the order made under sub-section (9) and
    direct further investigation to be made into the offence subject to such directions with regard to bail and
    other matters as he may specify.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the remand section — the backbone of how long a person can be kept in custody while police finish investigating. Section 58 gives police only 24 hours to produce an arrested person before a Magistrate; if the investigation needs more time, this section takes over. The officer must forward the accused, with case-diary extracts, to the nearest Magistrate, who can authorise custody (police or judicial) in blocks of up to 15 days at a time. But total police custody plus judicial custody together is capped — 90 days for the most serious offences (death, life imprisonment, or 10+ years) and 60 days for everything else. Once that outer cap is hit, the accused becomes entitled to bail as of right (so-called 'default bail'), regardless of the merits of the case. Crucial safeguards run throughout: the accused must be physically produced (or produced by video) each time custody is extended; second-class Magistrates can't authorise police custody without special High Court empowerment; a woman under 18 in custody must go to a remand home, not a jail; and if no Magistrate is available, an Executive Magistrate can grant a short-term 7-day custody as a stopgap, with the case then routed to a proper Judicial Magistrate. Sub-sections (9)-(10) add a separate check for minor (summons-triable) cases: if such an investigation drags past six months, the Magistrate must order it stopped unless there's a special-reasons justification — though a Sessions Judge can later revive it.
essential_elements: Triggered when arrest-to-24-hour deadline (section 58) can't be met and the investigation must continue
Officer (sub-inspector rank or above) must transmit case-diary entries and produce the accused before the nearest Magistrate
Magistrate may authorise detention in blocks up to 15 days at a time, within an overall scheme
Total detention capped at 90 days for offences punishable with death/life/10+ years imprisonment, 60 days for other offences
On expiry of the applicable cap, the accused is entitled to bail as of right if willing and able to furnish it (default bail)
Physical (or, for judicial custody, audio-video) production of the accused required at every extension of police custody
Only first-class (or specially empowered second-class) Magistrates may authorise police custody
Woman under 18 must be detained in a remand home or recognised social institution, not ordinary custody
Detention only in a police station (police custody), prison, or a place declared a prison — no informal detention sites
Fallback: Executive Magistrate may grant up to 7 days' custody when no Magistrate is available, later routed to a Judicial Magistrate
Magistrate must record reasons for authorising custody; non-Chief Judicial Magistrates must report their orders to the Chief Judicial Magistrate
For summons-triable cases, investigation must conclude within 6 months or be stopped absent special-reasons justification; a Sessions Judge may later revive it
exceptions_and_qualifications: The 90-day/60-day caps are absolute ceilings on custody pending investigation, not targets — once hit, bail becomes a right, not a discretion (subject to actually furnishing the bail bond, per Explanation I).
Executive Magistrate custody under sub-section (6) is a narrow, time-limited stopgap (7 days max) for when no Judicial/regular Magistrate is reachable, not a parallel remand track.
The six-month investigation-stopping rule in sub-sections (9)-(10) applies only to summons-triable cases, not to warrant-triable or serious offences covered by the 60/90-day scheme.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a dense, high-stakes bail/remand provision. Read sub-section (1) as the trigger, (2)-(3) as the custody-authorisation and default-bail scheme (the most litigated part), (4)-(5) as production and Magistrate-rank safeguards, the Explanations and provisos as clarifications and protections (especially for women under 18), (6) as the Executive Magistrate stopgap, (7)-(8) as accountability/reporting duties, and (9)-(10) as the separate six-month rule for minor cases.

sections.title: Report of investigation by subordinate police officer
sections.raw_text:
188. Report of investigation by subordinate police officer.—When any subordinate police officer
    has made any investigation under this Chapter, he shall report the result of such investigation to the officer
    in charge of the police station.

breakdown.plain_summary: A simple internal reporting rule: if a subordinate officer (not the station house officer) carried out the investigation, they must report what they found back to the officer in charge of the station, who remains the responsible point of contact for the case going forward (including for the section 173 FIR record and the eventual report to the Magistrate under sections 189-190).
essential_elements: Applies whenever a subordinate police officer (not the officer in charge) conducts the investigation
That subordinate officer must report the result to the officer in charge of the police station
breakdown.how_to_read: A short administrative-chain-of-command provision — read it as connective tissue between the various investigating officers who might act under this Chapter and the single officer-in-charge who remains accountable for the case.

sections.title: Release of accused when evidence deficient
sections.raw_text:
189. Release of accused when evidence deficient.—If, upon an investigation under this Chapter, it
    appears to the officer in charge of the police station that there is not sufficient evidence or reasonable round
    of suspicion to justify the forwarding of the accused to a Magistrate, such officer shall, if such person is in
    custody, release him on his executing a bond or bail bond, as such officer may direct, to appear, if and when
    so required, before a Magistrate empowered to take cognizance of the offence on a police report, and to try
    the accused or commit him for trial.

breakdown.plain_summary: If, after investigating, the police conclude there isn't enough evidence or reasonable suspicion to actually put the case before a Magistrate, they cannot simply keep holding the accused. Anyone still in custody must be released — but not unconditionally: they must first execute a bond (with or without sureties, i.e., a bail bond) promising to show up before a Magistrate later if required. This keeps the door open in case further evidence surfaces, without keeping a person in jail on a weak case.
essential_elements: Applies where, after investigation, the officer in charge finds insufficient evidence or reasonable ground of suspicion
Only engages if the accused is currently in custody
Release must be conditioned on executing a bond or bail bond as the officer directs
The bond obliges appearance before a Magistrate if and when later required
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a police-level release, not a judicial acquittal or discharge — it doesn't bar future proceedings if fresh evidence emerges; the bond exists precisely so the person can be recalled.
breakdown.how_to_read: Pair this with section 190 as the two possible endpoints of a completed investigation: insufficient evidence leads here (conditional release), sufficient evidence leads to section 190 (forwarding to a Magistrate).

sections.title: Cases to be sent to Magistrate, when evidence is sufficient
sections.raw_text:
190. Cases to be sent to Magistrate, when evidence is sufficient.—(1) If, upon an investigation under
    this Chapter, it appears to the officer in charge of the police station that there is sufficient evidence or
    reasonable ground as aforesaid, such officer shall forward the accused under custody to a Magistrate
    empowered to take cognizance of the offence upon a police report and to try the accused or commit him for
    trial, or, if the offence is bailable and the accused is able to give security, shall take security from him for
    his appearance before such Magistrate on a day fixed and for his attendance from day to day before such
    Magistrate until otherwise directed:
    Provided that if the accused is not in custody, the police officer shall take security from such person for
    his appearance before the Magistrate and the Magistrate to whom such report is forwarded shall not refuse
    to accept the same on the ground that the accused is not taken in custody.
    (2) When the officer in charge of a police station forwards an accused person to a Magistrate or takes
    security for his appearance before such Magistrate under this section, he shall send to such Magistrate any
    weapon or other article which it may be necessary to produce before him, and shall require the complainant
    (if any) and so many of the persons who appear to such officer to be acquainted with the facts and
    circumstances of the case as he may think necessary, to execute a bond to appear before the Magistrate as
    thereby directed and prosecute or give evidence (as the case may be) in the matter of the charge against the
    accused.
    (3) If the Court of the Chief Judicial Magistrate is mentioned in the bond, such Court shall be held to
    include any Court to which such Magistrate may refer the case for inquiry or trial, provided reasonable
    notice of such reference is given to such complainant or persons.
    (4) The officer in whose presence the bond is executed shall deliver a copy thereof to one of the persons
    who executed it, and shall then send to the Magistrate the original with his report.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the mirror image of section 189: where the investigation does turn up sufficient evidence or reasonable ground, the case must move forward to a Magistrate rather than being closed at the police level. If the offence is not bailable, the accused is forwarded in custody. If it is bailable and the accused can give security, they're released on that security instead, bound to keep appearing before the Magistrate — and this security route is available even if the accused isn't in custody at all (the Magistrate can't refuse to accept it just because the person was never held). Alongside the accused, the police must also send any physical evidence (weapons, articles) that will be needed in court, and bind the complainant and key witnesses by bond to show up and give evidence or prosecute when the case is called — otherwise the prosecution's own witnesses might simply not appear.
essential_elements: Applies where investigation reveals sufficient evidence or reasonable ground of suspicion
Non-bailable offences: accused forwarded to Magistrate in custody
Bailable offences: accused may instead be released on security to appear before the Magistrate
Security route available even for an accused not in custody — Magistrate cannot refuse it on that ground
Officer must send to the Magistrate any weapons/articles needed as evidence
Complainant and material witnesses must be bound by bond to appear and prosecute/give evidence
Bonds naming the Chief Judicial Magistrate's Court extend to any court that Magistrate refers the case to, with notice to the bound persons
A copy of the executed bond goes to the person who executed it; the original goes to the Magistrate with the officer's report
exceptions_and_qualifications: The 'not in custody' proviso is significant — it means a person who was never arrested, but is implicated by sufficient investigation evidence, can still be brought into the process via a security bond rather than arrest.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read this as the standard closing act of a completed investigation with a positive result: accused (or security) forwarded, evidence forwarded, witnesses bound — everything needed to actually commence proceedings before the Magistrate is assembled in one section.

sections.title: Complainant and witnesses not to be required to accompany police officer and not to be subject to restraint
sections.raw_text:
191. Complainant and witnesses not to be required to accompany police officer and not to be
    subject to restraint.—No complainant or witness on his way to any Court shall be required to accompany
    a police officer, or shall be subjected to unnecessary restraint or inconvenience, or required to give any
    security for his appearance other than his own bond:
    Provided that if any complainant or witness refuses to attend or to execute a bond as directed in section
    190, the officer in charge of the police station may forward him in custody to the Magistrate, who may
    detain him in custody until he executes such bond, or until the hearing of the case is completed.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section protects ordinary complainants and witnesses from being treated like suspects. When they're on their way to court, police cannot force them to physically accompany an officer, subject them to needless restraint or inconvenience, or demand any security beyond their own personal bond (no sureties, no bail-like conditions). The only exception is narrow: if a complainant or witness simply refuses to attend court or refuses to execute the section 190 bond at all, the police may forward them into custody before the Magistrate, who can then detain them only until they execute the bond or until the case hearing concludes — a coercive last resort, not a routine practice.
essential_elements: Applies to complainants and witnesses travelling to court, not to accused persons
No requirement to physically accompany a police officer
No unnecessary restraint or inconvenience may be imposed
Security for appearance, if any, is limited to the person's own bond — no sureties demanded
Exception: refusal to attend or execute the section 190 bond allows the police to forward the person in custody to the Magistrate
Magistrate may detain such a person only until the bond is executed or the hearing concludes
exceptions_and_qualifications: The custody power in the proviso is triggered only by outright refusal to cooperate, not by ordinary reluctance or scheduling difficulty.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read the main clause as the general rule (freedom from coercion for prosecution witnesses) and the proviso as the narrow enforcement mechanism against genuine non-cooperation, tying back to the bond obligation created under section 190.

sections.title: Diary of proceedings in investigation
sections.raw_text:
192. Diary of proceedings in investigation.—(1) Every police officer making an investigation under
    this Chapter shall day by day enter his proceedings in the investigation in a diary, setting forth the time at
    which the information reached him, the time at which he began and closed his investigation, the place or
    places visited by him, and a statement of the circumstances ascertained through his investigation.
    (2) The statements of witnesses recorded during the course of investigation under section 180 shall be
    inserted in the case diary.
    (3) The diary referred to in sub-section (1) shall be a volume and duly paginated.
    (4) Any Criminal Court may send for the police diaries of a case under inquiry or trial in such Court,
    and may use such diaries, not as evidence in the case, but to aid it in such inquiry or trial.
    (5) Neither the accused nor his agents shall be entitled to call for such diaries, nor shall he or they be
    entitled to see them merely because they are referred to by the Court; but, if they are used by the police
    officer who made them to refresh his memory, or if the Court uses them for the purpose of contradicting
    such police officer, the provisions of section 148 or section 164, as the case may be, of the Bharatiya
    Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, shall apply.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the case diary — a mandatory day-by-day investigation log every investigating officer must keep, recording when information arrived, when the investigation started and stopped each day, where the officer went, and what was found out. Section 180 witness statements get folded into this same diary. It must be a proper bound, paginated volume — not loose or reconstructible pages. Courts can call for and use the diary to help understand a case during inquiry or trial, but critically, it is not evidence in itself — it's a background aid for the court, not something either side can build their case on directly. The accused has no general right to see the diary just because the court referred to it; but if the police officer uses it to refresh their memory on the stand, or the court uses it to catch the officer contradicting themselves, then the ordinary evidence-law rules on refreshing memory (BSA section 148) or contradicting a witness (BSA section 164) kick in and open it up for that limited purpose.
essential_elements: Every investigating officer must maintain a day-by-day diary of investigation proceedings
Must record: time information reached the officer, start/stop times of investigation, places visited, circumstances ascertained
Section 180 witness statements recorded during investigation are inserted into the case diary
The diary must be a properly bound, paginated volume
Criminal Courts may call for and use the diary to aid an inquiry or trial — but not as evidence
Accused/agents have no general right to see or call for the diary merely because the court referred to it
Exception: if the officer uses the diary to refresh memory, or the court uses it to contradict the officer, ordinary BSA rules on refreshing memory/contradiction apply
exceptions_and_qualifications: The diary's non-evidentiary status is the key protective feature — it prevents either side from using unverified daily notes as substantive proof, while still letting courts benefit from the officer's contemporaneous record.
The accused's access is need-based and rule-gated (BSA sections 148/164), not automatic.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read sub-sections (1)-(3) as the recording obligations, and (4)-(5) as the evidentiary status and access rules — the tension between judicial usefulness and non-evidentiary status is the section's core idea.

sections.title: Report of police officer on completion of investigation
sections.raw_text:
193. Report of police officer on completion of investigation.—(1) Every investigation under this
    Chapter shall be completed without unnecessary delay.
    (2) The investigation in relation to an offence under sections 64, 65, 66, 67, 68, 70, 71 of the Bharatiya
    Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 or under sections 4, 6, 8 or section 10 of the Protection of Children from Sexual
    Offences Act, 2012 shall be completed within two months from the date on which the information was
    recorded by the officer in charge of the police station.
    (3) (i) As soon as the investigation is completed, the officer in charge of the police station shall forward,
    including through electronic communication to a Magistrate empowered to take cognizance of the offence
    on a police report, a report in the form as the State Government may, by rules provide, stating—
        (a) the names of the parties;
        (b) the nature of the information;
        (c) the names of the persons who appear to be acquainted with the circumstances of the case;
        (d) whether any offence appears to have been committed and, if so, by whom;
        (e) whether the accused has been arrested;
        (f) whether the accused has been released on his bond or bail bond;
        (g) whether the accused has been forwarded in custody under section 190;
        (h) whether the report of medical examination of the woman has been attached where investigation
    relates to an offence under sections 64, 65, 66, 67, 68, 70 or section 71 of the Bharatiya Nyaya
    Sanhita, 2023;
        (i) the sequence of custody in case of electronic device;
        (ii) the police officer shall, within a period of ninety days, inform the progress of the investigation
    by any means including through electronic communication to the informant or the victim;
        (iii) the officer shall also communicate, in such manner as the State Government may, by rules,
    provide, the action taken by him, to the person, if any, by whom the information relating to the
    commission of the offence was first given.
    (4) Where a superior officer of police has been appointed under section 177, the report shall, in any
    case in which the State Government by general or special order so directs, be submitted through that officer,
    and he may, pending the orders of the Magistrate, direct the officer in charge of the police station to make
    further investigation.
    (5) Whenever it appears from a report forwarded under this section that the accused has been released
    on his bond or bail bond, the Magistrate shall make such order for the discharge of such bond or bail bond
    or otherwise as he thinks fit.
    (6) When such report is in respect of a case to which section 190 applies, the police officer shall forward
    to the Magistrate along with the report—
        (a) all documents or relevant extracts thereof on which the prosecution proposes to rely other than
    those already sent to the Magistrate during investigation;
        (b) the statements recorded under section 180 of all the persons whom the prosecution proposes to
    examine as its witnesses.
    (7) If the police officer is of opinion that any part of any such statement is not relevant to the subject
    matter of the proceedings or that its disclosure to the accused is not essential in the interests of justice and
    is inexpedient in the public interest, he shall indicate that part of the statement and append a note requesting
    the Magistrate to exclude that part from the copies to be granted to the accused and stating his reasons for
    making such request.
    (8) Subject to the provisions contained in sub-section (7), the police officer investigating the case shall
    also submit such number of copies of the police report along with other documents duly indexed to the
    Magistrate for supply to the accused as required under section 230:
    Provided that supply of report and other documents by electronic communication shall be considered
    as duly served.
    (9) Nothing in this section shall be deemed to preclude further investigation in respect of an offence
    after a report under sub-section (3) has been forwarded to the Magistrate and, where upon such
    investigation, the officer in charge of the police station obtains further evidence, oral or documentary, he
    shall forward to the Magistrate a further report or reports regarding such evidence in the form as the State
    Government may, by rules, provide; and the provisions of sub-sections (3) to (8) shall, as far as may be,
    apply in relation to such report or reports as they apply in relation to a report forwarded under
    sub-section (3):
    Provided that further investigation during the trial may be conducted with the permission of the Court
    trying the case and the same shall be completed within a period of ninety days which may be extended with
    the permission of the Court.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the chargesheet section — the formal report police file to close out an investigation and hand the case to a Magistrate. Investigations generally must finish without unnecessary delay, and for specified serious sexual and child-abuse offences, there's a hard two-month deadline from when the FIR was recorded. The report itself is detailed: parties' names, the nature of the case, likely witnesses, whether an offence appears committed and by whom, the accused's custody/bail status, and — a new BNSS-era addition — the chain of custody for any electronic device seized. The investigating officer also has fresh victim-communication duties: informing the informant/victim of investigation progress within 90 days, and separately communicating what action was taken. If the case is going to trial (section 190 territory), the police must hand over all the evidence and witness statements the prosecution intends to rely on — but they can flag (with reasons) any part of a witness statement they think should be withheld from the accused's copy, subject to the Magistrate's oversight.
