Investigation doesn't have to stop just because a report was filed — the sub-section (9) 'further investigation' route lets police submit supplementary reports if new evidence turns up, even mid-trial, subject to the trial court's permission and (for the trial-stage version) a 90-day completion window.
essential_elements: Investigation must be completed without unnecessary delay generally
Hard 2-month deadline for specified BNS sexual-offence sections and POCSO Act offences, from date information was recorded

Report must state parties, nature of information, likely witnesses, whether an offence appears committed and by whom, custody/bail status, and (for the listed offences) confirmation of the medical examination report
New requirement: the sequence of custody for any electronic device must be documented
Police must update the informant/victim on investigation progress within 90 days, and separately communicate action taken
For section 190 cases, the report must be accompanied by prosecution evidence/documents and all section 180 witness statements
Police may request exclusion of irrelevant or sensitive parts of a statement from the accused's copy, with reasons noted for the Magistrate
Copies of the report and documents must be supplied to the accused per section 230; electronic service counts as valid service
Filing a report doesn't bar further investigation; fresh evidence can be reported via supplementary reports
Further investigation during trial requires the trial court's permission and must generally finish within 90 days (extendable by the court)
exceptions_and_qualifications: The 2-month completion deadline applies only to the specifically listed sexual/child-offence provisions — not to investigations generally, which are subject only to the looser 'without unnecessary delay' standard.
Withholding part of a witness statement from the accused (sub-section 7) requires the Magistrate's concurrence — police cannot unilaterally decide what the defence sees.
Further investigation during an ongoing trial is not automatic — it needs the trial court's permission and is time-boxed to 90 days (extendable), unlike pre-cognizance further investigation.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a long, structurally important section. Treat sub-sections (1)-(2) as the timing rules, (3) as the content of the report itself, (4)-(5) as administrative routing and bond-discharge consequences, (6)-(8) as the evidence-disclosure package for trial-track cases (the practical discovery mechanism for the defence), and (9) as the standing power to keep investigating and supplement the record even after the report is filed or the trial has begun.

sections.title: Police to enquire and report on suicide, etc.
sections.raw_text:
194. Police to enquire and report on suicide, etc.—(1) When the officer in charge of a police station
    or some other police officer specially empowered by the State Government in that behalf receives
    information that a person has committed suicide, or has been killed by another or by an animal or by
    machinery or by an accident, or has died under circumstances raising a reasonable suspicion that some other
    person has committed an offence, he shall immediately give intimation thereof to the nearest Executive
    Magistrate empowered to hold inquests, and, unless otherwise directed by any rule made by the State
    Government, or by any general or special order of the District or Sub-divisional Magistrate, shall proceed
    to the place where the body of such deceased person is, and there, in the presence of two or more respectable
    inhabitants of the neighbourhood, shall make an investigation, and draw up a report of the apparent cause
    of death, describing such wounds, fractures, bruises, and other marks of injury as may be found on the body,
    and stating in what manner, or by what weapon or instrument (if any), such marks appear to have been
    inflicted.
    (2) The report shall be signed by such police officer and other persons, or by so many of them as concur
    therein, and shall be forwarded to the District Magistrate or the Sub-divisional Magistrate within twenty-
    four hours.
    (3) When—
        (i) the case involves suicide by a woman within seven years of her marriage; or
        (ii) the case relates to the death of a woman within seven years of her marriage in any circumstances
    raising a reasonable suspicion that some other person committed an offence in relation to such
    woman; or
        (iii) the case relates to the death of a woman within seven years of her marriage and any relative of
    the woman has made a request in this behalf; or
        (iv) there is any doubt regarding the cause of death; or
        (v) the police officer for any other reason considers it expedient so to do,
    he shall, subject to such rules as the State Government may prescribe in this behalf, forward the body, with
    a view to its being examined, to the nearest Civil Surgeon, or other qualified medical person appointed in
    this behalf by the State Government, if the state of the weather and the distance admit of its being so
    forwarded without risk of such putrefaction on the road as would render such examination useless.
    (4) The following Magistrates are empowered to hold inquests, namely, any District Magistrate or Sub-
    divisional Magistrate and any other Executive Magistrate specially empowered in this behalf by the State
    Government or the District Magistrate.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the inquest section — the procedure police follow for suicides, unnatural deaths, and deaths under suspicious circumstances (killed by another person, an animal, machinery, or accident). The officer must immediately notify the nearest inquest-empowered Executive Magistrate, then go to where the body is and, with at least two respectable local residents present as witnesses to the process, prepare a report on the apparent cause of death — noting wounds, fractures, bruises, and how they seem to have been caused. This report must reach the District or Sub-divisional Magistrate within 24 hours. Certain categories of death trigger a mandatory forwarding of the body for post-mortem examination by a Civil Surgeon: notably, any suicide or suspicious/requested death of a woman within seven years of marriage (echoing the dowry-death concerns embedded across criminal law), any case where the cause of death is doubtful, or simply where the officer thinks it's warranted — subject to a practical caveat that the body must actually be transportable without decomposing to the point of making the examination useless.
essential_elements: Triggered by information of suicide, killing (by person/animal/machinery/accident), or death under suspicious circumstances
Officer must immediately notify the nearest inquest-empowered Executive Magistrate
Must proceed to the body's location and investigate with two or more respectable local inhabitants present
Must draw up a report on apparent cause of death, describing injuries and how they appear to have been inflicted
Report must be forwarded to the District/Sub-divisional Magistrate within 24 hours

Mandatory post-mortem forwarding for: a woman's suicide within 7 years of marriage; a woman's suspicious death within 7 years of marriage; such a death where a relative requests it; any doubtful cause of death; or wherever the officer considers it expedient
Forwarding for post-mortem is subject to practical feasibility (weather/distance risk of putrefaction)
Only District Magistrates, Sub-divisional Magistrates, and specially empowered Executive Magistrates may hold inquests
exceptions_and_qualifications: The seven-years-of-marriage categories mirror the special scrutiny given to suspicious deaths of married women elsewhere in Indian criminal law (evidentiary presumptions, dowry-death provisions) — this section is the investigative trigger for that scrutiny.
The body-forwarding duty is not absolute — it yields to genuine practical impossibility (distance/weather causing putrefaction), but that exception must be grounded in fact, not convenience.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read sub-sections (1)-(2) as the base inquest procedure and timeline, sub-section (3) as the mandatory post-mortem triggers (with the woman-within-seven-years-of-marriage categories as the most legally significant), and sub-section (4) as defining who counts as an inquest-empowered Magistrate.

sections.title: Power to summon persons
sections.raw_text:
195. Power to summon persons.—(1) A police officer proceeding under section 194 may, by order in
    writing, summon two or more persons as aforesaid for the purpose of the said investigation, and any other
    person who appears to be acquainted with the facts of the case and every person so summoned shall be
    bound to attend and to answer truly all questions other than questions the answers to which would have a
    tendency to expose him to a criminal charge or to a penalty or forfeiture:
    Provided that no male person under the age of fifteen years or above the age of sixty years or a woman
    or a mentally or physically disabled person or a person with acute illness shall be required to attend at any
    place other than the place where such person resides:
    Provided further that if such person is willing to attend and answer at the police station, such person
    may be permitted so to do.
    (2) If the facts do not disclose a cognizable offence to which section 190 applies, such persons shall not
    be required by the police officer to attend a Magistrate's Court.

breakdown.plain_summary: This gives the officer conducting a section 194 death inquiry the power to summon the two-plus respectable local witnesses, plus anyone else who seems to know relevant facts, and compel their attendance and truthful answers — subject to the same self-incrimination exception found throughout this Chapter (section 180's witness-examination rule echoed here). The same protected-category exemptions apply as with ordinary witness-attendance rules elsewhere in the Sanhita: males under 15 or over 60, women, disabled persons, and the acutely ill cannot be compelled to attend anywhere but their own residence, though they may volunteer to attend the police station. Sub-section (2) adds an important limiter: if the inquiry doesn't actually disclose a cognizable offence that would go forward under section 190, these summoned persons cannot then be dragged further into a Magistrate's Court — their obligation is confined to the inquest-stage inquiry.
essential_elements: Applies to a police officer conducting a section 194 death inquiry
May summon, by written order, the inquest witnesses and any other person acquainted with the facts
Summoned persons must attend and answer truly, except where answers would incriminate them or expose them to a penalty/forfeiture
Protected categories (males under 15/over 60, women, disabled persons, acutely ill) cannot be compelled to attend anywhere but their residence
Such protected persons may still voluntarily choose to attend at the police station
If no cognizable offence under section 190 is disclosed, summoned persons cannot be further required to attend a Magistrate's Court
exceptions_and_qualifications: This power is scoped specifically to section 194 death-inquiry investigations, not general criminal investigations — the latter are governed by sections 179-180.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read this alongside sections 179-180 (which it closely mirrors) as the inquest-specific version of the general witness-attendance and examination powers, with sub-section (2) marking the boundary between a mere death inquiry and a full cognizable-offence investigation.

sections.title: Inquiry by Magistrate into cause of death
sections.raw_text:
196. Inquiry by Magistrate into cause of death.—(1) When the case is of the nature referred to in
    clause (i) or clause (ii) of sub-section (3) of section 194, the nearest Magistrate empowered to hold inquests
    shall, and in any other case mentioned in sub-section (1) of section 194, any Magistrate so empowered may
    hold an inquiry into the cause of death either instead of, or in addition to, the investigation held by the
    police officer; and if he does so, he shall have all the powers in conducting it which he would have in
    holding an inquiry into an offence.
    (2) Where,—
        (a) any person dies or disappears; or
        (b) rape is alleged to have been committed on any woman, while such person or woman is in the
    custody of the police or in any other custody authorised by the Magistrate or the Court, under this
    Sanhita in addition to the inquiry or investigation held by the police, an inquiry shall be held by the
    Magistrate within whose local jurisdiction the offence has been committed.
    (3) The Magistrate holding such an inquiry shall record the evidence taken by him in connection
    therewith in any manner hereinafter specified according to the circumstances of the case.
    (4) Whenever such Magistrate considers it expedient to make an examination of the dead body of any
    person who has been already interred, in order to discover the cause of his death, the Magistrate may cause
    the body to be disinterred and examined.
    (5) Where an inquiry is to be held under this section, the Magistrate shall, wherever practicable, inform
    the relatives of the deceased whose names and addresses are known, and shall allow them to remain present
    at the inquiry.
    (6) The Magistrate or the Executive Magistrate or the police officer holding an inquiry or investigation
    under sub-section (2) shall, within twenty-four hours of the death of a person, forward the body with a view
    to its being examined to the nearest Civil Surgeon or other qualified medical person appointed in this behalf
    by the State Government, unless it is not possible to do so for reasons to be recorded in writing.
    Explanation.—In this section, the expression "relative" means parents, children, brothers, sisters and
    spouse.

breakdown.plain_summary: This closes Chapter XIII by adding a judicial layer on top of the police inquest of section 194. For the most serious categories — a woman's suicide or suspicious death within seven years of marriage — the nearest inquest-empowered Magistrate MUST personally hold an inquiry (not just may), either instead of or alongside the police investigation, wielding full offence-inquiry powers. For other section 194 deaths, the Magistrate has discretion to step in. A separate, especially serious trigger is custodial death or disappearance, or a custodial rape allegation — any death, disappearance, or alleged rape of someone in police or court-authorised custody automatically requires a Magistrate's inquiry, reflecting the heightened accountability owed by the State when someone is in its custody. The Magistrate can even order a buried body exhumed if that's needed to determine the cause of death, and must, wherever practical, notify and let the deceased's relatives (a defined list: parents, children, siblings, spouse) attend the inquiry. As with the police-level inquest, the body must generally reach a Civil Surgeon within 24 hours of death for examination, unless genuinely impossible, with reasons recorded. This section, together with section 194, forms the full unnatural-death/custodial-death accountability mechanism, before Chapter XIV opens with the ordinary rules on where offences are tried.
essential_elements: Mandatory Magistrate inquiry for the seven-years-of-marriage suicide/suspicious-death categories under section 194(3)(i)-(ii)
Discretionary Magistrate inquiry for other section 194(1) deaths
Magistrate conducting such an inquiry has the full powers of an inquiry into an offence
Mandatory Magistrate inquiry for any death, disappearance, or alleged rape of a person in police or authorised custody
Magistrate may order disinterment and examination of an already-buried body if expedient
Relatives of the deceased (parents, children, siblings, spouse) must be informed and allowed to attend, wherever practicable
The body must generally be forwarded to a Civil Surgeon within 24 hours of death, absent recorded reasons for impossibility
exceptions_and_qualifications: The custodial-death/disappearance/rape trigger in sub-section (2) applies regardless of which section 194 category the case would otherwise fall into — custody status alone is enough to mandate a Magistrate's inquiry.

"May" for ordinary section 194(1) deaths versus "shall" for the seven-years-of-marriage and custodial categories is the key mandatory/discretionary distinction to note when advising on whether a judicial inquiry is legally compulsory.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read sub-section (1) as calibrating mandatory-versus-discretionary Magistrate involvement based on the type of section 194 death, sub-section (2) as the separate and especially weighty custodial-death/rape trigger, and sub-sections (3)-(6) as the procedural machinery (evidence recording, disinterment power, family notice, medical examination timeline) for conducting that inquiry once triggered.

sections.title: Ordinary place of inquiry and trial
sections.raw_text:
197. Ordinary place of inquiry and trial.—Every offence shall ordinarily be inquired into and tried
    by a Court within whose local jurisdiction it was committed.

breakdown.plain_summary: This opens Chapter XIV, the Sanhita's rules on where a case should be heard. The default, common-sense rule is territorial: a case is normally inquired into and tried by the court whose geographic jurisdiction covers the place where the offence actually happened. Everything else in this Chapter carves out special situations — offences spanning multiple areas, offences with effects felt elsewhere, offences committed electronically, and so on — where this simple rule doesn't cleanly apply.
essential_elements: The general/default rule for venue in criminal cases
The relevant court is the one with local jurisdiction over the place where the offence was committed
Applies unless one of the Chapter's special venue rules displaces it
exceptions_and_qualifications: The word "ordinarily" signals this is a default, not an absolute rule — the sections that follow displace it for specific fact patterns.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat this as the baseline against which every other section in this Chapter is an exception or clarification for a particular kind of case.

sections.title: Place of inquiry or trial
sections.raw_text:
198. Place of inquiry or trial.—(a) When it is uncertain in which of several local areas an offence was
    committed; or
    (b) where an offence is committed partly in one local area and partly in another; or
    (c) where an offence is a continuing one, and continues to be committed in more local areas than
    one; or
    (d) where it consists of several acts done in different local areas, it may be inquired into or tried by a
    Court having jurisdiction over any of such local areas.

breakdown.plain_summary: This handles offences that don't neatly belong to a single place. If it's unclear exactly which area the offence occurred in, if it straddles two areas, if it's a continuing offence unfolding across multiple areas over time, or if it's really a series of acts spread across different places, then any one of the courts covering those areas can validly hear the case — the prosecution isn't stuck guessing the single 'correct' venue.
essential_elements: Applies to four scenarios: uncertain location, offence spanning two areas, continuing offence across multiple areas, and offences made up of several acts in different areas
In any of these scenarios, a court with jurisdiction over any of the areas involved may inquire into or try the case
breakdown.how_to_read: Read the four clauses (a)-(d) as a checklist of multi-location fact patterns, all resolved the same way: jurisdiction attaches to any of the implicated areas, giving flexibility rather than a single fixed venue.

sections.title: Offence triable where act is done or consequence ensues
sections.raw_text:
199. Offence triable where act is done or consequence ensues.—When an act is an offence by reason
    of anything which has been done and of a consequence which has ensued, the offence may be inquired into
    or tried by a Court within whose local jurisdiction such thing has been done or such consequence has
    ensued.

breakdown.plain_summary: Some offences are defined by both an act and a resulting consequence — for example, an assault (the act) that causes death (the consequence) elsewhere. This section says the case can be tried either where the act was done or where the consequence occurred, whichever is more convenient — the prosecution isn't forced to prove venue only at the place of the original act if the harm actually materialised somewhere else.
essential_elements: Applies where an offence is defined by an act plus a consequence that flows from it
Venue may be either where the act was done or where the consequence ensued
breakdown.how_to_read: A classic example is where an injury is inflicted in one place but the victim dies in another — either location's court has jurisdiction under this rule.

sections.title: Place of trial where act is an offence by reason of relation to other offence
sections.raw_text:
200. Place of trial where act is an offence by reason of relation to other offence.—When an act is
    an offence by reason of its relation to any other act which is also an offence or which would be an offence
    if the doer were capable of committing an offence, the first-mentioned offence may be inquired into or tried
    by a Court within whose local jurisdiction either act was done.

breakdown.plain_summary: Some offences (like abetment, or receiving stolen property) are only offences because of their relationship to another act — the underlying crime. This section allows the case about the dependent offence to be tried either where that offence itself happened or where the related underlying act happened, even covering the situation where the person who did the underlying act couldn't themselves be prosecuted (for instance, a minor or someone of unsound mind) — the relational offence can still be tried at either location.
essential_elements: Applies where an act is criminal only because of its relation to another act that is (or would be) an offence
Covers the situation where the person doing the related act wasn't capable of committing an offence (e.g., minority, unsoundness of mind)
Venue lies in the jurisdiction where either act was done
breakdown.how_to_read: Think of this as the venue rule for accessory-type offences (abetment, receiving stolen property, harbouring an offender) whose criminality derives from another act — jurisdiction follows either location.

sections.title: Place of trial in case of certain offences
sections.raw_text:
201. Place of trial in case of certain offences.—(1) Any offence of dacoity, or of dacoity with murder,
    of belonging to a gang of dacoits, or of escaping from custody, may be inquired into or tried by a Court
    within whose local jurisdiction the offence was committed or the accused person is found.
    (2) Any offence of kidnapping or abduction of a person may be inquired into or tried by a Court within
    whose local jurisdiction the person was kidnapped or abducted or was conveyed or concealed or detained.
    (3) Any offence of theft, extortion or robbery may be inquired into or tried by a Court within whose
    local jurisdiction the offence was committed or the stolen property which is the subject of the offence was
    possessed by any person committing it or by any person who received or retained such property knowing
    or having reason to believe it to be stolen property.
    (4) Any offence of criminal misappropriation or of criminal breach of trust may be inquired into or tried
    by a Court within whose local jurisdiction the offence was committed or any part of the property which is
    the subject of the offence was received or retained, or was required to be returned or accounted for, by the
    accused person.
    (5) Any offence which includes the possession of stolen property may be inquired into or tried by a
    Court within whose local jurisdiction the offence was committed or the stolen property was possessed by
    any person who received or retained it knowing or having reason to believe it to be stolen property.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section lays down bespoke, offence-specific venue rules for crimes that inherently involve movement — of people, of stolen goods, or of offenders themselves. Dacoity (gang robbery), dacoity with murder, belonging to a gang of dacoits, and escape from custody can be tried either where committed or wherever the accused is later found — recognising that these offenders often flee. Kidnapping/abduction can be tried anywhere along the chain: where the person was taken, conveyed, concealed, or detained — not just the original abduction spot. Theft, extortion, and robbery can be tried where committed or wherever the stolen property later turns up in someone's possession. The same possession-based venue applies to criminal misappropriation/breach of trust (tied to where entrusted property was received, retained, or was due to be accounted for) and to standalone possession-of-stolen-property offences.
essential_elements: Dacoity/dacoity-with-murder/gang-membership/escape from custody: venue where committed OR where the accused is found
Kidnapping/abduction: venue where the person was kidnapped, abducted, conveyed, concealed, or detained
Theft/extortion/robbery: venue where committed OR where the stolen property was possessed, received, or retained by anyone (offender or handler)
Criminal misappropriation/breach of trust: venue where committed OR where the entrusted property was received, retained, or was due to be accounted for
Possession of stolen property (as a standalone offence): venue where committed OR where the property was possessed by a knowing/suspecting receiver
exceptions_and_qualifications: These are deliberately broad, multi-venue rules designed to prevent offenders who move goods or victims across jurisdictions from evading trial through venue technicalities.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat each sub-section as a distinct offence-category rule; the common thread across all five is that venue follows wherever the person, property, or offender physically ends up, not just the original crime scene.

sections.title: Offences committed by means of electronic communications, letters, etc.
sections.raw_text:
202. Offences committed by means of electronic communications, letters, etc.—(1) Any offence
    which includes cheating, may, if the deception is practised by means of electronic communications or letters
    or telecommunication messages, be inquired into or tried by any Court within whose local jurisdiction such
    electronic communications or letters or messages were sent or were received; and any offence of cheating
    and dishonestly inducing delivery of property may be inquired into or tried by a Court within whose local
    jurisdiction the property was delivered by the person deceived or was received by the accused person.
    (2) Any offence punishable under section 82 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 may be inquired
    into or tried by a Court within whose local jurisdiction the offence was committed or the offender last
    resided with his or her spouse by the first marriage, or the wife by the first marriage has taken up permanent
    residence after the commission of the offence.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the modern, remote-crime venue rule. Where cheating is committed via electronic communication, letters, or telecom messages — the classic online fraud or phishing scenario — the case can be tried wherever those messages were sent OR wherever they were received, covering both the offender's and the victim's ends. For the specific offence of cheating that induces someone to hand over property, venue also extends to wherever the deceived person delivered the property or wherever the accused received it. Sub-section (2) handles bigamy (BNS section 82): venue can be where the offence was committed, where the offender last lived with their first spouse, or where the first wife has since taken up permanent residence — recognising that a bigamous second marriage might happen far from where the abandoned first spouse now lives, and she shouldn't have to travel to a distant court to pursue the case.
essential_elements: Cheating via electronic communication/letters/telecom: venue where messages were sent OR received
Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property: venue also extends to where property was delivered or received
Bigamy (BNS section 82): venue where committed, where the offender last resided with the first spouse, or where the first wife has taken up permanent residence after the offence
exceptions_and_qualifications: This section reflects deliberate modernisation for digital-era offences, giving victims of remote/online cheating a local venue option rather than forcing them to travel to the offender's location.
The bigamy venue rule is specifically protective of the first wife's convenience, letting her pursue the case near her own current residence.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read sub-section (1) as the general remote-communication cheating rule (both ends of the communication, plus both ends of any property transfer), and sub-section (2) as a distinct, victim-protective venue rule specific to bigamy.

sections.title: Offence committed on journey or voyage
sections.raw_text:
203. Offence committed on journey or voyage.—When an offence is committed whilst the person by
    or against whom, or the thing in respect of which, the offence is committed is in the course of performing
    a journey or voyage, the offence may be inquired into or tried by a Court through or into whose local
    jurisdiction that person or thing passed in the course of that journey or voyage.

breakdown.plain_summary: For offences that happen while someone (or something) is travelling — on a train, bus, ship, or any journey — pinning down a single 'scene of the crime' can be impractical, since the exact location at the moment of the offence may be unclear or constantly moving. This section allows the case to be tried by any court whose jurisdiction the traveller or the relevant thing passed through during that journey, not just wherever the offence is provable to have technically occurred.
essential_elements: Applies where the offender, victim, or the thing involved in the offence was in the course of a journey or voyage when the offence occurred
Venue lies with any court whose local jurisdiction that person or thing passed through during the journey
breakdown.how_to_read: A practical rule for transit-based offences (e.g., theft on a train) — it avoids disputes over the exact coordinates of the offence by allowing trial anywhere along the travelled route.

sections.title: Place of trial for offences triable together
sections.raw_text:
204. Place of trial for offences triable together.—Where—
    (a) the offences committed by any person are such that he may be charged with, and tried at one
    trial for, each such offence by virtue of the provisions of section 242, section 243 or section 244; or
    (b) the offence or offences committed by several persons are such that they may be charged with
    and tried together by virtue of the provisions of section 246, the offences may be inquired into or tried
    by any Court competent to inquire into or try any of the offences.

breakdown.plain_summary: Elsewhere in the Sanhita (sections 242, 243, 244, and 246), multiple offences by one person, or offences by several people acting together, can be combined into a single trial for efficiency. This section makes sure venue doesn't undo that efficiency: if offences qualify for a joint trial, any court that's competent to try any one of those offences can try all of them together, rather than forcing separate trials in separate courts purely because of jurisdictional technicalities.
essential_elements: Applies to offences joinable in one trial under sections 242, 243, or 244 (same person, multiple offences)
Also applies to offences joinable under section 246 (several persons tried together)
Venue for the combined trial lies in any court competent to try any one of the joined offences
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a venue-facilitation rule that piggybacks on the separate joinder-of-charges/joinder-of-persons rules found later in the Sanhita — read it alongside sections 242-244 and 246 for the full picture of when joint trials are permitted.

sections.title: Power to order cases to be tried in different sessions divisions
sections.raw_text:
205. Power to order cases to be tried in different sessions divisions.—Notwithstanding anything
    contained in the preceding provisions of this Chapter, the State Government may direct that any case or
    class of cases committed for trial in any district may be tried in any sessions division:
    Provided that such direction is not repugnant to any direction previously issued by the High Court or
    the Supreme Court under the Constitution, or under this Sanhita or any other law for the time being in force.

breakdown.plain_summary: This gives the State Government an override power to redirect where a case is tried, moving it out of the district it would ordinarily be tried in and into a different sessions division altogether — useful for situations like sensitive or high-profile cases where local conditions (community pressure, security concerns, logistical issues) make trial in the home district impractical. This power isn't absolute: it cannot contradict any direction already issued by the High Court or Supreme Court on the same matter.
essential_elements: State Government may direct that a case or class of cases be tried in a different sessions division than the district it was committed in
Overrides the preceding territorial-jurisdiction rules in this Chapter
Cannot be repugnant to a prior direction of the High Court or Supreme Court on the same matter
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is an executive override subject to a hard constitutional-and-judicial-supremacy constraint — the State Government cannot use it to contradict a higher court's own venue-related directions (for example, a transfer order).
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat this as an administrative escape valve from the ordinary territorial rules, useful in extraordinary cases, but always subordinate to judicial directions from the High Court or Supreme Court.

sections.title: High Court to decide, in case of doubt, district where inquiry or trial shall take place
sections.raw_text:
206. High Court to decide, in case of doubt, district where inquiry or trial shall take place.—
    Where two or more Courts have taken cognizance of the same offence and a question arises as to which of
    them ought to inquire into or try that offence, the question shall be decided—
    (a) if the Courts are subordinate to the same High Court, by that High Court;
    (b) if the Courts are not subordinate to the same High Court, by the High Court within the local
    limits of whose appellate criminal jurisdiction the proceedings were first commenced, and thereupon
    all other proceedings in respect of that offence shall be discontinued.

breakdown.plain_summary: Sometimes, because of the flexible multi-venue rules in this Chapter, two or more courts might each validly take cognizance of the very same offence — creating a conflict over which one should actually proceed. This section resolves that conflict by escalating it to a High Court: if both courts answer to the same High Court, that High Court decides. If they fall under different High Courts, the High Court where proceedings were first started gets to decide, and once it does, every other pending proceeding on that same offence must stop — ensuring only one court ultimately handles the case.
essential_elements: Triggered when two or more courts have taken cognizance of the same offence
If both courts are subordinate to the same High Court, that High Court decides which should proceed
If subordinate to different High Courts, the High Court where proceedings were first commenced decides
Once decided, all other proceedings on that offence must be discontinued
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a jurisdictional tie-breaker, not a venue-choice mechanism for the parties — it only engages once an actual conflict between courts has already arisen.
breakdown.how_to_read: A conflict-resolution safety valve for the flexible, multi-venue framework built by sections 198-204 — read it as the mechanism that prevents parallel prosecutions of the same offence in different courts.

sections.title: Power to issue summons or warrant for offence committed beyond local jurisdiction
sections.raw_text:
207. Power to issue summons or warrant for offence committed beyond local jurisdiction.—(1)
    When a Magistrate of the first class sees reason to believe that any person within his local jurisdiction has
    committed outside such jurisdiction (whether within or outside India) an offence which cannot, under the
    provisions of sections 197 to 205 (both inclusive), or any other law for the time being in force, be inquired
    into or tried within such jurisdiction but is under any law for the time being in force triable in India, such
    Magistrate may inquire into the offence as if it had been committed within such local jurisdiction and
    compel such person in the manner hereinbefore provided to appear before him, and send such person to the
    Magistrate having jurisdiction to inquire into or try such offence, or, if such offence is not punishable with
    death or imprisonment for life and such person is ready and willing to give bail to the satisfaction of the
    Magistrate acting under this section, take a bond or bail bond for his appearance before the Magistrate
    having such jurisdiction.
    (2) When there are more Magistrates than one having such jurisdiction and the Magistrate acting under
    this section cannot satisfy himself as to the Magistrate to or before whom such person should be sent or
    bound to appear, the case shall be reported for the orders of the High Court.

breakdown.plain_summary: This lets a first-class Magistrate act as a practical stopgap when someone physically present in their jurisdiction has committed an offence elsewhere (even outside India) that isn't triable by this Magistrate under the ordinary venue rules, but is triable somewhere in India under some law. Rather than doing nothing while the proper court is far away, the Magistrate can treat the offence as if it happened locally just enough to compel the person's appearance, then either physically forward them to the Magistrate who actually has jurisdiction, or — for offences not punishable by death or life imprisonment, and if the person is willing to furnish bail — simply take a bail bond binding them to appear before the proper Magistrate. If there happen to be multiple Magistrates who could have jurisdiction and it's unclear which one the person should be sent to, the local Magistrate refers the question up to the High Court rather than guessing.
essential_elements: Applies to a first-class Magistrate who believes a person within their jurisdiction committed an offence elsewhere (in or outside India)
The offence must not be triable within this Magistrate's jurisdiction under sections 197-205 or other law, but must be triable somewhere in India
Magistrate may inquire as if the offence occurred locally, solely to compel the person's appearance
Person is then either forwarded to the Magistrate with actual jurisdiction, or (for offences not punishable by death/life imprisonment, with willing bail) released on a bond to appear there
If multiple Magistrates could have jurisdiction and it's unclear which, the matter is reported to the High Court for orders
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Magistrate's inquiry power is a narrow, compelling-appearance-only power — it does not let them actually try the offence itself; that remains with the Magistrate having true jurisdiction.
The bail-instead-of-custody route is unavailable for offences punishable with death or life imprisonment.
breakdown.how_to_read: Think of this as a jurisdictional 'holding' mechanism — it bridges the gap between where an offender happens to be found and where the offence must actually be tried, without letting either consideration block the person being brought to justice.

sections.title: Offence committed outside India
sections.raw_text:
208. Offence committed outside India.—When an offence is committed outside India—
    (a) by a citizen of India, whether on the high seas or elsewhere; or
    (b) by a person, not being such citizen, on any ship or aircraft registered in India,
    he may be dealt with in respect of such offence as if it had been committed at any place within India at
    which he may be found or where the offence is registered in India:
    Provided that notwithstanding anything in any of the preceding sections of this Chapter, no such offence
    shall be inquired into or tried in India except with the previous sanction of the Central Government.

breakdown.plain_summary: This closes Chapter XIV with India's extraterritorial jurisdiction rule for criminal procedure: an Indian citizen who commits an offence anywhere outside India (including on the high seas), or any person — citizen or not — who commits an offence aboard an Indian-registered ship or aircraft, can be tried in India as though the offence happened at whichever Indian place they're found, or wherever the offence gets formally registered in India. But this power is deliberately reined in: no such prosecution can actually begin without the Central Government's prior sanction — a diplomatic and policy safeguard, given the international sensitivities of prosecuting conduct that happened on foreign or international territory.
essential_elements: Applies to offences committed outside India by an Indian citizen (anywhere, including the high seas)
Also applies to offences committed by anyone (citizen or not) aboard a ship or aircraft registered in India
Such offences may be dealt with in India as if committed at the place where the person is found, or where registered in India
Mandatory precondition: prior sanction of the Central Government before any such inquiry or trial can proceed
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Central Government sanction requirement is an absolute precondition, not a formality — it overrides every other provision in this Chapter for extraterritorial offences.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read the substantive jurisdiction-extending rule in the main text alongside its proviso as a package: India can reach extraterritorial conduct by citizens and on its own registered vessels/aircraft, but only with Central Government sanction acting as a gatekeeper before any court gets involved.

sections.title: Receipt of evidence relating to offences committed outside India
sections.raw_text:
209. Receipt of evidence relating to offences committed outside India.—When any offence alleged
    to have been committed in a territory outside India is being inquired into or tried under the provisions of
    section 208, the Central Government may, if it thinks fit, direct that copies of depositions made or exhibits
    produced, either in physical form or in electronic form, before a judicial officer, in or for that territory or
    before a diplomatic or consular representative of India in or for that territory shall be received as evidence
    by the Court holding such inquiry or trial in any case in which such Court might issue a commission for
    taking evidence as to the matters to which such depositions or exhibits relate.

breakdown.plain_summary: This closes Chapter XIV by solving a practical problem created by section 208's extraterritorial jurisdiction: if India is trying someone for an offence committed abroad, how does evidence from that foreign territory get before an Indian court? Rather than requiring witnesses to travel to India or the court to issue a formal evidence commission every time, the Central Government can direct that depositions or exhibits already taken before a judicial officer abroad, or before an Indian diplomatic/consular official there (physical or electronic copies), be accepted directly as evidence — provided the situation is one where the trial court could otherwise have issued a commission to take that very evidence anyway.
essential_elements: Applies to trials of offences under section 208 (extraterritorial jurisdiction)
Central Government may direct acceptance of depositions/exhibits taken before a foreign judicial officer or an Indian diplomatic/consular representative abroad
Covers both physical and electronic-form copies
Only applies where the trial court could otherwise have issued a commission to take that evidence
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a Central-Government-gated evidentiary shortcut, not an automatic rule — it requires an affirmative direction, and only substitutes for what a commission for evidence would otherwise achieve.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read this as the evidentiary companion to section 208 — it exists solely to make extraterritorial prosecutions practically workable once the Central Government has sanctioned them.

sections.title: Cognizance of offences by Magistrate
sections.raw_text:
210. Cognizance of offences by Magistrate.—(1) Subject to the provisions of this Chapter, any
    Magistrate of the first class, and any Magistrate of the second class specially empowered in this behalf
    under sub-section (2), may take cognizance of any offence—
    (a) upon receiving a complaint of facts, including any complaint filed by a person authorised under
    any special law, which constitutes such offence;
    (b) upon a police report (submitted in any mode including electronic mode) of such facts;
    (c) upon information received from any person other than a police officer, or upon his own
    knowledge, that such offence has been committed.
    (2) The Chief Judicial Magistrate may empower any Magistrate of the second class to take cognizance
    under sub-section (1) of such offences as are within his competence to inquire into or try.

breakdown.plain_summary: This opens Chapter XV, on how criminal proceedings formally get started. A Magistrate can take cognizance of an offence — that is, formally apply their judicial mind to the facts so as to begin proceeding — through any of three routes: (a) a private complaint of facts constituting the offence, including complaints by persons specially authorised under a special law; (b) a police report (the chargesheet under section 193), which can now be submitted electronically; or (c) information from someone other than the police, or even the Magistrate's own personal knowledge, that an offence has occurred. First-class Magistrates can always do this; second-class Magistrates need to be specially empowered by the Chief Judicial Magistrate for offences within their competence.
essential_elements: First-class Magistrates may take cognizance of any offence via any of three routes
Route (a): a complaint of facts constituting the offence, including complaints by persons authorised under special laws
Route (b): a police report, submittable in any mode including electronic
Route (c): information from a non-police source, or the Magistrate's own knowledge
Second-class Magistrates may take cognizance only if specially empowered by the Chief Judicial Magistrate, and only for offences within their competence
exceptions_and_qualifications: "Subject to the provisions of this Chapter" signals that later sections (e.g., sanction requirements, complaint-specific procedures) can further condition or restrict when cognizance may actually be taken.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the foundational cognizance provision — the three routes in sub-section (1) are the three doors through which a criminal case can formally enter the judicial system, and sub-section (2) is the gatekeeping mechanism for lower-tier Magistrates.

sections.title: Transfer on application of accused
sections.raw_text:
211. Transfer on application of accused.—When a Magistrate takes cognizance of an offence under
    clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 210, the accused shall, before any evidence is taken, be informed
    that he is entitled to have the case inquired into or tried by another Magistrate, and if the accused or any of
    the accused, if there be more than one, objects to further proceedings before the Magistrate taking
    cognizance, the case shall be transferred to such other Magistrate as may be specified by the Chief Judicial
    Magistrate in this behalf.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is a specific fairness safeguard for the third cognizance route (section 210(1)(c)) — where the Magistrate acted on information from someone else or their own personal knowledge, rather than a complaint or police report. Because the Magistrate here is, in a sense, closer to being both an information-source and the decision-maker, the accused must be told, before any evidence is taken, that they have a right to have the case heard by a different Magistrate instead. If the accused (or any one of multiple accused) objects to continuing before this Magistrate, the case must be transferred to whichever Magistrate the Chief Judicial Magistrate designates.
essential_elements: Applies only where cognizance was taken under section 210(1)(c) — non-police information or the Magistrate's own knowledge
Accused must be informed of the right to transfer before any evidence is taken
If the accused (or any one of several accused) objects to proceeding before that Magistrate, transfer is mandatory
The Chief Judicial Magistrate specifies which Magistrate the case is transferred to
exceptions_and_qualifications: This right is triggered automatically by that specific mode of cognizance and doesn't need to be separately justified by the accused — a bare objection is enough to require transfer.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a targeted natural-justice safeguard: read it as balancing the flexibility of the own-knowledge/third-party-information cognizance route against the perceived risk of a Magistrate who is less neutral than one acting purely on a complaint or police report.

sections.title: Making over of cases to Magistrates
sections.raw_text:
212. Making over of cases to Magistrates.—(1) Any Chief Judicial Magistrate may, after taking
    cognizance of an offence, make over the case for inquiry or trial to any competent Magistrate subordinate
    to him.
    (2) Any Magistrate of the first class empowered in this behalf by the Chief Judicial Magistrate may,
    after taking cognizance of an offence, make over the case for inquiry or trial to such other competent
    Magistrate as the Chief Judicial Magistrate may, by general or special order, specify.

breakdown.plain_summary: Taking cognizance and actually conducting the inquiry or trial don't have to be done by the same Magistrate. This section lets a Chief Judicial Magistrate, after taking cognizance, hand the case off to any competent subordinate Magistrate to actually inquire into or try it — a routine case-management and workload-distribution tool. A specially empowered first-class Magistrate can do the same, but only within the specific routing scheme the Chief Judicial Magistrate has set (by general or special order) for where such cases should go.
essential_elements: Chief Judicial Magistrate may make over a case (after taking cognizance) to any competent subordinate Magistrate
A specially empowered first-class Magistrate may also make over a case, but only to a Magistrate specified via the Chief Judicial Magistrate's general or special order
breakdown.how_to_read: A purely administrative case-distribution provision — cognizance and trial are functionally separable, and this section is the mechanism for that separation within the Magistracy's hierarchy.

sections.title: Cognizance of offences by Court of Session
sections.raw_text:
213. Cognizance of offences by Court of Session.—Except as otherwise expressly provided by this
    Sanhita or by any other law for the time being in force, no Court of Session shall take cognizance of any
    offence as a Court of original jurisdiction unless the case has been committed to it by a Magistrate under
    this Sanhita.

breakdown.plain_summary: Unlike a Magistrate, a Court of Session generally cannot start a case from scratch on its own — it can only take cognizance of an offence as a trial court of first instance if a Magistrate has already committed the case to it through the Sanhita's committal procedure. This structural rule keeps the Sessions Court's original-jurisdiction workload flowing through the Magistracy's initial screening, except where some other provision of the Sanhita or another law expressly says otherwise.
essential_elements: General rule: a Court of Session cannot take original cognizance of an offence on its own
It may act only where a Magistrate has committed the case to it under the Sanhita's committal procedure
Exception: where this Sanhita or another law expressly provides a different route
exceptions_and_qualifications: This reinforces the Magistracy's role as the standard entry-point/screening layer for the criminal justice system, with the Sessions Court reserved for cases that clear that initial screening (or are exempted by special statute).
breakdown.how_to_read: Pair this with the committal provisions found later in the Sanhita — this section is the rule that makes committal necessary in the first place for original Sessions Court jurisdiction.

sections.title: Additional Sessions Judges to try cases made over to them
sections.raw_text:
214. Additional Sessions Judges to try cases made over to them.—An Additional Sessions Judge
    shall try such cases as the Sessions Judge of the division may, by general or special order, make over to
    him for trial or as the High Court may, by special order, direct him to try.

breakdown.plain_summary: This defines how an Additional Sessions Judge gets their caseload: not independently, but only through cases specifically made over by the Sessions Judge of that division (via general or special order), or through a specific High Court direction. This keeps case allocation within the Sessions Court hierarchy centrally controlled by the Sessions Judge (or, exceptionally, the High Court), rather than the Additional Sessions Judge selecting or receiving cases independently.
essential_elements: An Additional Sessions Judge tries only cases made over by the division's Sessions Judge (general or special order)
Or cases the High Court specially directs the Additional Sessions Judge to try
breakdown.how_to_read: A short administrative provision — read it as the Sessions Court-level counterpart to section 212's Magistracy case-allocation rule.

sections.title: Prosecution for contempt of lawful authority of public servants, for offences against public justice and for offences relating to documents given in evidence
sections.raw_text:
215. Prosecution for contempt of lawful authority of public servants, for offences against public
    justice and for offences relating to documents given in evidence.—(1) No Court shall take cognizance—
        (a) (i) of any offence punishable under sections 206 to 223 (both inclusive but excluding section
    209) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023; or
        (ii) of any abetment of, or attempt to commit, such offence; or
        (iii) of any criminal conspiracy to commit such offence,
    except on the complaint in writing of the public servant concerned or of some other public servant to
    whom he is administratively subordinate or of some other public servant who is authorised by the
    concerned public servant so to do;
        (b) (i) of any offence punishable under any of the following sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya
    Sanhita, 2023, namely, sections 229 to 233 (both inclusive), 236, 237, 242 to 248 (both inclusive) and
    267, when such offence is alleged to have been committed in, or in relation to, any proceeding in any
    Court; or
        (ii) of any offence described in sub-section (1) of section 336, or punishable under sub-section (2)
    of section 340 or section 342 of the said Sanhita, when such offence is alleged to have been committed
    in respect of a document produced or given in evidence in a proceeding in any Court; or
        (iii) of any criminal conspiracy to commit, or attempt to commit, or the abetment of, any offence
    specified in sub-clause (i) or sub-clause (ii),
    except on the complaint in writing of that Court or by such officer of the Court as that Court may authorise
    in writing in this behalf, or of some other Court to which that Court is subordinate.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is a gatekeeping provision protecting two distinct interests from private, freelance prosecutions. Clause (a) covers offences against the lawful authority of public servants — obstruction, disobedience, and similar offences under BNS sections 206-223 (excluding 209) — which can only be prosecuted if the affected public servant (or their administrative superior, or someone they authorise) files a written complaint; a private citizen cannot initiate such a case. Clause (b) covers offences against public justice committed in or in relation to court proceedings (like giving false evidence or fabricating evidence, under a specified list of BNS sections) and offences relating to documents produced in evidence — these can only be prosecuted on the written complaint of the court itself, an officer the court authorises, or a superior court. The underlying policy is to prevent courts and public servants from being harassed by vexatious private prosecutions for offences that are essentially about their own official functioning — only they (or their institutional superior) are positioned to judge whether prosecution is warranted.
essential_elements: Clause (a): offences under BNS sections 206-223 (excluding 209) against public servants' lawful authority — cognizance only on written complaint of the public servant concerned, their administrative superior, or someone authorised by the concerned public servant

Clause (b): specified offences against public justice (BNS 229-233, 236, 237, 242-248, 267) committed in relation to court proceedings, and offences involving documents given in evidence (BNS 336(1), 340(2), 342) — cognizance only on written complaint of that Court, an officer it authorises, or a superior Court
Both clauses extend the bar to abetment, attempt, and criminal conspiracy to commit the listed offences
exceptions_and_qualifications: This bar applies specifically to the listed sections — it does not bar prosecution of unrelated offences arising from the same facts.
The complaint must be in writing; an oral report or FIR alone will not satisfy this requirement for the listed offences.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read this as the institutional-standing requirement: for offences that are essentially attacks on a public servant's or a court's own functioning, only that institution (or its authorised representative or superior) can set prosecution in motion — ordinary complainants are shut out for these specific offence categories.

sections.title: Procedure for witnesses in case of threatening, etc.
sections.raw_text:
216. Procedure for witnesses in case of threatening, etc.—A witness or any other person may file a
    complaint in relation to an offence under section 232 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.

breakdown.plain_summary: This short section is a witness-protection clarification sitting between the two gatekeeping provisions (sections 215 and 217). It confirms that a witness — or indeed any other person — who is threatened or intimidated (the offence defined in BNS section 232) can directly file a complaint about that threat, without needing to route it through any special sanctioning authority. It exists to make clear that the complaint-only restrictions of section 215 do not extend to this particular offence.
essential_elements: Applies specifically to the offence of threatening under BNS section 232
A witness or any other person (not just the direct target) may file the complaint
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat this as a narrow carve-out/clarification protecting witnesses' direct access to court for threats made against them, distinct from the general sanction requirements surrounding it.

sections.title: Prosecution for offences against State and for criminal conspiracy to commit such offence
sections.raw_text:
217. Prosecution for offences against State and for criminal conspiracy to commit such
    offence.—(1) No Court shall take cognizance of—
        (a) any offence punishable under Chapter VII or under section 196, section 299 or sub-section (1)
    of section 353 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023; or
        (b) a criminal conspiracy to commit such offence; or
        (c) any such abetment, as is described in section 47 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, except
    with the previous sanction of the Central Government or of the State Government.
    (2) No Court shall take cognizance of—
        (a) any offence punishable under section 197 or sub-section (2) or sub-section (3) of section 353
    of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023; or
        (b) a criminal conspiracy to commit such offence, except with the previous sanction of the Central
    Government or of the State Government or of the District Magistrate.
    (3) No Court shall take cognizance of the offence of any criminal conspiracy punishable under
    sub-section (2) of section 61 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, other than a criminal conspiracy to
    commit an offence punishable with death, imprisonment for life or rigorous imprisonment for a term of two
    years or upwards, unless the State Government or the District Magistrate has consented in writing to the
    initiation of the proceedings:
    Provided that where the criminal conspiracy is one to which the provisions of section 215 apply, no
    such consent shall be necessary.
    (4) The Central Government or the State Government may, before according sanction under
    sub-section (1) or sub-section (2) and the District Magistrate may, before according sanction under
    sub-section (2) and the State Government or the District Magistrate may, before giving consent under
    sub-section (3), order a preliminary investigation by a police officer not being below the rank of Inspector,
    in which case such police officer shall have the powers referred to in sub-section (3) of section 174.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section erects a high government-sanction barrier before offences against the State itself can be prosecuted — recognising that such offences (sedition-adjacent and related offences under BNS Chapter VII, plus specified public-order offences) carry serious political and public-order sensitivity, so a private complainant or even the police cannot single-handedly trigger prosecution. Sub-section (1) requires Central or State Government sanction for the most serious category (Chapter VII offences and specified sections) plus conspiracy and abetment to commit them. Sub-section (2) requires the same sanction, but also allows a District Magistrate to grant it, for a second, somewhat less serious category. Sub-section (3) is a general safety-valve for criminal conspiracy prosecutions generally — requiring State Government or District Magistrate written consent unless the conspiracy is to commit a very serious offence (death, life imprisonment, or 2+ years' rigorous imprisonment), in which case no consent is needed (ordinary criminal process applies), and this consent requirement is itself switched off where section 215 already governs the conspiracy. Sub-section (4) lets the sanctioning/consenting authority order a preliminary police investigation (by at least an Inspector, with search powers) before deciding whether to grant sanction or consent — a controlled fact-finding step short of a full investigation.
essential_elements: Sub-section (1): Chapter VII offences, sections 196/299/353(1), their conspiracy, and section 47 abetment — need Central or State Government sanction
Sub-section (2): section 197 and section 353(2)/(3) offences and their conspiracy — need Central Government, State Government, or District Magistrate sanction

Sub-section (3): criminal conspiracy generally (section 61(2)) needs State Government/District Magistrate written consent, UNLESS the planned offence carries death/life/2+ years' rigorous imprisonment (no consent needed) or section 215 already applies (no consent needed)
Sub-section (4): before granting sanction or consent, the authority may order a preliminary investigation by an Inspector-or-above police officer, with search powers under section 174(3)
exceptions_and_qualifications: The severity-based carve-out in sub-section (3) means the most serious conspiracies bypass the consent requirement entirely — ordinary process applies to them.
Sub-section (3)'s proviso explicitly avoids double-gatekeeping: if section 215 already governs a conspiracy, section 217(3)'s consent requirement doesn't additionally apply.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read the four sub-sections as graduated layers: (1) and (2) are offence-specific sanction requirements for State-security and public-order offences, (3) is a general conspiracy-prosecution consent filter with a serious-offence exception, and (4) is a shared procedural tool (preliminary investigation) available to whichever authority is deciding sanction or consent under any of the above.

sections.title: Prosecution of Judges and public servants
sections.raw_text:
218. Prosecution of Judges and public servants.—(1) When any person who is or was a Judge or
    Magistrate or a public servant not removable from his office save by or with the sanction of the Government
    is accused of any offence alleged to have been committed by him while acting or purporting to act in the
    discharge of his official duty, no Court shall take cognizance of such offence except with the previous
    sanction save as otherwise provided in the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 (1 of 2014)—
        (a) in the case of a person who is employed or, as the case may be, was at the time of commission
    of the alleged offence employed, in connection with the affairs of the Union, of the Central
    Government;
        (b) in the case of a person who is employed or, as the case may be, was at the time of commission
    of the alleged offence employed, in connection with the affairs of a State, of the State Government:
    Provided that where the alleged offence was committed by a person referred to in clause (b) during the
    period while a Proclamation issued under clause (1) of article 356 of the Constitution was in force in a
    State, clause (b) will apply as if for the expression "State Government" occurring therein, the expression
    "Central Government" were substituted:
    Provided further that such Government shall take a decision within a period of one hundred and twenty
    days from the date of the receipt of the request for sanction and in case it fails to do so, the sanction shall
    be deemed to have been accorded by such Government:
    Provided also that no sanction shall be required in case of a public servant accused of any offence
    alleged to have been committed under section 64, section 65, section 66, section 68, section 69, section 70,
    section 71, section 74, section 75, section 76, section 77, section 78, section 79, section 143, section 199 or
    section 200 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
    (2) No Court shall take cognizance of any offence alleged to have been committed by any member of
    the Armed Forces of the Union while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of his official duty, except
    with the previous sanction of the Central Government.
    (3) The State Government may, by notification, direct that the provisions of sub-section (2) shall apply
    to such class or category of the members of the Forces charged with the maintenance of public order as
    may be specified therein, wherever they may be serving, and thereupon the provisions of that sub-section
    will apply as if for the expression "Central Government" occurring therein, the expression "State
    Government" were substituted.
    (4) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (3), no Court shall take cognizance of any
    offence, alleged to have been committed by any member of the Forces charged with the maintenance of
    public order in a State while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of his official duty during the period
    while a Proclamation issued under clause (1) of article 356 of the Constitution was in force therein, except
    with the previous sanction of the Central Government.
    (5) The Central Government or the State Government, may determine the person by whom, the manner
    in which, and the offence or offences for which, the prosecution of such Judge, Magistrate or public servant
    is to be conducted, and may specify the Court before which the trial is to be held.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the constitutional-grade shield protecting judicial officers, tenured public servants, and armed forces personnel from being dragged into court over acts done in their official capacity, without prior government sanction. Sub-section (1) requires sanction from the Central Government (for Union-affairs employees) or the State Government (for State-affairs employees) before any Court can take cognizance of an offence a Judge, Magistrate, or protected public servant is accused of committing while acting or purporting to act in official duty — unless the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act already governs the situation. During President's Rule (an Article 356 Proclamation), the sanctioning authority for State employees shifts to the Central Government, since the State Government itself is not functioning normally. A firm 120-day deadline forces the sanctioning government to decide — if it doesn't, sanction is deemed granted by default, preventing indefinite stonewalling. Certain serious offences (a specific list of BNS sections covering sexual offences and related provisions) are explicitly exempted from the sanction requirement altogether — protecting victims from being blocked by bureaucratic sanction delays in these especially serious cases. Sub-sections (2)-(4) apply an analogous sanction shield to the Armed Forces of the Union and, by State notification, to public-order forces, with the same President's-Rule Central-Government substitution. Sub-section (5) gives the sanctioning government control over how the prosecution actually proceeds — who conducts it, how, for what offences, and before which Court.
essential_elements: Sub-section (1): sanction (Central for Union employees, State for State employees) required before prosecuting a Judge/Magistrate/tenured public servant for official-duty offences
During an Article 356 Proclamation in a State, the Central Government becomes the sanctioning authority in place of the State Government
120-day deemed-sanction rule: if the government doesn't decide within 120 days of the sanction request, sanction is deemed granted
No sanction required at all for the specifically listed BNS sections (64-79 etc., 143, 199, 200) — mostly serious sexual and bodily-harm offences
Sub-section (2): Central Government sanction required for Armed Forces of the Union personnel's official-duty offences
Sub-sections (3)-(4): State Government may extend the sanction requirement to public-order forces by notification, but during President's Rule the Central Government resumes that sanctioning role
Sub-section (5): sanctioning government controls prosecutor, manner, offences charged, and trial court
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 carve-out means this section's sanction scheme yields to that Act's own procedure where applicable.
The third proviso's exemption list is a deliberate victim-protective override — sanction delays cannot be used to stall prosecution of these serious offences.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read sub-section (1) as the general framework (who sanctions, when Centre substitutes for State, the 120-day deadline, and the no-sanction-needed exemption list), and sub-sections (2)-(4) as the parallel, largely mirrored scheme for armed and public-order forces — sub-section (5) then applies across both schemes to control how any sanctioned prosecution is actually run.

sections.title: Prosecution for offences against marriage
sections.raw_text:
219. Prosecution for offences against marriage.—(1) No Court shall take cognizance of an offence
    punishable under sections 81 to 84 (both inclusive) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 except upon a
    complaint made by some person aggrieved by the offence:
    Provided that—
        (a) where such person is a child, or is of unsound mind or is having intellectual disability requiring
    higher support needs, or is from sickness or infirmity unable to make a complaint, or is a woman who,
    according to the local customs and manners, ought not to be compelled to appear in public, some other
    person may, with the leave of the Court, make a complaint on his or her behalf;
        (b) where such person is the husband and he is serving in any of the Armed Forces of the Union
    under conditions which are certified by his Commanding Officer as precluding him from obtaining
    leave of absence to enable him to make a complaint in person, some other person authorised by the
    husband in accordance with the provisions of sub-section (4) may make a complaint on his behalf;
        (c) where the person aggrieved by an offence punishable under section 82 of the Bharatiya Nyaya
    Sanhita, 2023 is the wife, complaint may be made on her behalf by her father, mother, brother, sister,
    son or daughter or by her father's or mother's brother or sister, or, with the leave of the Court, by any
    other person related to her by blood, marriage or adoption.
    (2) For the purposes of sub-section (1), no person other than the husband of the woman shall be deemed
    to be aggrieved by any offence punishable under section 84 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
    (3) When in any case falling under clause (a) of the proviso to sub-section (1), the complaint is sought
    to be made on behalf of a child or of a person of unsound mind by a person who has not been appointed or
    declared by a competent authority to be the guardian of the child, or of the person of unsound mind, and
    the Court is satisfied that there is a guardian so appointed or declared, the Court shall, before granting the
    application for leave, cause notice to be given to such guardian and give him a reasonable opportunity of
    being heard.
    (4) The authorisation referred to in clause (b) of the proviso to sub-section (1), shall be in writing, shall
    be signed or otherwise attested by the husband, shall contain a statement to the effect that he has been
    informed of the allegations upon which the complaint is to be founded, shall be countersigned by his
    Commanding Officer, and shall be accompanied by a certificate signed by that Officer to the effect that
    leave of absence for the purpose of making a complaint in person cannot for the time being be granted to
    the husband.
    (5) Any document purporting to be such an authorisation and complying with the provisions of
    sub-section (4), and any document purporting to be a certificate required by that sub-section shall, unless
    the contrary is proved, be presumed to be genuine and shall be received in evidence.
    (6) No Court shall take cognizance of an offence under section 64 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita,
    2023, where such offence consists of sexual intercourse by a man with his own wife, the wife being under
    eighteen years of age, if more than one year has elapsed from the date of the commission of the offence.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section governs who may set prosecution in motion for offences against marriage (BNS sections 81-84, covering things like bigamy-type offences and dishonestly inducing a woman to believe she is lawfully married). The default rule is strict complainant-standing: only the person actually aggrieved by the offence may complain — no third party or police-initiated case will do. But the proviso builds in sensible flexibility: if the aggrieved person is a child, of unsound mind, has an intellectual disability, is physically unable to complain, or is a woman whom local custom shields from appearing in public, someone else may complain on their behalf with the Court's leave. A special rule handles a serving military husband who cannot get leave to appear — his Commanding Officer's certification lets someone else, formally authorised in writing, complain for him. For the specific offence under section 82, the wife's own family members (a defined list) can complain on her behalf. Sub-section (2) restricts standing for section 84 offences to the husband alone. Sub-section (3) adds a natural-justice safeguard: if someone without formal guardianship status tries to complain for a child or person of unsound mind, and a proper guardian actually exists, that guardian must be notified and heard before leave is granted. Sub-sections (4)-(5) set out the paperwork requirements for a serving husband's authorised representative, with a presumption of genuineness to ease proof. Sub-section (6) imposes a firm one-year limitation period on prosecuting a man for consummating a marriage with his wife when she is under eighteen — after one year, cognizance is barred entirely regardless of complainant.
essential_elements: General rule: only the aggrieved person may complain of a BNS sections 81-84 offence
Exception (a): another person may complain with Court's leave, for children, persons of unsound mind, persons with intellectual disability, the physically unable, or women shielded by local custom
Exception (b): for a husband serving in the Armed Forces unable to get leave, a formally authorised representative (with Commanding Officer certification) may complain
Exception (c): for section 82 offences, the wife's listed family members may complain on her behalf
Sub-section (2): only the husband is deemed 'aggrieved' for section 84 offences
Sub-section (3): existing guardians must be notified and heard before leave is granted to a non-guardian complainant
Sub-section (6): one-year limitation bar on cognizance of section 64 offences involving a wife under eighteen
exceptions_and_qualifications: The one-year bar in sub-section (6) is an absolute cognizance bar, not merely a defence — the Court cannot take cognizance at all once the period lapses.
Authorisation documents meeting sub-section (4)'s formal requirements enjoy a rebuttable presumption of genuineness under sub-section (5), easing the evidentiary burden at the cognizance stage.
