breakdown.how_to_read: Treat sub-section (1) and its three-clause proviso as the core standing rules, sub-sections (2)-(5) as supporting mechanics for specific proviso clauses, and sub-section (6) as a wholly separate, freestanding limitation bar tacked onto the same section because it also concerns marital offences under BNS Chapter VI.

sections.title: Prosecution of offences under section 85 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
sections.raw_text:
220. Prosecution of offences under section 85 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.— No Court shall
    take cognizance of an offence punishable under section 85 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 except
    upon a police report of facts which constitute such offence or upon a complaint made by the person
    aggrieved by the offence or by her father, mother, brother, sister or by her father's or mother's brother or
    sister or, with the leave of the Court, by any other person related to her by blood, marriage or adoption.

breakdown.plain_summary: BNS section 85 punishes cruelty by a husband or his relatives towards a wife (the successor to the familiar matrimonial-cruelty offence). This section broadens standing beyond the strict aggrieved-person-only rule seen in section 219: cognizance can be taken either on a full police report (meaning the police can investigate and formally report the matter, functioning like any ordinary cognizable-offence pathway) or on a complaint by the aggrieved wife herself, or by a defined circle of her close relatives (parents, siblings, or her parents' siblings), or, with the Court's leave, by any other person related to her by blood, marriage, or adoption. This wider circle reflects the practical reality that victims of domestic cruelty are often unable or unwilling to personally initiate a complaint, so trusted family members are given standing to act for her.
essential_elements: Two independent pathways to cognizance: a police report, OR a complaint
Complaint may be made by the aggrieved wife, her father, mother, brother, sister, or her parents' siblings
With the Court's leave, any other blood/marriage/adoption relative may also complain
exceptions_and_qualifications: Unlike section 219's default (aggrieved-person-only, with narrow exceptions), section 220 opens a police-report route and a much wider family-complainant circle from the outset.
breakdown.how_to_read: Note the structural contrast with section 219 immediately preceding it — section 220 is deliberately more permissive about who can trigger prosecution, in recognition of the practical barriers facing victims of domestic cruelty.

sections.title: Cognizance of offence
sections.raw_text:
221. Cognizance of offence.— No Court shall take cognizance of an offence punishable under
    section 67 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 where the persons are in a marital relationship, except
    upon prima facie satisfaction of the facts which constitute the offence upon a complaint having been filed
    or made by the wife against the husband.

breakdown.plain_summary: BNS section 67 addresses sexual intercourse by a husband with his wife during separation (that is, without her consent while they are living apart, short of marriage having ended) — a narrowly defined offence within the marital context. This section sets a two-part gate before a Court can take cognizance in such a case: the complaint must be filed or made specifically by the wife against the husband (no one else can trigger this prosecution), and the Court must reach prima facie satisfaction that the facts constituting the offence are actually made out before proceeding — a slightly heightened threshold compared with the routine cognizance standard, reflecting the sensitivity of prosecuting conduct within an ongoing marital relationship.
essential_elements: Applies specifically to BNS section 67 offences where the parties are in a marital relationship
Complaint must be filed or made by the wife against the husband — no other complainant is competent
The Court must find prima facie satisfaction of the constituent facts before taking cognizance
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a narrower, more tightly gated cognizance rule than either section 219 or 220 — both complainant identity and an evidentiary threshold are fixed by statute.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read this as a deliberately cautious cognizance filter: standing is restricted strictly to the wife, and the Court must do more than passively receive the complaint — it must satisfy itself prima facie that the offence is made out before the case can proceed.

sections.title: Prosecution for defamation
sections.raw_text:
222. Prosecution for defamation.—(1) No Court shall take cognizance of an offence punishable under
    section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 except upon a complaint made by some person aggrieved
    by the offence:
    Provided that where such person is a child, or is of unsound mind or is having intellectual disability or
    is from sickness or infirmity unable to make a complaint, or is a woman who, according to the local customs
    and manners, ought not to be compelled to appear in public, some other person may, with the leave of the
    Court, make a complaint on his or her behalf.
    (2) Notwithstanding anything contained in this Sanhita, when any offence falling under section 356 of
    the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 is alleged to have been committed against a person who, at the time of
    such commission, is the President of India, the Vice-President of India, the Governor of a State, the
    Administrator of a Union territory or a Minister of the Union or of a State or of a Union territory, or any
    other public servant employed in connection with the affairs of the Union or of a State in respect of his
    conduct in the discharge of his public functions, a Court of Session may take cognizance of such offence,
    without the case being committed to it, upon a complaint in writing made by the Public Prosecutor.
    (3) Every complaint referred to in sub-section (2) shall set forth the facts which constitute the offence
    alleged, the nature of such offence and such other particulars as are reasonably sufficient to give notice to
    the accused of the offence alleged to have been committed by him.
    (4) No complaint under sub-section (2) shall be made by the Public Prosecutor except with the previous
    sanction—
        (a) of the State Government,—
            (i) in the case of a person who is or has been the Governor of that State or a Minister of that
        Government;
            (ii) in the case of any other public servant employed in connection with the affairs of the State;
        (b) of the Central Government, in any other case.
    (5) No Court of Session shall take cognizance of an offence under sub-section (2) unless the complaint
    is made within six months from the date on which the offence is alleged to have been committed.
    (6) Nothing in this section shall affect the right of the person against whom the offence is alleged to
    have been committed, to make a complaint in respect of that offence before a Magistrate having jurisdiction
    or the power of such Magistrate to take cognizance of the offence upon such complaint.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section, which closes Chapter XV, governs prosecutions for defamation (BNS section 356) through two distinct tracks. The ordinary track (sub-section (1)) mirrors the pattern seen throughout this Chapter: only the aggrieved person may complain, with the same familiar proviso allowing someone else to complain on their behalf (with Court leave) if they are a child, of unsound mind, disabled, unwell, or a woman shielded by local custom. The special track (sub-sections (2)-(5)) is reserved for defamation of very high constitutional and public office-holders — the President, Vice-President, Governors, Administrators, Union/State/Union-territory Ministers, and other public servants (regarding their official conduct). For this category, a Court of Session can take cognizance directly — skipping the normal committal-by-Magistrate requirement of section 213 — but only on a written complaint by the Public Prosecutor, not the office-holder personally, and only with prior government sanction (State Government for a Governor/State Minister or State public servant, Central Government for anyone else). This complaint must plead the facts, the offence, and enough particulars for the accused to understand the case, and is subject to a strict six-month limitation period from the date of the alleged offence. Sub-section (6) preserves the underlying individual's own right, alongside this special track, to instead go the ordinary route and complain directly to a Magistrate — the special Public Prosecutor track is an additional option, not an exclusive or mandatory substitute.
essential_elements: Sub-section (1): ordinary defamation prosecution — aggrieved person complains, with the standard vulnerable-complainant proviso

Sub-section (2): special track for defamation of the President, Vice-President, Governors, Administrators, and Ministers/public servants regarding official conduct — Court of Session may take direct cognizance (no committal needed) on the Public Prosecutor's written complaint
Sub-section (3): the Public Prosecutor's complaint must set out the facts, offence, and particulars sufficient to give the accused notice
Sub-section (4): the Public Prosecutor needs prior government sanction — State Government for Governors/State Ministers/State public servants, Central Government otherwise
Sub-section (5): six-month limitation period for the special-track complaint
Sub-section (6): the aggrieved office-holder retains the independent right to complain to an ordinary Magistrate instead
exceptions_and_qualifications: The special track under sub-section (2) is an alternative, not exclusive, remedy — sub-section (6) expressly preserves the ordinary Magistrate-complaint route for the same person.
The Court of Session's direct cognizance power here is a notable departure from section 213's general committal requirement, justified by the public-office context.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read sub-section (1) as the default rule (consistent with the rest of this Chapter), and sub-sections (2)-(5) as a self-contained special procedure for high-office defamation, with sub-section (6) confirming the special procedure supplements rather than displaces the ordinary one. This section completes Chapter XV; Chapter XVI (Complaints to Magistrates) follows.

sections.title: Examination of complainant
sections.raw_text:
223. Examination of complainant.—(1) A Magistrate having jurisdiction while taking cognizance of
    an offence on complaint shall examine upon oath the complainant and the witnesses present, if any, and the
    substance of such examination shall be reduced to writing and shall be signed by the complainant and the
    witnesses, and also by the Magistrate:
    Provided that no cognizance of an offence shall be taken by the Magistrate without giving the accused
    an opportunity of being heard:
    Provided further that when the complaint is made in writing, the Magistrate need not examine the
    complainant and the witnesses—
        (a) if a public servant acting or purporting to act in the discharge of his official duties or a Court
    has made the complaint; or
        (b) if the Magistrate makes over the case for inquiry or trial to another Magistrate under
    section 212:
    Provided also that if the Magistrate makes over the case to another Magistrate under section 212 after
    examining the complainant and the witnesses, the latter Magistrate need not re-examine them.
    (2) A Magistrate shall not take cognizance on a complaint against a public servant for any offence
    alleged to have been committed in course of the discharge of his official functions or duties unless—
        (a) such public servant is given an opportunity to make assertions as to the situation that led to the
    incident so alleged; and
        (b) a report containing facts and circumstances of the incident from the officer superior to such
    public servant is received.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section opens Chapter XVI and lays down the Magistrate's first procedural act on a complaint case: sworn examination. Ordinarily, the Magistrate must put the complainant and any present witnesses on oath, record the substance of what they say in writing, and have it signed by the complainant, the witnesses, and the Magistrate — creating a formal record before the case proceeds further. A cross-cutting safeguard requires that the accused be given a hearing opportunity before cognizance is taken at all. Three practical exceptions relieve the Magistrate of re-doing this examination: when the complaint is written and comes from a public servant or a Court (institutional complainants are presumed reliable), when the case is simply being transferred to another Magistrate under section 212 (no need to examine twice), and — specifically — when the receiving Magistrate under such a transfer inherits an already-completed examination. Sub-section (2) adds a distinct, important safeguard for complaints against public servants regarding their official conduct: cognizance cannot be taken unless that public servant is first given a chance to explain the circumstances, and a report is obtained from their superior officer — protecting officials from being hauled into court on unverified allegations about their official acts.
essential_elements: Default rule: Magistrate examines complainant and present witnesses on oath, records it in writing, signed by all
Cross-cutting safeguard: no cognizance without giving the accused a hearing opportunity
Exception: no re-examination needed for written complaints from a public servant or a Court
Exception: no examination needed when the case is simply made over to another Magistrate under section 212
Exception: the receiving Magistrate in a section 212 transfer need not repeat an examination already done
Sub-section (2): complaints against a public servant regarding official conduct require the public servant's own input and a superior officer's report before cognizance
exceptions_and_qualifications: The hearing-opportunity safeguard for the accused (first proviso) is a general requirement layered onto the examination process, not merely an exception affecting specific complainant types.
Sub-section (2)'s protection is specific to allegations arising from a public servant's official functions or duties — it does not shield purely private conduct.
breakdown.how_to_read: Separate the section into its examination mechanics (sub-section (1) and its three provisos) and its distinct public-servant safeguard (sub-section (2)) — the latter operates as an additional precondition layered on top of, not a substitute for, the general examination process.

sections.title: Procedure by Magistrate not competent to take cognizance of case
sections.raw_text:
224. Procedure by Magistrate not competent to take cognizance of case.—If the complaint is made
    to a Magistrate who is not competent to take cognizance of the offence, he shall,—
        (a) if the complaint is in writing, return it for presentation to the proper Court with an endorsement
    to that effect;
        (b) if the complaint is not in writing, direct the complainant to the proper Court.

breakdown.plain_summary: A simple traffic-direction rule for complaints filed at the wrong address. If a complainant mistakenly brings their complaint to a Magistrate who lacks competence to take cognizance of that particular offence (whether for territorial, pecuniary, or subject-matter reasons), the Magistrate does not simply reject or sit on the complaint. For a written complaint, the Magistrate returns it with an endorsement noting the lack of competence, so it can be presented to the correct Court without needing to be redrafted. For an oral complaint, the Magistrate simply directs the complainant to the correct Court. Either way, the complainant is pointed toward the right forum rather than being turned away empty-handed.
essential_elements: Written complaint at the wrong Magistrate: returned with an endorsement, for presentation to the proper Court
Oral complaint at the wrong Magistrate: complainant is directed to the proper Court
breakdown.how_to_read: A short administrative-mechanics section — read it as ensuring a complainant's mistake about forum doesn't cost them their complaint, only their time in redirecting it.

sections.title: Postponement of issue of process
sections.raw_text:
225. Postponement of issue of process.—(1) Any Magistrate, on receipt of a complaint of an offence
    of which he is authorised to take cognizance or which has been made over to him under section 212, may,
    if he thinks fit, and shall, in a case where the accused is residing at a place beyond the area in which he
    exercises his jurisdiction, postpone the issue of process against the accused, and either inquire into the case
    himself or direct an investigation to be made by a police officer or by such other person as he thinks fit, for
    the purpose of deciding whether or not there is sufficient ground for proceeding:
    Provided that no such direction for investigation shall be made,—
        (a) where it appears to the Magistrate that the offence complained of is triable exclusively by the
    Court of Session; or
        (b) where the complaint has not been made by a Court, unless the complainant and the witnesses
    present (if any) have been examined on oath under section 223.
    (2) In an inquiry under sub-section (1), the Magistrate may, if he thinks fit, take evidence of witnesses
    on oath:
    Provided that if it appears to the Magistrate that the offence complained of is triable exclusively by the
    Court of Session, he shall call upon the complainant to produce all his witnesses and examine them on oath.
    (3) If an investigation under sub-section (1) is made by a person not being a police officer, he shall
    have for that investigation all the powers conferred by this Sanhita on an officer in charge of a police station
    except the power to arrest without warrant.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section gives the Magistrate a screening tool before formally hauling an accused into court: the power (and, in one specific circumstance, the duty) to postpone issuing process and first inquire into or investigate the complaint to check whether there's actually sufficient ground to proceed. The postponement is discretionary generally, but becomes mandatory whenever the accused resides outside the Magistrate's own jurisdiction — protecting distant accused persons from being summoned to a far-off court on a complaint that hasn't even been screened yet. The Magistrate can either inquire personally or direct a police officer or any other suitable person to investigate. Two provisos restrict when a Magistrate can direct someone else to investigate: not for offences exclusively triable by a Court of Session (these need the Magistrate's own closer scrutiny), and not for non-Court complaints unless the complainant and witnesses have already been examined on oath under section 223 (ensuring some sworn basis exists first). Sub-section (2) lets the Magistrate take witness evidence on oath during this inquiry, and mandates it — requiring the complainant to produce and have examined all witnesses — specifically for Sessions-triable offences. Sub-section (3) equips a non-police investigator with an officer-in-charge's investigative powers, but withholds the power to arrest without warrant — a deliberate limit on delegating coercive power to non-police investigators.
essential_elements: Postponement of process is discretionary generally, but mandatory when the accused resides outside the Magistrate's jurisdiction
The Magistrate may inquire personally or direct investigation by a police officer or other suitable person
No investigation-direction where the offence is exclusively Court of Session-triable, or (for non-Court complaints) before section 223 sworn examination has occurred
Sub-section (2): witness evidence may be taken on oath; mandatory full witness examination for Sessions-triable offences
Sub-section (3): a non-police investigator gets officer-in-charge powers except the power of warrantless arrest
exceptions_and_qualifications: The mandatory-postponement trigger (accused residing outside jurisdiction) is purely about the accused's residence, independent of the offence's seriousness.
The withheld warrantless-arrest power for non-police investigators is a deliberate check on delegating coercive authority outside the police force.
breakdown.how_to_read: Track the two axes of variation: when postponement is discretionary versus mandatory (turns on the accused's residence), and when direction-to-investigate is available versus barred or converted into a mandatory full witness examination (turns on whether the offence is Sessions-exclusive and whether a sworn examination has already occurred).

sections.title: Dismissal of complaint
sections.raw_text:
226. Dismissal of complaint.—If, after considering the statements on oath (if any) of the complainant
    and of the witnesses and the result of the inquiry or investigation (if any) under section 225, the Magistrate
    is of opinion that there is no sufficient ground for proceeding, he shall dismiss the complaint, and in every
    such case he shall briefly record his reasons for so doing.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section closes Chapter XVI by giving the Magistrate an explicit off-ramp: if, after weighing the sworn statements of the complainant and witnesses and the outcome of any section 225 inquiry or investigation, the Magistrate concludes there simply isn't sufficient ground to proceed, the complaint must be dismissed — this isn't optional once that conclusion is reached. Critically, the Magistrate cannot just dismiss silently; reasons, even if brief, must be recorded in every such case. This reasoned-dismissal requirement matters practically because it creates a record that a complainant can point to (and potentially challenge, e.g., through revision) if they believe the dismissal was wrong.
essential_elements: Trigger: Magistrate's opinion, after considering sworn statements and any section 225 inquiry/investigation result, that there is no sufficient ground for proceeding
Consequence: the complaint must be dismissed
Mandatory requirement: reasons for dismissal must be briefly recorded in every case
exceptions_and_qualifications: The reason-recording duty is unconditional ('in every such case') — there's no shortcut allowing a bare, unreasoned dismissal.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat this as the natural end-point of the screening machinery in sections 223-225: if the process, examination, and any inquiry/investigation together fail to establish sufficient ground, dismissal (with recorded reasons) is the mandatory result. This completes Chapter XVI; Chapter XVII (Commencement of Proceedings before Magistrates) follows at Section 227.

sections.title: Issue of process
sections.raw_text:
227. Issue of process.—(1) If in the opinion of a Magistrate taking cognizance of an offence there is
    sufficient ground for proceeding, and the case appears to be—
        (a) a summons-case, he shall issue summons to the accused for his attendance; or
        (b) a warrant-case, he may issue a warrant, or, if he thinks fit, a summons, for causing the accused
    to be brought or to appear at a certain time before such Magistrate or (if he has no jurisdiction himself)
    some other Magistrate having jurisdiction:
    Provided that summons or warrants may also be issued through electronic means.
    (2) No summons or warrant shall be issued against the accused under sub-section (1) until a list of the
    prosecution witnesses has been filed.
    (3) In a proceeding instituted upon a complaint made in writing, every summons or warrant issued
    under sub-section (1) shall be accompanied by a copy of such complaint.
    (4) When by any law for the time being in force any process-fees or other fees are payable, no process
    shall be issued until the fees are paid and, if such fees are not paid within a reasonable time, the Magistrate
    may dismiss the complaint.
    (5) Nothing in this section shall be deemed to affect the provisions of section 90.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section opens Chapter XVII and is the pivot point where a screened complaint or cognizable report actually turns into active court proceedings against the accused. Once the Magistrate finds sufficient ground for proceeding, the type of process issued tracks the offence's seriousness: summons-cases (lighter offences) get a mandatory summons, while warrant-cases (more serious offences) give the Magistrate discretion to issue either a warrant or, if a lighter touch suffices, a summons instead — and either can now be issued electronically, a modernisation running throughout the Sanhita. Several safeguards attach: no summons or warrant can issue until the prosecution's witness list is filed (so the accused knows who will testify), a written complaint must be attached to any process issued on it (so the accused knows what they're accused of from the outset), and any applicable process-fees must be paid first, with non-payment within a reasonable time letting the Magistrate dismiss the complaint outright. Sub-section (5) is a savings clause preserving section 90 (which deals with a related summons mechanism) undisturbed by this section.
essential_elements: Summons-case: Magistrate shall issue summons to secure attendance
Warrant-case: Magistrate may issue a warrant or, at discretion, a summons instead
Summons/warrants may be issued electronically
No process issues before the prosecution witness list is filed
Written complaints must be attached to any process issued on them
Process-fee non-payment (within a reasonable time) permits dismissal of the complaint
Section 90 is expressly unaffected by this section
exceptions_and_qualifications: The witness-list-first requirement in sub-section (2) is an absolute precondition — process cannot issue without it, regardless of case type.
Sub-section (5)'s savings clause avoids any implied conflict with the separate summons mechanism under section 90.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat sub-section (1) as the core issue-of-process rule (summons-case vs. warrant-case, with electronic issuance available for both) and sub-sections (2)-(4) as sequential preconditions that must each be satisfied before process can actually go out.

sections.title: Magistrate may dispense with personal attendance of accused
sections.raw_text:
228. Magistrate may dispense with personal attendance of accused.—(1) Whenever a Magistrate
    issues a summons, he may, if he sees reason so to do, dispense with the personal attendance of the accused
    and permit him to appear by his advocate.
    (2) But the Magistrate inquiring into or trying the case may, in his discretion, at any stage of the
    proceedings, direct the personal attendance of the accused, and, if necessary, enforce such attendance in the
    manner hereinbefore provided.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section gives the Magistrate flexibility to spare an accused person the burden of personally attending every hearing in a summons case — they may instead appear through their advocate if the Magistrate sees good reason to allow it. This is purely discretionary and revocable: sub-section (2) makes clear the Magistrate retains full power, at any later stage of the same proceeding, to require the accused's personal attendance after all, and to enforce that attendance using the ordinary compulsion mechanisms (summons, warrant, etc.) available under the Sanhita. So dispensation is a convenience, not an entitlement locked in for the whole case.
essential_elements: Magistrate may, at his discretion, dispense with personal attendance and allow appearance by advocate
This dispensation may be reversed at any stage; personal attendance can be directed and, if necessary, enforced
exceptions_and_qualifications: The power to reverse dispensation exists 'at any stage of the proceedings' — there's no point after which the accused's exemption becomes irrevocable.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read the two sub-sections as a grant-and-reserve pair: sub-section (1) grants the convenience, sub-section (2) reserves the Magistrate's ongoing control to withdraw it whenever circumstances warrant.

sections.title: Special summons in cases of petty offence
sections.raw_text:
229. Special summons in cases of petty offence.—(1) If, in the opinion of a Magistrate taking
    cognizance of a petty offence, the case may be summarily disposed of under section 283 or section 284, the
    Magistrate shall, except where he is, for reasons to be recorded in writing of a contrary opinion, issue
    summons to the accused requiring him either to appear in person or by an advocate before the Magistrate
    on a specified date, or if he desires to plead guilty to the charge without appearing before the Magistrate,
    to transmit before the specified date, by post or by messenger to the Magistrate, the said plea in writing and
    the amount of fine specified in the summons or if he desires to appear by an advocate and to plead guilty
    to the charge through such advocate, to authorise, in writing, the advocate to plead guilty to the charge on
    his behalf and to pay the fine through such advocate:
    Provided that the amount of the fine specified in such summons shall not exceed five thousand rupees.
    (2) For the purposes of this section, "petty offence" means any offence punishable only with fine not
    exceeding five thousand rupees, but does not include any offence so punishable under the Motor Vehicles
    Act, 1988 (59 of 1988), or under any other law which provides for convicting the accused person in his
    absence on a plea of guilty.
    (3) The State Government may, by notification, specially empower any Magistrate to exercise the
    powers conferred by sub-section (1) in relation to any offence which is compoundable under section 359
    or any offence punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding three months, or with fine, or with
    both where the Magistrate is of opinion that, having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case, the
    imposition of fine only would meet the ends of justice.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section creates a streamlined, low-friction procedure for truly minor offences, sparing both the accused and the court system the full weight of a normal appearance-based process. For petty offences eligible for summary disposal, the default (unless the Magistrate records reasons otherwise) is a special summons offering the accused three options: appear in person or by advocate on a fixed date; skip appearing altogether and simply post or courier in a written guilty plea plus the fine (capped at five thousand rupees); or authorise an advocate in writing to plead guilty and pay the fine on their behalf without the accused personally showing up at all. Sub-section (2) precisely defines 'petty offence' as fine-only offences up to five thousand rupees, but carves out Motor Vehicles Act offences and any other law that already has its own in-absentia guilty-plea conviction mechanism — avoiding overlap with existing specialised schemes. Sub-section (3) lets the State Government extend this convenience procedure, via specially empowering a Magistrate, to compoundable offences or offences punishable with up to three months' imprisonment (or fine, or both), where the Magistrate believes a fine-only outcome would serve justice — broadening the reach of this efficient disposal route beyond the strict 'petty offence' definition when appropriate.
essential_elements: Default rule for petty offences eligible for summary disposal: special summons offering personal/advocate appearance, postal guilty plea with fine, or advocate-conducted guilty plea
Fine specified in the summons capped at five thousand rupees
'Petty offence' = fine-only offence up to five thousand rupees, excluding Motor Vehicles Act offences and offences under laws with their own in-absentia guilty-plea schemes
State Government may, by notification, extend this procedure to compoundable offences or offences punishable with up to three months' imprisonment/fine/both, at the Magistrate's discretion
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Magistrate can depart from issuing the special summons, but only for recorded reasons — this isn't an unfettered discretion to skip the streamlined route.
The Motor Vehicles Act carve-out in sub-section (2) avoids duplicating that Act's own dedicated guilty-plea conviction mechanism.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read sub-section (1) as the procedural menu offered to the accused, sub-section (2) as the eligibility gate (what counts as 'petty'), and sub-section (3) as a State-driven expansion mechanism letting the same convenience apply to a wider band of minor, compoundable, or short-imprisonment offences.

sections.title: Supply to accused of copy of police report and other documents
sections.raw_text:
230. Supply to accused of copy of police report and other documents.—In any case where the
    proceeding has been instituted on a police report, the Magistrate shall without delay, and in no case beyond
    fourteen days from the date of production or appearance of the accused, furnish to the accused and the
    victim (if represented by an advocate) free of cost, a copy of each of the following:—
        (i) the police report;
        (ii) the first information report recorded under section 173;
        (iii) the statements recorded under sub-section (3) of section 180 of all persons whom the
    prosecution proposes to examine as its witnesses, excluding therefrom any part in regard to which a
    request for such exclusion has been made by the police officer under sub-section (7) of section 193;
        (iv) the confessions and statements, if any, recorded under section 183;
        (v) any other document or relevant extract thereof forwarded to the Magistrate with the police report
    under sub-section (6) of section 193:
    Provided that the Magistrate may, after perusing any such part of a statement as is referred to in
    clause (iii) and considering the reasons given by the police officer for the request, direct that a copy of that
    part of the statement or of such portion thereof as the Magistrate thinks proper, shall be furnished to the
    accused:
    Provided further that if the Magistrate is satisfied that any such document is voluminous, he shall,
    instead of furnishing the accused and the victim (if represented by an advocate) with a copy thereof, may
    furnish the copies through electronic means or direct that he will only be allowed to inspect it either
    personally or through an advocate in Court:
    Provided also that supply of documents in electronic form shall be considered as duly furnished.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section closes out the initial appearance stage for police-report cases with a core fair-trial guarantee: the accused must be given free copies of the entire evidentiary package underlying the prosecution — the police report (chargesheet) itself, the original FIR, all prosecution witness statements recorded during investigation, any recorded confessions, and any other documents forwarded to the Magistrate with the police report — and this must happen without delay, with a firm outer limit of fourteen days from when the accused is produced or appears. Notably, the victim (if legally represented) is entitled to the same copies, extending the disclosure obligation beyond just the defence. Built-in flexibility handles two practical wrinkles: where police have specifically requested that part of a witness statement be withheld (typically for witness-protection reasons under section 193(7)), the Magistrate reviews that request and decides how much, if any, of that excluded portion should still be given to the accused; and where documents are voluminous, the Magistrate can furnish them electronically or simply allow inspection in Court rather than physical copying — with electronic supply explicitly treated as fully compliant with the furnishing requirement, another modernisation thread running through the Sanhita.
essential_elements: Applies only where proceedings are instituted on a police report
Free copies of: police report, FIR, prosecution witness statements, confessions/statements, and other forwarded documents
Firm fourteen-day outer limit from the accused's production or appearance
Victim (if represented by an advocate) is also entitled to the same copies
Witness-protection exclusions under section 193(7) are handled by Magistrate review, not automatic full disclosure
Voluminous documents may be furnished electronically or made available for inspection instead of physical copies
Electronic supply is deemed to satisfy the furnishing requirement
exceptions_and_qualifications: The witness-statement exclusion mechanism (first proviso) is a deliberate, court-supervised balance between full disclosure to the accused and protecting sensitive witness information.
The victim's entitlement to copies is conditional on being represented by an advocate — an unrepresented victim does not automatically receive this same disclosure under this section.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat this as the disclosure backbone of a police-report case: the fourteen-day deadline and the list of five document categories form the baseline obligation, with the two provisos supplying controlled exceptions (partial withholding for witness protection, electronic/inspection-only for bulk documents) rather than open-ended discretion to withhold.
